about: Every decision and why (ADRs) and the plans, of every project

rows.title: ADR-0001: A device is the app as Flutter web in Chromium, driven over CDP; one backend, a panel, a window and a terminal as fronts —…
rows.summary: editor, in a window or in a terminal, several at once, with hot reload and the editor's debugger.
body: - Positive: a device starts with what a Flutter developer already has (Flutter and a Chromium browser), in the
editor, in a window or in a terminal, several at once, with hot reload and the editor's debugger.
- Negative: it is Flutter web: no native plugins and no `dart:io`; a real phone is still needed for those. A device
costs a `flutter run` and a browser in memory.

rows.title: ADR-0001: A device is the app as Flutter web in Chromium, driven over CDP; one backend, a panel, a window and a terminal as fronts —…
rows.summary: Android Studio shows a running device inside the IDE (*Running Devices*).
body: Android Studio shows a running device inside the IDE (*Running Devices*). A Synapsis app in VS Code, or built from
a terminal, had no device of its own to run on: it needed an emulator, a phone or a plain browser tab beside the
tool. The question was what a device is, so that the editor and the command line show the same one.

rows.title: ADR-0001: A device is the app as Flutter web in Chromium, driven over CDP; one backend, a panel, a window and a terminal as fronts —…
rows.summary: `nuclear terminal-device` shows it inside the terminal.
body: **From the command line** `nuclear device [<device>]` runs the app in its own window, like an emulator, and
`nuclear terminal-device` shows it inside the terminal. Both share one backend (Flutter web in Chromium, the
emulation over CDP, input, hot reload); only the front changes. Several at once are numbered. The window takes the
device's ratio and at most 85 % of the screen's height; on a tiling window manager (Hyprland, Sway, i3) it floats.
The terminal draws with the best it supports: images (kitty, sixel), or colored blocks with the app's texts
written as letters in their exact place (given by the `synapsis` package in debug).

rows.title: ADR-0001: A device is the app as Flutter web in Chromium, driven over CDP; one backend, a panel, a window and a terminal as fronts —…
rows.summary: the Chrome DevTools Protocol: the screen's size and density, touch, orientation and the identity (user agent) of a phone or a tablet; the frames come back as a screencast and input goes in as CDP events.
body: **A device is the app running as Flutter web in a Chromium browser, with the device emulated and driven through
the Chrome DevTools Protocol**: the screen's size and density, touch, orientation and the identity (user agent) of
a phone or a tablet; the frames come back as a screencast and input goes in as CDP events. The same list of devices
everywhere, the one of the browsers' device toolbar (iPhone, Pixel, iPad, Galaxy, laptop, responsive).
**In the editor** the app runs inside VS Code, like Android Studio's *Running Devices*: a Flutter *custom device*
(`synapsis`, "Synapsis device") shipped with the extension appears in the device picker; launching on it runs
the app on Flutter's `chrome` device with a headless Chromium, and the panel shows its screen and sends input over
CDP, with breakpoints, hot reload and hot restart. A device bar like the browsers' (the devices, zoom, rotation)
sits over Chrome's device mode.

rows.title: ADR-0001: A device is the app as Flutter web in Chromium, driven over CDP; one backend, a panel, a window and a terminal as fronts —…
rows.summary: 1. Flutter's `web-server` device for the editor's panel: no breakpoints.
body: 1. Flutter's `web-server` device for the editor's panel: no breakpoints.
2. An engine of our own, without a browser (flutter-pi as a guide): postponed.
3. Flutter's `chrome` device with a Chromium we drive over CDP. Chosen.

rows.title: ADR-0001: Everything is written in English — Consequences
rows.summary: Consequences
body: - Positive: one language for every reader; an agent reads the same words in the code and in the documents.
- Negative: the user writes in Spanish and reads the documents in a second language.

rows.title: ADR-0001: Everything is written in English — Context and problem
rows.summary: The platform is open source and is read by agents and by people of any country.
body: The platform is open source and is read by agents and by people of any country. Documentation was first written
in Spanish while the code was in English, so two languages lived in one tree.

rows.title: ADR-0001: Everything is written in English — Decision
rows.summary: Everything is in English: code, comments, test names, diagnostics, the output of the command line tools, dialects (comments, notes, templates), examples, references, guides, context documents, ADRs and the website.
body: Everything is in English: code, comments, test names, diagnostics, the output of the command line tools, dialects
(comments, notes, templates), examples, references, guides, context documents, ADRs and the website. Spanish is a
later translation of the website. The chat with the user is in Spanish.
Exceptions: localization data (the `es` translations, the CLI motto with an `es` locale) and the tests of unicode.

rows.title: ADR-0001: Everything is written in English — Options considered
rows.summary: 1. Documentation in Spanish, code in English: two languages to keep in step, and half the readers lost.
body: 1. Documentation in Spanish, code in English: two languages to keep in step, and half the readers lost.
2. Everything in English.

rows.title: ADR-0002: One repository; each project in its folder, with its own documents — Consequences
rows.summary: builds from one tree.
body: - Positive: a task needs the root map and one project's documents; a change and its documents are in one commit.
- Negative: the nine public repositories that are now folders are archived, and their links change; a release
builds from one tree.

rows.title: ADR-0002: One repository; each project in its folder, with its own documents — Context and problem
rows.summary: The platform was split into eleven repositories checked out inside one another, while the context of all of them was written in one tree at the root: a map in layers (`docs/context/`), one numbering for every decision (108 ADRs), a single state file loaded whole in every session, a folder `spec/`…
body: The platform was split into eleven repositories checked out inside one another, while the context of all of them
was written in one tree at the root: a map in layers (`docs/context/`), one numbering for every decision (108
ADRs), a single state file loaded whole in every session, a folder `spec/` beside a folder `specs/`. Code crossed
the repositories' borders (a framework dialect depends on the compiler, the CLI on both), and an agent that touched
one project read the documents of all. Features came out wrong.

rows.title: ADR-0002: One repository; each project in its folder, with its own documents — Decision
rows.summary: 1. One git repository holds the whole tree.
body: 1. **One git repository** holds the whole tree. A project is a folder: `nuclearlang/` (the language, with each
dialect under `dialects/<language>/`), `nuclear-synapsis-framework/` (with `platforms/<platform>/`), `tools/`
(`cli/`, `code_generator/`, `mcp/`), `extensions/`, `device-emulators/`, `nuclear-agents/`,
`nuclear-graph-storage/`, `installer/`. One Cargo workspace builds every Rust crate.
2. **Each project documents itself**: an `AGENTS.md` and a `docs/` laid out the same way in every project
(`docs/README.md` is the standard). A project's documents, decisions and pending work describe that project only.
3. **The root holds only what is about the whole platform** and the map that routes to each project.
4. **Decisions are numbered per project** and cited with the project's key (`ADR-lang-0007`).
5. **No file lists the state of the whole platform.** A project's pending work is its `docs/01-product/roadmap.md`.
6. **Documents are short**: one is read in one go, or it is split.

rows.title: ADR-0002: One repository; each project in its folder, with its own documents — Options considered
rows.summary: 1. A repository per project, checked out inside one another: the borders did not match what depends on what, and every check needed the whole tree anyway.
body: 1. A repository per project, checked out inside one another: the borders did not match what depends on what, and
every check needed the whole tree anyway.
2. One repository with one documentation tree in layers: every agent loaded the context of every project.
3. One repository, a project per folder, documents inside each project.

rows.title: ADR-0003: The AI loop: a private knowledge base, local agents, one MCP server and a pipeline tool — Consequences
rows.summary: measured and corrected.
body: - Positive: most of the work runs on the developer's machine; what the agents know is data that can be read,
measured and corrected.
- Negative: every change to an agent, a prompt or the knowledge base is a new round of the evaluation; the
knowledge base must follow the tree.

rows.title: ADR-0003: The AI loop: a private knowledge base, local agents, one MCP server and a pipeline tool — Context and problem
rows.summary: The user wants spec-driven work inside the editor: a spec goes through plan, tests, code, verification, security, artifacts and deploy on the developer's machine, and the same pipeline runs on a server.
body: The user wants spec-driven work inside the editor: a spec goes through plan, tests, code, verification, security,
artifacts and deploy on the developer's machine, and the same pipeline runs on a server. A frontier model must not
do all the work: it leads, and hands each piece to a local model of at most 3B parameters, as a lead hands work to
a junior. A model that small cannot hold much context, and the machine has no GPU to train one.

rows.title: ADR-0003: The AI loop: a private knowledge base, local agents, one MCP server and a pipeline tool — Decision
rows.summary: a frontier model answers a task bank once, its answers that pass the compiler become examples of the graph, and the local agents are measured against it.
body: - **Local models have at most 3B parameters.** They learn by retrieval and distillation, not by training weights:
a frontier model answers a task bank once, its answers that pass the compiler become examples of the graph, and
the local agents are measured against it. A failure is fixed with a general rule or knowledge in the graph, never
with the answer.
- **The local agents write only Nuclear.** They name a platform (`backend`, `mobile`, `web`), never a dialect or a
target language, and read only what is written for them.
- **The tools write; the agents think the business logic.** The compiler writes the project's map, the platform
says where each kind goes and its smallest file, the generators write what is standard.
- **Over MCP the local developer works first**: a frontier model gives every task that writes `.nuc` to the local
developer, then validates, corrects and records its review.
- **The agents' prompts are files** of the graph, never text inside the agents' code.
- **A failure is diagnosed before it is retried**: what may pass on a second try is retried with backoff; a
compiler error or a failing test goes to the repair rounds.

rows.title: ADR-0003: The AI loop: a private knowledge base, local agents, one MCP server and a pipeline tool — Decision
rows.summary: Four projects, each with its own documents: 1. The Smart Graph (`nuclear-graph-storage/`): the knowledge base of the whole platform, on the developer's machine.
body: Four projects, each with its own documents:
1. **The Smart Graph** (`nuclear-graph-storage/`): the knowledge base of the whole platform, on the developer's
machine. It is private: only its server opens the store, it listens on the loopback address, each program asks
for access and the user allows it, and what it stores is encrypted.
2. **The MCP server** (`tools/mcp/`): one server gives any agent the graph, the compiler, a project's commands and
the local developer.
3. **The Nuclear Developer** (`nuclear-agents/nuclear_developer/`): the local agents, written in Nuclear. Each runs
fixed steps (recall from the graph, write, check with the compiler, repair), because a small model follows steps
better than it chooses tools.
4. **The pipeline tool** (`extensions/tools/nuclear-builder/`): the spec form, the runs and the pipeline in the
editor, and the same engine as a command.
Rules that hold across the four:

rows.title: ADR-0003: The AI loop: a private knowledge base, local agents, one MCP server and a pipeline tool — Options considered
rows.summary: 1. A frontier model does everything: every token is paid and the code leaves the machine.
body: 1. A frontier model does everything: every token is paid and the code leaves the machine.
2. Training the local model's weights: days per round without a GPU.
3. Retrieval and distillation over a local knowledge base, with a frontier model as lead.

rows.title: ADR-platform-0004: A product is made with the platform's tools, never by porting code by hand — Consequences
rows.summary: code; the generated code stays as fast and as uniform as the generators make it.
body: - Positive: every product is a test of the tools; a gap shows up as a roadmap item instead of hidden hand-written
code; the generated code stays as fast and as uniform as the generators make it.
- Negative: a feature a tool cannot make yet waits for the tool, or is written by hand with the gap recorded.

rows.title: ADR-platform-0004: A product is made with the platform's tools, never by porting code by hand — Context and problem
rows.summary: NuclearLang exists to prove that a language, its framework and its tools let people and agents build software.
body: NuclearLang exists to prove that a language, its framework and its tools let people and agents build software.
An agent that writes a feature by hand in the target's language (React, Node.js, Python/FastAPI, Dart), or that
translates such code into Nuclear by itself, proves nothing: the product works, but nobody learns whether the
transpiler, the generators, the MCP server or the type definitions would have made it. It also hides every gap of
the tools behind work no one sees.
A **product** is any software made from Nuclear: an app, a backend, the website of the tree, an example, a tool of
the tree written in Nuclear.

rows.title: ADR-platform-0004: A product is made with the platform's tools, never by porting code by hand — Decision
rows.summary: A product is made with the tools of the platform, and every agent (Claude Code, the local Nuclear Developer, any agent reading the MCP server) follows it: 1. The code is Nuclear and the target code comes from the transpiler.
body: A product is made with the tools of the platform, and every agent (Claude Code, the local Nuclear Developer, any
agent reading the MCP server) follows it:
1. **The code is Nuclear and the target code comes from the transpiler.** No agent writes, edits or patches target
code (`.ts`, `.dart`, `.py` of `build/`, or any native file of a product) to make a feature.
2. **No agent migrates code by hand.** Code of a native dialect (React, Node.js, Python/FastAPI, Dart) is never
translated into Nuclear by the agent itself. What exists as a library is added with `nuclear add <package>` and
used through its generated type definitions; what is standard is written by the generators.
3. **The tools come first, in this order:** `nuclear new`, `nuclear gen` and `nuclear make` (the code generator),
the MCP server's tools, `nuclear add` (a library and its definitions), `nuclear fix` (the compiler's exact fixes);
only what they leave is written by hand, in Nuclear.
4. **By hand, outside Nuclear, only when strictly necessary**: when a product cannot work otherwise, or when the
work is on Nuclear itself (the compiler, a dialect, a runtime package, a tool that cannot yet be written in
Nuclear: the root `AGENTS.md`, rule 9). The agent says so, and the missing capability becomes an item of the roadmap
of the tool that should have done it, in the same change.

rows.title: ADR-platform-0004: A product is made with the platform's tools, never by porting code by hand — Options considered
rows.summary: 1. The tools first, by hand only when strictly necessary, every gap recorded (chosen).
body: 1. The tools first, by hand only when strictly necessary, every gap recorded (chosen).
2. Let agents write whatever is fastest: products ship sooner, and the platform is never tested.

rows.title: ADR-platform-0004: A product is made with the platform's tools, never by porting code by hand — References
rows.summary: the skill), `tools/mcp/server.nuc`, `nuclear-agents/nuclear_developer/AGENTS.md`.
body: - The root `AGENTS.md`, hard rule 13; the agents' instructions: `tools/cli/agent-files/` (the project section and
the skill), `tools/mcp/server.nuc`, `nuclear-agents/nuclear_developer/AGENTS.md`.

rows.summary: every other repository is a folder inside it (`synapsis-web/`, `synapsis-backend/`, `editors/`…), ignored by the root's git, as `editors/` and `cli/` are today.
body: **Layout of the working tree (decided 2026-11-10 with the pilot):** the root folder is the `nuclear` repository and
every other repository is a folder inside it (`synapsis-web/`, `synapsis-backend/`, `editors/`…), ignored by the
root's git, as `editors/` and `cli/` are today. `nuclear_dialect::source_roots(root)` lists the root and each
`synapsis-*` folder with `dialects/`; the CLI, the LSP, the tests, `install.sh`, the editors' bundles and the website
merge the `dialects/`, `defs/`, `spec/`, `docs/` and `examples/` of every source root. A CI of a platform repository
checks out `nuclear` and places itself inside it.
Commits and pushes are made with the user's own GitHub user (decided 2026-11-10).

rows.title: 006 — Public repositories: the organization `nuclearlang` — 2. Stages
rows.summary: 1. Local reorganization (no network): one future repository at a time, moved under a working folder `nuclearlang/<repo>/`; after each move `cargo test`, clippy, the check scripts and `./install.sh` green; every path in the tests, scripts, `install.sh` and `docs/context/` updated.
body: 1. **Local reorganization** (no network): one future repository at a time, moved under a working folder
`nuclearlang/<repo>/`; after each move `cargo test`, clippy, the check scripts and `./install.sh` green; every path
in the tests, scripts, `install.sh` and `docs/context/` updated. The compiler's tests that build the platforms'
examples (`crates/nuclear-transpile/tests/projects.rs`) move to the platform repositories or read them from the
sibling folder; the `nuclear` repository keeps language-only tests. `editors/` and `cli/` keep their history
(`git` of their own today): their sessions are told before each move (rule 7).
2. **Publishing files** in every repository: `LICENSE` (Apache-2.0), `README.md`, `CONTRIBUTING.md`, `CHANGELOG.md`,
`.gitignore` (build/, target/, node_modules/, .dart_tool/, .venv/, dist/), CI (GitHub Actions: the checks run by
hand today), the Zed manifest's `repository` pointing to GitHub.
3. **Create and push** with the user's GitHub session (`gh auth login`): the repositories in `nuclearlang`, the first
commit of each, CI green.
4. Then (still step 1 of "Next"): packages on pub.dev / PyPI / npm, extensions in the marketplaces, binaries for
macOS and Windows, a one-command installer, the 1.0 spec.

(`00-context` … `06-runbooks`) plus `07-reference` (the normative text: a language's rules, a dialect's

rows.title: Spec 008: restructure the tree — Design — How the loader finds things
rows.summary: `platforms/<platform>/platform.toml`, found in the loader's platform folders.
body: - A dialect is `dialects/<language>/` or `dialects/<language>/frameworks/<name>/`; its name is the folder's.
- A framework dialect names its platform (`platform = "backend"` in `dialect.toml`); the contract is
`platforms/<platform>/platform.toml`, found in the loader's platform folders.
- Type definitions are `dialects/<language>/defs/<package>/<version>/`. A project's own `defs/` and the cache keep
`<language>/<package>/<version>/`.
- An install has the same two folders: `$NUCLEAR_HOME/dialects` and `$NUCLEAR_HOME/platforms`.

rows.title: Spec 008: restructure the tree — Design — Risks
rows.summary: Risks
body: | Risk | Mitigation |
| A move loses uncommitted work of the 11 repositories | A copy of the whole tree before the first move: `~/Documents/projects/nuclearlang-backup-2026-11-16-pre-restructure.tar.gz` |
| A path in code, a script or CI still names an old folder | After each phase: `cargo test`, clippy, and a search of the tree for the old names |
| The installed commands and services stop | They run from `~/.local/share/nuclearlang`, not from the tree; reinstalled once at the end |
| The knowledge base describes the old tree | Rebuilt and ingested once, when the docs are in place (phase 3) |

rows.summary: `agent-context-docs-implementation.md`, describing that project only.
body: - [ ] THE SYSTEM SHALL keep each project in the folder of the target tree (`design.md`) and nowhere else.
- [ ] THE SYSTEM SHALL give each project an `AGENTS.md` and a `docs/` in the layout of
`agent-context-docs-implementation.md`, describing that project only.
- [ ] THE SYSTEM SHALL keep at the root only what is about the whole platform, and a map to each project.
- [ ] THE SYSTEM SHALL number each project's ADRs from 0001 and consolidate them by theme.
- [ ] THE SYSTEM SHALL keep no state file that every session loads whole; a project's pending work is in its docs.
- [ ] WHEN a file of context is written THE SYSTEM SHALL keep it short enough to read at once.
- [ ] THE SYSTEM SHALL name the framework Synapsis (`nuclear-synapsis-framework`), the pipeline tool
`nuclear-builder` and the protocol client `nuclear-http-connections`, everywhere.
- [ ] THE SYSTEM SHALL have one command line tool, `nuclear`; the `dragonfly` command does not exist.
- [ ] WHEN a phase of `tasks.md` ends THE SYSTEM SHALL pass `cargo test` and `cargo clippy --all-targets`.

rows.title: ADR-0001: One language server and one base extension per editor; a framework's tools go in an extension of that framework — Consequences
rows.summary: device and hot reload parts of Synapsis projects (`../01-product/roadmap.md`).
body: - Positive: the base extension serves any dialect, because what it needs from one is data of the dialect.
- Negative: until the framework extensions exist, the base extensions of VS Code and JetBrains carry the run, debug,
device and hot reload parts of Synapsis projects (`../01-product/roadmap.md`).

rows.title: ADR-0001: One language server and one base extension per editor; a framework's tools go in an extension of that framework — Context and…
rows.summary: The same `.nuc` language is turned into several targets, and each framework brings tools of its own: how an app is run and debugged, its devices, its hot reload.
body: The same `.nuc` language is turned into several targets, and each framework brings tools of its own: how an app is
run and debugged, its devices, its hot reload. An editor needs the language for every dialect, and those tools only
for the projects of one framework.

rows.title: ADR-0001: One language server and one base extension per editor; a framework's tools go in an extension of that framework — Decision
rows.summary: One language server (`nuclearlang/crates/nuclear-lsp`) and one base extension, "NuclearLang", per editor.
body: One language server (`nuclearlang/crates/nuclear-lsp`) and one base extension, "NuclearLang", per editor. The base
extension gives, for any dialect: syntax, highlighting, the theme, the code metrics, diagnostics, completion and the
line map between a `.nuc` and its generated file.
Each file's dialect comes from its project: `nuclear.toml`, `config.nuc`, or the dialect's `[project] marker`.
What depends on a framework's tools (run, debug, devices, hot reload) goes in one extension per framework, which
depends on the base. Only the base registers the language, the grammar and the language server. A framework
extension activates on its dialect's `[project] marker` and prefixes everything it contributes with its dialect, so
two framework extensions never collide (ADR-platform-0002).
What an editor needs from a language is declared by the dialect: `[docs]` and `[project] marker` / `output`.

rows.title: ADR-0002: The Nuclear workspace in the editor: projects and tools as tabs, one thing on screen, keyboard first — Consequences
rows.summary: time; every action has a key.
body: - Positive: one place for every Nuclear feature; projects side by side without windows; the screen for one thing at a
time; every action has a key.
- Negative:
- The HTTP tree and the file tree are drawn by the webview, not native trees: the file tree has no git decorations
and no drag and drop (the user adds the folder to the VS Code workspace for those).
- A component panel's memory lives in the window, not on disk.
- The editors remembered per workspace are text editors; an unsaved editor is not closed by a switch (no save
prompt: it stays open until saved).
- The Dart extension launches Flutter only for a project inside the workspace folders, so Run, Debug and Device of
a mobile project opened as a tab first add its folder to them: the window reloads once and the user state
`nuclear.workspace.pendingAction` continues the action.
- The editor title bar is the only toolbar an extension can fill, so the actions show only while an editor is open
(not on the welcome page).
- The terminals the actions open are named per project and action, but not swapped with the workspace.
- `Ctrl+1` … `Ctrl+9` replace VS Code's "focus editor group N"; a desktop environment may take a
`Ctrl+Alt+<letter>` (the user rebinds).

rows.title: ADR-0002: The Nuclear workspace in the editor: projects and tools as tabs, one thing on screen, keyboard first — Context and problem
rows.summary: Every Nuclear feature in the editor was a view of its own: the HTTP client in one activity bar container, the device in a panel, the projects as VS Code windows.
body: Every Nuclear feature in the editor was a view of its own: the HTTP client in one activity bar container, the device
in a panel, the projects as VS Code windows. Working on a backend and its apps meant several windows, or a sidebar
cut into small sections that take space from the code. The user wants one place where everything of Nuclear meets,
like a tiling window manager: each project and each tool is a tab, the whole screen goes to one thing at a time and
the keyboard moves between them. VS Code's own explorer, search and git stay as they are unless the user wants them.

rows.title: ADR-0002: The Nuclear workspace in the editor: projects and tools as tabs, one thing on screen, keyboard first — Decision
rows.summary: its own locked editor group to the right of the code (like Android Studio) and is never merged into the code's tab group.
body: its own locked editor group to the right of the code (like Android Studio) and is never merged into the code's tab
group. A device streams at the physical pixels the panel shows, so a 3x phone stays sharp on a HiDPI screen.
5. **A project is a tab, not a window, and shares nothing with the others.** *Open a project as a tab* remembers the
folder (user state) and shows its files in the workspace view; it does not touch the VS Code workspace folders.
One command adds the active project's folder to them when the user wants the explorer, search and git on it.
6. **The actions of a project's platform sit in the editor title bar**, as a toolbar, never inside the file tree
(asked by the user), each with a shortcut VS Code shows in its tooltip. Each platform has its own set and nothing
of one platform is offered to another (context key `nuclear.platform`; no buttons while a tool is the active tab):
- mobile: ▷ Run, ◉ Debug, ↻ Reload, ▭ Device, Build, Test, Check;
- backend: ▷ Serve (`nuclear run`; the server restarts on each build), ◉ Debug (debugpy for fastapi, node with
source maps for nestjs), Test, Build, Check, ⇄ API (its routes in the HTTP Connections tool);
- web: ▷ Serve (`nuclear run`, Vite), ▭ Device, ◉ Debug, ↻ Reload, Build, Test, Check.

rows.title: ADR-0002: The Nuclear workspace in the editor: projects and tools as tabs, one thing on screen, keyboard first — Decision
rows.summary: 7. Every platform runs, debugs and reloads pre-configured, as Flutter does.
body: 7. **Every platform runs, debugs and reloads pre-configured, as Flutter does.** Saving a `.nuc` of a backend or web
project builds it, so the running server or page reloads (`nuclear.buildOnSave`); `install` runs first when the app
has no packages. `nuclear build` writes `build/<name>.code-workspace` for every platform (the tasks build,
install, run, test, check and the dialect's debug launch), and every `nuclear build` writes `.nuclear/lines.json`,
so a breakpoint in a `.nuc` stops in every debugger and the paused line shows in the `.nuc`.
8. **The tools are workspaces too, independent of the projects.**
- The HTTP Connections tool works like Bruno: its pane is the endpoints tree of every project (platform → project → contracts
/ components → endpoints, OpenAPI documents, the environment); a component is an editor tab and each endpoint a
tab inside it, so the tab bar never fills with requests. A component panel keeps its tabs, forms and responses
while its workspace is left. Environments belong to the window (`<first folder>/.nuclear/http.json`, else the
extension's storage).
- The Devices tool lists the open Synapsis devices with their state and opens as many as wanted (a preset each),
each in its own locked editor group tiled horizontally with its own app, so several users can be signed in at

rows.title: ADR-0002: The Nuclear workspace in the editor: projects and tools as tabs, one thing on screen, keyboard first — Decision
rows.summary: throttling (fast 4G, slow 3G, offline), no cache; a dock with the page's Console (errors counted, a line's source opens the generated file) and Network (method, status, address, type, size, time), filtered; a screenshot into `build/screenshots/`; ◉ Debug attaches VS Code's JavaScript debugger to…
body: throttling (fast 4G, slow 3G, offline), no cache; a dock with the page's Console (errors counted, a line's source
opens the generated file) and Network (method, status, address, type, size, time), filtered; a screenshot into
`build/screenshots/`; ◉ Debug attaches VS Code's JavaScript debugger to that page.
10. **The file tree is the explorer's equal.** It wears the Chernobyl icon theme with VS Code's own lookup (file
name, longest extension, folder name, open or closed) and hides what `files.exclude` hides.
11. **Keyboard first.** Fixed bindings: `Ctrl+1` … `Ctrl+9` the project tabs, `Ctrl+Alt+N` the container,
`Ctrl+Alt+O` open a project, `Ctrl+Alt+W` the welcome page, one `Ctrl+Alt+<letter>` per tool (`H`, `V`, `P`, `D`,
`M`, `A`, `S`) and per action (`R`, `G`, `L`, `B`, `T`, `C`). Clicking a tab or an action does the same and shows
a short toast with its shortcut, so the mouse teaches the keys. The user may rebind any of them.
12. **A welcome page at startup** (`nuclear.workspace.welcome`, on by default, only when the window restored no
editor) explains the workspace, lists the projects with their shortcut and the tools, and can turn itself off.
13. **The other editors.** Android Studio gets tool windows and actions with shortcuts (the HTTP Connections tool window,
`Alt+Shift+H`). Zed cannot contribute keybindings or views.

rows.title: ADR-0002: The Nuclear workspace in the editor: projects and tools as tabs, one thing on screen, keyboard first — Decision
rows.summary: The VS Code extension first; Android Studio and Zed follow as far as their platform allows.
rows.body: The VS Code extension first; Android Studio and Zed follow as far as their platform allows.

rows.title: ADR-0002: The Nuclear workspace in the editor: projects and tools as tabs, one thing on screen, keyboard first — Decision
rows.summary: 1. One container.
body: 1. **One container.** A single activity bar container, `Nuclear`, with one *Workspace* webview view. No other
Nuclear container or sidebar view: the sidebar is a strip of tabs and a pane that depends on the active tab; the
editor area is for one thing at a time.
2. **The strip.** A vertical strip beside the pane: the projects at the top (the Nuclear projects of the workspace
folders, then the ones opened as tabs, and a `+` slot; each tab shows the platform's glyph with the dialect's icon
as a badge) and the tools at the bottom. A tool that is not built has a template page that says what it will do:
the layout and its shortcut come first, the tool later.
3. **Every tab is a workspace of its own**, a project or a tool. Switching swaps the editor area: the editors of the
tab left are remembered per window and closed, those of the tab entered are reopened.
4. **The devices are the exception.** They stay beside the code in the mobile workspaces and in the Devices tool, like
emulators, because hot reload is watched while coding. Entering a backend, a web or another tool workspace parks
them: the panel closes, the app keeps running headless with its session, and the next mobile workspace gives it a
panel again. Every switch parks the devices and takes them back after the code is reopened, so each device lands in

rows.title: ADR-0002: The Nuclear workspace in the editor: projects and tools as tabs, one thing on screen, keyboard first — Decision
rows.summary: once.
body: once. A project's ▭ Device offers the open devices, a new one or the Devices workspace; ▷ Run and ◉ Debug of a
mobile project offer the same plus *Other Flutter device…* (Flutter's own picker). A run that names no device
takes a free one or opens a new one, never a running one; a device's ▷ run restarts its own app.
- **An app lives on its own.** Closing a device tab only hides it (the app and its session go on; the Devices
workspace lists it as hidden and shows it again). The ✕ of the Devices workspace, the panel's ■ or the end of
its session end it at once (session, page connection, browser, Flutter). A watchdog runs every minute: a device
nobody looked at for 30 minutes ends, and any Flutter or browser process of this window that no device owns is
killed. Devices take the lowest free number; a session is named after its device.
9. **The web device.** ▭ Device of a web project opens the app beside the code in a headless Chromium the editor
drives, with the mobile device's machinery: desktop, laptop, tablet and phone sizes (user agent and touch for
tablets and phones), rotation, *Responsive* with any size, zoom; an address bar with back, forward, reload (Shift:
without cache), the page in the user's browser and Chrome's DevTools of the page; `prefers-color-scheme`, network

rows.title: ADR-0002: The Nuclear workspace in the editor: projects and tools as tabs, one thing on screen, keyboard first — Options considered
rows.summary: 1. One webview with the strip and the pane (chosen).
body: 1. **One webview with the strip and the pane (chosen).**
2. Multi-root workspace folders as the project tabs: the first added folder reloads the window and VS Code's explorer
shows every folder at once; the user asked not to touch VS Code's own system unless wanted.
3. The native explorer beside the strip: a built-in view cannot be placed inside an extension's container, and the
views of a container stack vertically, so a strip and a tree side by side need one webview.
4. A horizontal tab row above a native tree: it fits the sidebar's stacking, but not the vertical strip the user drew.

rows.title: ADR-0001: A release is one archive per system, installed by a one-line installer into the user's folders — Consequences
rows.summary: (`NUCLEAR_DOWNLOAD`) serves the same files, which is also how an installer is tested.
body: - Positive: one command installs NuclearLang on the three systems, with no rights beyond the user's; a mirror
(`NUCLEAR_DOWNLOAD`) serves the same files, which is also how an installer is tested.
- Negative: the installers work only once a release exists (a tag `v<version>` built by the workflow); six targets
are built for every release.

rows.title: ADR-0001: A release is one archive per system, installed by a one-line installer into the user's folders — Context and problem
rows.summary: NuclearLang was installed only from its source tree, with Rust on the machine.
body: NuclearLang was installed only from its source tree, with Rust on the machine. The user asked to install it with
one command on Linux, macOS and Windows, as Claude Code or Ollama do. An installation is more than binaries: the
dialects, the platforms' contracts and documents, the runtime packages, the definitions generator and the agents'
skill travel with them, and the binaries find them from their own location.

rows.title: ADR-0001: A release is one archive per system, installed by a one-line installer into the user's folders — Decision
rows.summary: 1. One layout.
body: 1. **One layout.** `installer/release/stage.sh` assembles an installation; the installer from source
(`installer/install.sh`) and the release archives use the same script, so both give the same folders.
2. **One archive per system and architecture.** `installer/release/package.sh` makes
`nuclearlang-<version>-<os>-<arch>.tar.gz` (`.zip` for Windows) with its `.sha256`.
3. **One-line installers.** `install.sh` (`curl … | sh`) and `install.ps1` (`irm … | iex`) download the release of
the system from GitHub, check the SHA-256, install into the user's folders (no sudo, no administrator), set the
PATH, copy the agents' skill and the VS Code extension, and uninstall.
4. **The release is a workflow.** `.github/workflows/release.yml` builds Linux (musl: static binaries for any
distribution; x86_64 and aarch64), macOS (x86_64, arm64) and Windows (x86_64, arm64) on a tag `v<version>` and
publishes the archives, the extension and both installers in the GitHub release.
5. **The website serves both installers at its root.**

rows.title: ADR-0001: A release is one archive per system, installed by a one-line installer into the user's folders — Options considered
rows.summary: 1. A package manager per system (Homebrew, winget, apt) first: three formats to maintain before there is a release; they can wrap the same archives later.
body: 1. A package manager per system (Homebrew, winget, apt) first: three formats to maintain before there is a
release; they can wrap the same archives later.
2. `cargo install`: it needs Rust on the user's machine and does not ship the dialects, the runtimes or the skill.
3. Archives of one layout and a script per shell. Chosen.

rows.title: ADR-0001: A release is one archive per system, installed by a one-line installer into the user's folders — References
rows.summary: line tools keep; this ADR holds its installers.
body: - Decided together with running and debugging a project from the dialect's data: `ADR-cli-0001`, which the command
line tools keep; this ADR holds its installers.
- The AI services the installers set up at their end: ADR-installer-0002.

rows.title: ADR-0002: The AI services come with the installer: a set-up in steps, a profile for the machine, the services at every login — Consequences
rows.summary: questions of the set-up); from VS Code alone, the wizard installs NuclearLang too.
body: - Positive: one command installs everything (`curl -fsSL https://nuclearlang.github.io/install.sh | sh`, then the
questions of the set-up); from VS Code alone, the wizard installs NuclearLang too. A machine with 8 GB gets local
agents that fit it, instead of a set that does not load. The services survive a restart of the machine and work
with the editor closed (MCP clients, `nuclear-builder`). From the source tree, `installer/install.sh --ai` is the
same set-up over the tree's own folders (the graph installed editable, the Developer built in place).
- Negative, the limits:
- The set-up is in VS Code and in a terminal. Android Studio has no wizard: `nuclear-builder setup`.
- macOS and Windows are written and not run: the launch agents, the Startup script, `winget` and Homebrew for
Ollama. Only Linux with systemd ran.
- No GPU is recognised except NVIDIA's (`nvidia-smi`) and Apple silicon: on other machines the set-up says that
no GPU with memory of its own was found, although Ollama may use an integrated one.
- The first load of the knowledge base asks Ollama for an embedding of every row: about two minutes.
- The models are Ollama's files in the user's folder: several users of one machine download them once each.
- `lite` and the assistant's part of `medium` are not fully measured: the wizard says so in their cards.

rows.title: ADR-0002: The AI services come with the installer: a set-up in steps, a profile for the machine, the services at every login — Context and…
rows.summary: The Smart Graph and the Nuclear Developer were installed from the source tree only, followed by nine commands typed by hand: pull three models, start the graph, build and ingest the knowledge base, connect two clients, start the Developer.
body: The Smart Graph and the Nuclear Developer were installed from the source tree only, followed by nine commands
typed by hand: pull three models, start the graph, build and ingest the knowledge base, connect two clients, start
the Developer. The release installers brought `nuclear-builder` and nothing else. The services were processes started
by hand: after a restart of the machine nothing answered. And there was one set of models for every machine: 9.7
GB, of which the assistant's model is 7.2 GB and leaves a 16 GB machine with under 1 GB of memory.
The user asked for every service the extension brings to be installed locally by the installer; for the hardware
to be analysed and the choices `lite`, `medium` and `hard` offered step by step, the best one for the machine
suggested, the user deciding what is downloaded and warned how far each choice works; for the services to start at
login; and for Ollama to be detected, installed as one of the steps or replaced by something better, with a user
who does not want it choosing the remote agents alone.

rows.title: ADR-0002: The AI services come with the installer: a set-up in steps, a profile for the machine, the services at every login — Decision
rows.summary: embeddings behind one address, an open licence, no window that must stay open.
body: embeddings behind one address, an open licence, no window that must stay open. Where the models run is one
address (`OLLAMA_URL`): changing the program later touches the Developer's connection, not the set-up.
7. **Remote agents only** is a choice of the first step: nothing runs on the machine. The MCP server is installed
alone (`nuclear-graph[mcp]`, 33 MB instead of 405), offers the generators, the compiler, the command line and
the internet tools, takes away the tools that need the graph or the local developer, and its instructions ask
the model to write what the generators do not. The wizard says what that costs: every line is paid tokens.
8. **The choice is one file**: `~/.config/nuclearlang/ai.env` (`%APPDATA%\nuclearlang\ai.env`), `KEY=value` lines:
the mode, the profile, its models. The services start with it; the Builder and the editor take their default models
from it; the MCP server reads the mode from it. A model set in the editor's settings wins there and is written
to the file when the editor restarts a service.
9. **The services start at every login**, with the system's own means and no administrator rights: two systemd
user units on Linux (`nuclear-graph`, `nuclear-developer`, restarted when they fail), two launch agents on
macOS, a script in the Startup folder on Windows. The editor's Start and Restart go through them. A system

rows.summary: reason; the user chooses, also one that does not fit.

Ollama, LM Studio, Jan and others run the same engine (llama.cpp), so on the same model and quantization the

that leaves a service running, models pulled by name, a model loaded when asked and freed afterwards, chat and

rows.title: ADR-0002: The AI services come with the installer: a set-up in steps, a profile for the machine, the services at every login — Decision
rows.summary: without a user service manager gets the services started now and is told so.
body: without a user service manager gets the services started now and is told so. A service started by hand that
holds the port stops the set-up with the command that stops it.
10. **A service that starts at login runs before the keyring opens.** The graph writes down the names of the
secrets its keyring keeps (`.keyring` of its data folder, no secret in it): a keyring that does not answer for
one of them is closed, so the secret is waited for (90 s) and then refused, and the unit starts again until the
keyring opens. No second secret is ever made, and a file made while the keyring was closed is not read.
(Without this, the graph found no owner's token, made another one in a file, and the user's tools, which read
the keyring's, were answered 401.)
11. **An update keeps the choice.** The environments live inside the installation, so an installer that replaces
it runs the set-up again with the profile the machine has, without questions. `--no-ai` skips it,
`--profile <id>` takes one without questions, and without a terminal (CI) nothing is asked or downloaded.
12. **Uninstalling** takes away what starts the services, the graph's tool, the Developer's launcher and the file
of the choice (`nuclear-builder setup --remove`, called by `--uninstall`). Ollama, its models and the graph's data
stay: they are the user's.

rows.title: ADR-0001: A strategy for each kind of request: the agent recognises what it is asked and follows the plan of that kind — Consequences
rows.summary: model.
body: - Positive: a request in plain words reaches the generators, each call shown before it runs.
- Positive: a compile error is repaired without planning; a failing test without generating; a rename without a
model.
- Positive: a run says which kind of request it understood and why, at its first stage: a wrong reading is seen
before any file is written, and the spec can name the right strategy.
- Positive: a lead model gets the same routing (`graph_strategy`) and the same plans.
- Positive: adding a kind of request, or changing how one is handled, is a row and its test requests.
- Negative: the selection reads words. A request that names its kind in an unusual way is classified by meaning
alone, which a small embedding model does less well than an exact sign.
- Negative: `refactor-move-extract`, `remove` and `beyond` need a lead: the local agents do their mechanical steps
only.
- Negative: a rename by the tool covers declarations and the names built from them, not fields or methods; the
file of a renamed declaration keeps its path; a rename runs no security review.
- Negative: a bug whose failure names only its test stops at *Verification*: where the cause is needs a lead or
the user.
- Negative: a model asked about a request that lists no field invents them, so the analyst's one model call is
made only when the request lists some, and its answer is held to that list.

rows.title: ADR-0001: A strategy for each kind of request: the agent recognises what it is asked and follows the plan of that kind — Context and problem
rows.summary: The local agent treated every request the same way.
body: The local agent treated every request the same way. The planner had one prompt for everything, and the Builder ran
the same nine stages for a whole system, a rename and a compile error: a bug went through *Generate*, *Plan* and
*Tests first* as if it were a feature. The spec's `Use case` field was kept and changed nothing. The knowledge
base (ADR-graph-0001) had its playbooks, found only when someone searched for them. And the generators (old
ADR-0103), which write most of a feature without a model, were reached only by a spec that wrote a `GET <url>` line
or a `Resources` section: a request in plain words ("an order has a total and a status") went to a 2B model, which
planned badly.
A small model follows steps better than it chooses them. So choosing what to do with a request cannot be the
model's work.

rows.title: ADR-0001: A strategy for each kind of request: the agent recognises what it is asked and follows the plan of that kind — Decision
rows.summary: (`nuclear fix`) come before any repair; a rename is done by a tool (every file that writes the name as a word, and with it the project's names built from it) and no model writes; the files a change starts in are found by the project's declarations, not planned.
body: **Tools before models, in every strategy.** A generator writes what is standard; the compiler's exact fixes
(`nuclear fix`) come before any repair; a rename is done by a tool (every file that writes the name as a word, and
with it the project's names built from it) and no model writes; the files a change starts in are found by the
project's declarations, not planned. A model writes only a piece of one file that no tool can write.
**The Builder follows the strategy.** The analysis is the last step of the *Specification* stage. Then the stages the
strategy has no use for are skipped; *Generate* runs the spec's own resources and the calls the analysis derived;
*Plan* takes the pieces the tools gave, and asks the planner only when the strategy's pieces come from a plan;
*Code* writes a piece a tool already wrote as it is, and afterwards wires each use case the coder wrote with
`nuclear gen usecase`; *Verification*, for a bug, repairs the file the failure names whoever wrote it, and never
the test. A Developer without an analyst leaves the run as it was: every stage.
**The classification is tested like the rest of the knowledge base.** `questions.toml` holds requests in English
and Spanish (`request = true`), none of them among the `asks` of its row; `nuclear-graph knowledge ask` gives each
to the selection and its first strategy must be the expected one.

rows.title: ADR-0001: A strategy for each kind of request: the agent recognises what it is asked and follows the plan of that kind — Decision
rows.summary: kind of request a user makes.
body: **A strategy is a row of the knowledge base** (`strategy:<name>`, type `strategy`, on the playbooks shelf): one per
kind of request a user makes. It holds how the kind is recognised (exact signs as regular expressions, trigger
words, the ways people ask), its plan step by step with the tool of every step, and what it asks of a run (its
mode, the stages of the Builder it runs, where its pieces come from, the generators it calls, the facts it cannot
start without, whether it needs a frontier model as lead). Changing how a kind of request is handled is changing a
row, never code.
**The kinds of request**, in five families:
| Family | Strategies |
| create | `system`, `project`, `component`, `resource-api`, `resource-db`, `client-of-backend`, `interface`, `repository`, `usecase`, `endpoint`, `declaration` |
| change | `member`, `refactor-rename`, `refactor-move-extract`, `refactor-architecture`, `data-migration`, `configuration`, `remove` |
| fix | `bug-compile`, `bug-failing-test`, `bug-behaviour`, `bug-runtime`, `bug-data-contract`, `bug-interface`, `bug-environment` |
| verify and explain | `tests`, `security-review`, `document`, `question`, `operate` |
| beyond | `beyond` |

rows.title: ADR-0001: A strategy for each kind of request: the agent recognises what it is asked and follows the plan of that kind — Decision
rows.summary: between strategies with no exact sign, or the same ones; whether the project has the names the request writes moves the score.
body: **The selection asks no model.** An exact sign of the request outweighs any closeness of meaning; meaning decides
between strategies with no exact sign, or the same ones; whether the project has the names the request writes moves
the score. The answer says which signs chose the strategy. A run of the Builder cannot follow a strategy without
stages (a question, a command): such a strategy comes first for a run only when an exact sign chose it. A spec may
name its strategy itself (`- Strategy: usecase`).
**The analyst** runs before anything is generated or planned, in fixed steps: the project's files say which names
of the request exist; the graph gives the strategy; the strategy gives the stages, the source of the pieces and the
facts it needs. A model is asked for one thing only: the resources a request in plain words describes. Each line
becomes a `nuclear gen resource` call and is kept only if its `--dry-run` accepts it. A fact the request lacks is
a question for the user and stops the run: nothing is guessed.

rows.title: ADR-0001: A strategy for each kind of request: the agent recognises what it is asked and follows the plan of that kind — Decision
rows.summary: the repository's method and the controller's route too (merged member by member); it refuses a search of a stored resource, because which column is searched is a decision.
body: **A generator finishes what it starts on a resource that exists.** `nuclear gen resource` with a new action adds
the repository's method and the controller's route too (merged member by member); it refuses a search of a stored
resource, because which column is searched is a decision.

rows.title: ADR-0001: A strategy for each kind of request: the agent recognises what it is asked and follows the plan of that kind — Options considered
rows.summary: 1. One prompt and one pipeline for every request: what was there.
body: 1. One prompt and one pipeline for every request: what was there.
2. A model classifies the request and chooses the steps: a small model follows steps better than it chooses them.
3. Rows of the knowledge base, one per kind of request, chosen by exact signs and then by meaning.

rows.title: 007 — A LoRA of the local coder trained on Nuclear and Synapsis — How the dataset is made (the compiler is the judge)
rows.summary: 1. A task generator, not hand-written tasks.
body: 1. **A task generator, not hand-written tasks.** The platforms already describe every kind (`docs.toml`, `[layout]`,
`[skeletons]`, the briefs): a script crosses kinds × business domains (library, shop, clinic, school…) × variations
(fields, relations, rules, errors) into thousands of task texts with acceptance texts.
2. **Answers validated by NuclearLang itself.** Every answer must pass `nuclear check` (as a project for features) and
its acceptance texts; nothing else enters the dataset. Wrong answers with their errors become repair pairs.
3. **Where the answers come from — to decide with the user:**
- *Self-distillation* (no external terms): the local model samples many answers per task, the compiler keeps the
ones that pass, and those train the next round (rejection sampling). Free, slower to start.
- *A frontier model*: Claude answers the tasks (≈ USD 0.02–0.03 per answer with Sonnet: ≈ USD 100–300 for 5–10k;
the user approved USD 20 so far). **Before using Claude's answers as training data, check Anthropic's terms for
training models on outputs** (the commercial terms restrict building competing models).
- *The tree's own code*: every example, test and generated docs (`.nuclear/map.md` descriptions → their code).
4. **Only Nuclear in the data.** No target language (Python, TypeScript, Dart) ever appears in a pair: the model

rows.title: 007 — A LoRA of the local coder trained on Nuclear and Synapsis — Order
rows.summary: 1. The task generator and the compiler-validated pipeline (no GPU): grow the eval bank to ~300 tasks first.
body: 1. The task generator and the compiler-validated pipeline (no GPU): grow the eval bank to ~300 tasks first.
2. Self-distillation round 1 on CPU-sized data (a few hundred pairs) to test the pipeline end to end.
3. A rented GPU run (QLoRA, 2–3 epochs), GGUF, Ollama; the eval against the retrieval-only coder.
4. Keep retrieval on top of the LoRA (the graph still gives the project's own names and the map).
Done when the LoRA coder passes the held-out features the retrieval-only coder fails, with no loss on single files.

Qwen2.5 has had a different license from the 1.5B and 7B ones).
- Alternatives within 3B with permissive licenses to compare on the eval: `qwen2.5-coder:1.5b`, `llama3.2:3b`,

rows.title: 007 — A LoRA of the local coder trained on Nuclear and Synapsis — What is needed
rows.summary: What is needed
body: | Need | Today | For a strong LoRA |

| Training pairs (task → validated `.nuc`) | 39 validated reference answers, 26 graph examples, ~280 `.nuc` files of the tree (~4k lines) | 5 000–10 000 pairs over every kind of the three platforms, single files and features |
| Repair pairs (code + compiler errors → fixed code) | the eval's traces | 1 000–2 000: they teach the check-and-repair loop the Developer runs |

| Hardware | Radeon 880M iGPU (no ROCm support for its gfx1150), 15 GB shared memory: CPU training takes days per round | one NVIDIA GPU with 12–24 GB (QLoRA of a 3B in 1–3 h per epoch), or a rented A10/L4/A100 (≈ USD 1–2 per hour, ≈ USD 5–15 per run) |
| Tooling | — | Unsloth or HF PEFT + TRL (SFT), then `llama.cpp` to GGUF and an Ollama `Modelfile` (`nuclear-coder:3b`) |
| Measure | `eval/run.py` (45 tasks, 18 held out) | the same bank grown to ~300 tasks, the held-out split never trained on |

rows.title: ADR-0001: The Smart Graph is a library of typed, linked, versioned rows — Context and problem
rows.summary: The knowledge base of the AI loop (ADR-platform-0003) was two collections made by cutting every markdown file of the tree into pieces of 1400 characters.
body: The knowledge base of the AI loop (ADR-platform-0003) was two collections made by cutting every markdown file of the
tree into pieces of 1400 characters. A piece knew its file and little else. Asking "what is nuclear" answered the
agent skill and a chapter about modules; "advantages" answered an editor's README; an error code found its table
cut in the middle. Nothing said what the ecosystem is for, what it can and cannot do, which tool does what, how a
task is done or what an error has to do with another. The log of the project's state was read by the local agents.
And nothing kept the base in step with the code: it was rebuilt when someone remembered.
The user asks for a library that knows the theory, the documentation, the rules, the purpose and every tool; what
Nuclear can and cannot do; every error and how errors relate; organised as JSON assets with their metadata in
Chroma collections designed for what Chroma can do; with versions, updated with every feature; tested with the
questions people ask; good enough to replace the markdown files one day.

rows.title: ADR-0001: The Smart Graph is a library of typed, linked, versioned rows — Context and problem
rows.summary: Chroma gives collections with their own metadata, rows with a vector, a document and metadata of texts, numbers, booleans and lists of texts, filters over that metadata (`$contains` on a list) and lookup by id.
body: Chroma gives collections with their own metadata, rows with a vector, a document and metadata of texts, numbers,
booleans and lists of texts, filters over that metadata (`$contains` on a list) and lookup by id. Its full-text
filters read the document, which this graph stores encrypted, so they are of no use here; it has no keyword index.

rows.title: ADR-0001: The Smart Graph is a library of typed, linked, versioned rows — Decision
rows.summary: `language`, `platforms`, `tools`, `errors`, `capabilities`, `playbooks`, `examples`, `docs`.
body: **Shelves.** One Chroma collection per kind of question, each with its own row types and filters: `concepts`,
`language`, `platforms`, `tools`, `errors`, `capabilities`, `playbooks`, `examples`, `docs`. `shelves.nuc` is the
schema; the base carries it as `schema.json`. `prompts` (the prompt files of the package) and `memory` (what an
agent keeps about a project) are collections outside the base. The catalogue of exact questions, `queries`, is a
tenth shelf (ADR-graph-0002).
**A row is a card.** `id` (`<prefix>:<name>`; a prefix belongs to one shelf, so an id is fetched without a search),
`type`, `title`, `summary`, `body`, `keys` (exact names in lower case), `asks` (the questions it answers, as people
write them), `tags`, `platforms`, `agents`, `links` (`{rel, to}`), `sources`, `meta` (the shelf's own filters),
`data`. The metadata is stored in clear, as the vectors are; the document, encrypted, is the card. What is embedded
is not the document: the title in the embedding model's title slot, with the summary and the first 1200 characters
of the body; each `ask` is one more entry that points to its card.

rows.title: ADR-0001: The Smart Graph is a library of typed, linked, versioned rows — Decision
rows.summary: shelf: ADR-developer-0001.
body: ## References
- Replaces: ADR-0104
- The AI loop this base serves: ADR-platform-0003. The `queries` shelf: ADR-graph-0002. The strategies on the `playbooks`
shelf: ADR-developer-0001.
- State: `../02-architecture/shelves.md`, `../02-architecture/search.md`, `../02-architecture/knowledge-base.md`.

rows.title: ADR-0001: The Smart Graph is a library of typed, linked, versioned rows — Decision
rows.summary: row each must return among the first; `nuclear-graph knowledge ask` runs them against the running graph.
body: **Retrieval is tested with people's questions.** `questions.toml` lists questions, in English and Spanish, and the
row each must return among the first; `nuclear-graph knowledge ask` runs them against the running graph. Every
```` ```nuclear ```` block of a hand-written row is compiled by `nuclear-graph knowledge examples`.
## Options considered
1. Document pieces: every markdown file cut into pieces, in one collection for everyone and one for the local
agents. What was there; a piece answers no question whole.
2. A library of rows on shelves, generated where a structured source exists and curated where none does.
3. For the search, Chroma's approximate index against comparing every stored vector: the index lost cards after
rows were replaced.

rows.title: ADR-0001: The Smart Graph is a library of typed, linked, versioned rows — Decision
rows.summary: examples of that kind and the pitfalls of that kind; a repair gets the card of each error code by id.
body: ## Consequences
- Positive: the local agents stop reading document pieces. A coder gets the card of the kind it writes, validated
examples of that kind and the pitfalls of that kind; a repair gets the card of each error code by id.
- Positive: a new command, MCP tool, kind, decorator, diagnostic, version or example reaches the base by building
it; the check says when a hand-written row must be read again.
- Positive: the chat can answer what the ecosystem is for, what it can do and where the agent stops.
- Negative: a new capability, limit, failure or procedure needs its row written by hand.
- Negative: the help of the commands is read from the installed binaries: a changed command is installed before
the base is built.
- Negative: keys are exact: a name written with a typo is found by meaning only.
- Negative: a curated row without `sources` is never asked for a review; one whose source is a long section is
asked often.
- The pending work of the projects is not in the base: it changes with every task. What matters of it for a reader
of the graph is in `capabilities` rows that name its sections as sources.

rows.title: ADR-0001: The Smart Graph is a library of typed, linked, versioned rows — Decision
rows.summary: answers its closest rows.
body: **Search is by meaning and by exact name, over several shelves.** The query is embedded once and every shelf asked
answers its closest rows. The runs of one to four words of the query are looked up in the rows' `keys`: a row that
carries one is brought in and moves up, so a code, a command or a kind reaches its card whatever the rest of the
sentence says and whatever its language. Entries are ranked together, each card once; a `docs` row yields to a
card. A card is also read by id.
**The search is exact.** The vector Chroma keeps of every item a filter matches is compared with the query's;
Chroma's own index (HNSW) is not asked. It is approximate, and once rows were replaced it did not reach every item
it held, differently at every start. A shelf holds hundreds of items, so comparing them all costs milliseconds.
**Two readers, one flag.** `agents: false` marks what only frontier models and people read: the target languages,
the dialects underneath, the runtimes, the decisions, the state. A row the local agents read holds no code of a
target language.
**Assets.** The knowledge base is a folder of `assets/<shelf>/<name>.json`. A row with a structured source is
generated by `nuclear-graph knowledge build` and never written by hand; a row no file says in one place is curated
by hand and names its sources; an overlay merges hand-written fields into generated rows by id.

rows.title: ADR-0001: The Smart Graph is a library of typed, linked, versioned rows — Decision
rows.summary: duplicated id, a prefix or a type of another shelf, a filter the shelf does not have, a missing title, summary or body, target-language code in an agents' row, a diagnostic without documentation, a document no section claims.
body: **The base is valid or it is not built.** `build` and `ingest` refuse a link to a row that does not exist, a
duplicated id, a prefix or a type of another shelf, a filter the shelf does not have, a missing title, summary or
body, target-language code in an agents' row, a diagnostic without documentation, a document no section claims.
**Versions.** `manifest.json` holds the schema, the revision (one more whenever any row changes, is added or is
removed), each row's hash and, for each curated row, the hash of each of its sources at its last review.
`revisions.json` is the log. The graph says which revision it holds.
**The base never stays behind the code.** `nuclear-graph knowledge check` fails when a generated file is not what
the tree gives now, a row is invalid, a source of a curated row changed since its review, or the running graph
holds another revision. The end-of-turn hook of the working tree runs it. The procedure is itself a row
(`playbook:update-the-knowledge-base`).
**What agents write at run time survives.** `POST /v1/documents` writes only `memory` and `examples`, as rows of
`origin: runtime` that an ingest keeps; the rows of the base are written by ingest alone.

rows.title: ADR-0002: Questions with one right answer are answered from exact facts by a query planner; the Smart Graph is written in Nuclear —…
rows.summary: "what does N0114 mean", "the stages of the Builder" are answered with every row, the same on every run, whatever the model.
body: - Positive: "which tools does the MCP have", "the parameters of `generate_resource`", "how is a use case created",
"what does N0114 mean", "the stages of the Builder" are answered with every row, the same on every run, whatever
the model.
- Positive: a new kind of fact is a view; a new question is a row of the catalogue with an entry of
`questions.toml`: no code.
- Negative: the facts are only as complete as the structured fields of the generated rows: what only a curated
card's prose says is still found by meaning.
- Negative: a small model can still misread a question the rows answer (its explanation may dwell on the wrong
rows); the rows under it are right and complete.
- Negative: an answer with exact facts is long: the model's explanation and then every row.
- Negative: a graph that starts makes its facts at the first question (a read of every card of the store, once).

rows.title: ADR-0002: Questions with one right answer are answered from exact facts by a query planner; the Smart Graph is written in Nuclear —…
rows.summary: The local assistant answered every question from the four cards closest to it by meaning.
body: The local assistant answered every question from the four cards closest to it by meaning. That is right for *what
is* and *how*, and wrong for *which*, *how many* and *what are*: the answer of "every tool of the MCP server" is 27
rows, and no search by meaning gives all of something. The model (2–4 B parameters) filled what was missing from
memory: a partial list, a command that does not exist. The knowledge was there: the generated rows of the base
(ADR-graph-0001) already carry each command, tool, parameter, kind and diagnostic as structured fields.
The Smart Graph itself was 6,000 lines of Python written by hand, in an ecosystem whose language transpiles to
Python.

rows.title: ADR-0002: Questions with one right answer are answered from exact facts by a query planner; the Smart Graph is written in Nuclear — Decision
rows.summary: query whose parameter the question names is run from further away than one it only resembles, with thresholds measured on `questions.toml`.
body: **The planner asks no model.** It matches the question to the catalogue by meaning and by the names it writes; a
query whose parameter the question names is run from further away than one it only resembles, with thresholds
measured on `questions.toml`. The shelves decide whether a question is exact at all: a query runs only when its
exact question is closer to what was asked than the closest card, because a name alone is a weak sign (the things
of the ecosystem share names). The question's own words fill the parameters; a follow-up that names nothing takes
them from the user's earlier messages. A needed parameter no word gives is not guessed: the query is answered
under `needs`. What is left of the question is searched in the shelves. The answer is `facts`, `knowledge` and
`needs`.
**The rows reach the reader as they are.** The chat calls the planner before the model; the prompt has an "Exact
facts" section above the documentation, left out whole with its instructions when no query ran (a 2B model copies
instructions about rows it was not given into its answer). The model explains the rows; the rows themselves end the
answer, put there by the assistant's code and never rewritten by the model (measured: a 2B model given 27 rows
retold them whole in one run and as six groups in the next). The step is in the trace.

rows.title: ADR-0002: Questions with one right answer are answered from exact facts by a query planner; the Smart Graph is written in Nuclear — Decision
rows.summary: rows of the base without their bodies: `cards`, `platforms`, `keys`, `links`, `fields` and `items` (every value of a row's `meta` and `data`, flattened), `about` (the revision).
body: **The exact facts are a relational database** (SQLite, in the standard library of the target). Its tables are the
rows of the base without their bodies: `cards`, `platforms`, `keys`, `links`, `fields` and `items` (every value of
a row's `meta` and `data`, flattened), `about` (the revision). One view per thing a question can list (`commands`,
`mcp_tools`, `mcp_params`, `routes`, `kinds`, `diagnostics`, `strategies`...). The generated rows carry what the
views read as structured `data`.
**The database lives in memory only.** The store's rule is encryption at rest; a SQLite file would keep names and
summaries in clear. The graph's process makes the database from the cards the store keeps sealed, at the first
question after it starts and again at every ingest, marks it read-only, and writes nothing of it to disk. It holds
no body and nothing an agent kept at run time.
**The questions are data: the `queries` shelf.** A row is one question with one right answer: the ways people ask
it (English and Spanish), its parameters, and its SQL over the views. A parameter names the query that lists what
people write and the value it means: no word list lives in code. The build runs every query against empty tables
and refuses a base whose query does not run, names a parameter it does not declare, or declares one it never uses.

rows.title: ADR-0002: Questions with one right answer are answered from exact facts by a query planner; the Smart Graph is written in Nuclear — Decision
rows.summary: the expected one.
body: **Acceptance.** `questions.toml` has `exact = true` entries: the planner's first query for the question must be
the expected one. An open question that reads like an exact one has `exact = false`: besides finding its card, the
planner must run no query for it. The entries with `says` are also asked to the assistant.
**The Smart Graph is a Nuclear project** of the `python` dialect. Its `.nuc` files are the source; `nuclear build`
writes the package `build/nuclear_graph` that `pyproject.toml` packages; the set-up builds before it installs; the
tests are `tests/*.nuc`. `[project] package` of `nuclear.toml` names the package the files are emitted into. This
came with the platform's rule "Nuclear and Synapsis first" (the root `AGENTS.md`): what the language could not
express while the graph was written is a finding of the compiler, kept in the roadmap of the language
(`nuclearlang/docs/01-product/roadmap.md`), never a reason to write a piece in the target language.

rows.title: ADR-0002: Questions with one right answer are answered from exact facts by a query planner; the Smart Graph is written in Nuclear —…
rows.summary: 1. More cards closer to the question: a search by meaning still gives the closest, never all.
body: 1. More cards closer to the question: a search by meaning still gives the closest, never all.
2. A SQLite file on disk: it would keep names and summaries in clear beside an encrypted store.
3. Word lists and question patterns in code: every new question would be a change of code.
4. A database in memory made from the sealed cards, with the questions as rows of the base.
