rows.title: ADR-0001: Synapsis is Nuclear's framework: a concept independent of the target language, and a project is only `.nuc` — Consequences
rows.summary: generated is ever mixed with what a person or an agent writes.
body: - Positive: one architecture to learn for every target; a project is read and reviewed as Nuclear only; nothing
generated is ever mixed with what a person or an agent writes.
- Positive: a dialect declares its `[toolchain]`, so the command needs no code for that dialect's language.
- Negative: everything the command does with a target has to be declared as data of the dialect.
- Later decisions added folders that are not `.nuc` beside the sources, each written or read by a tool: the copy of
a url contract in `contracts/<name>/contract.json` (ADR-synapsis-0006), kind packages in `kinds/<name>/`
(ADR-synapsis-0004), generated type definitions in `defs/` (ADR-lang-0008) and `migrations/` in a backend (ADR-backend-0001).

rows.title: ADR-0001: Synapsis is Nuclear's framework: a concept independent of the target language, and a project is only `.nuc` — Context and problem
rows.summary: Writing an app usually means choosing and wiring many packages: state, JSON, injection, http, routing, translations, tests.
body: Writing an app usually means choosing and wiring many packages: state, JSON, injection, http, routing,
translations, tests. Nuclear is a minimal language for agents and people, so that wiring cannot be the user's work,
and it cannot be different in every target the transpiler writes. Two things had to be fixed: what the framework is
(the companion of one target, or part of the language), and what a project made with it holds.

rows.title: ADR-0001: Synapsis is Nuclear's framework: a concept independent of the target language, and a project is only `.nuc` — Decision
rows.summary: other framework is needed.
body: **The framework is called Synapsis and it comes with the language.** It is to Nuclear what Actix is to Rust: no
other framework is needed. In Nuclear only the business logic is written; constructors, overrides, injection,
JSON, http, states, modules and imports are written by the transpiler. What a target framework lacks is added by a
runtime package of Synapsis in the target language (the first one: the Dart package `synapsis`, with the classes
and features Flutter lacks).
**It is a framework concept, not a target.** Synapsis is components, layers and architecture kinds; each dialect
applies it to its technology. The `nuclear` command knows no language: what it needs from each one (how to
install, run, test, migrate, add a package) is declared by the dialect in `[toolchain]`.
**The `.nuc` files are a project of their own.** They are separate from the target app, which is generated complete
in another folder (`build/`; `build/app` for a Flutter app) and is never edited.
**A project is only `.nuc`.** No `nuclear.toml` and no files of other types, except the dictionaries of
translations in `assets/` (ADR-synapsis-0005). The manifest is Nuclear too: `config.nuc` (ADR-mobile-0001, ADR-synapsis-0002).
Everything generated goes to `build/`.

rows.title: ADR-0001: Synapsis is Nuclear's framework: a concept independent of the target language, and a project is only `.nuc` — Options considered
rows.summary: 1. Synapsis as the framework of the `flutter` dialect only, with its Dart package: the first form of the decision, generalized.
body: 1. Synapsis as the framework of the `flutter` dialect only, with its Dart package: the first form of the decision,
generalized.
2. Synapsis as a framework concept every dialect applies to its technology: chosen.

rows.title: ADR-0001: Synapsis is Nuclear's framework: a concept independent of the target language, and a project is only `.nuc` — References
rows.summary: References
rows.body: - Replaces: ADR-0041, ADR-0045, ADR-0050, ADR-0072

rows.title: ADR-0002: Synapsis has exactly three platforms; dialects are grouped under them and never show in the Nuclear code — Consequences
rows.summary: once; the rule is the hard rule 11 of the root `AGENTS.md`.
body: - Positive: the same project builds as a Python service or as a TypeScript service; an agent learns a platform
once; the rule is the hard rule 11 of the root `AGENTS.md`.
- Positive: `Manifest` carries `platform`, read from `synapsis(...)` in `config.nuc`, so every tool knows what a
project is without knowing its language.
- Negative: a kind, a decorator or a plugin exists in a platform only when it is in the contract, and a kind only
when every dialect of the platform implements it.
- "The library is the target's" (ADR-lang-0002) is reversed for the base types by ADR-lang-0009: the standard library
is Nuclear's own and every dialect translates it.

rows.title: ADR-0002: Synapsis has exactly three platforms; dialects are grouped under them and never show in the Nuclear code — Context and problem
rows.summary: Dialects were created so that each language could use its own things (ADR-lang-0007, ADR-lang-0002).
body: Dialects were created so that each language could use its own things (ADR-lang-0007, ADR-lang-0002). With a Python
backend (ADR-python-0002) and a TypeScript backend (ADR-typescript-0001) written for the same framework, the Nuclear code of
the two examples came out different: `@get("/{id}")` against `@get(":id")`, `SQLite(url =
"sqlite+aiosqlite:///x.db")` against `SQLite(storage = "x.db")`, `len(xs)` against `xs.length`, `tests/` against
`test/`. That loses the real potential of Nuclear: anyone could build projects that make Nuclear incompatible with
itself. The differences that matter are between a web app, a mobile app and a backend, not between the languages
that run them ("of what use is the state management of Flutter in an HTTP API?").

rows.title: ADR-0002: Synapsis has exactly three platforms; dialects are grouped under them and never show in the Nuclear code — Decision
rows.summary: prints the base, the language, the platform and the dialect.
body: prints the base, the language, the platform and the dialect. One brief per platform plus the dialect's notes.
7. **A platform is one folder of the framework**, `nuclear-synapsis-framework/platforms/<platform>/`, holding its
contract, its reference and guides, its runtime packages, its examples and its checks. Its dialects and their
type definitions are with their language, in `nuclearlang/dialects/<language>/`.
8. **The backend platform, unified** (what its two dialects had decided differently):
- routes: `@controller("tasks")`, `@get()`, `@get("{id}")`, `@post("plan")`: segments without a leading slash,
`{name}` placeholders bound to the parameter of that name; the dialect writes `/tasks/:id` or `/tasks/{id}`;
- connections: `SQLite(file = "tasks.sqlite")` (`":memory:"` in tests), `Postgres(url)`, `MySQL(url)`,
`MariaDB(url)`, each with `createTables = true` for development; `Redis(url)`, `Kafka(servers, group)`,
`Ollama(model, baseUrl)`, `OpenAI(model)`, `Chroma(collection)`, `env("VAR", "default")`;
- plugins: `sqlite`, `postgres`, `mysql`, `mariadb`, `redis`, `kafka`, `events`, `ai`, `openai`, `ollama`,
`chroma` in every backend dialect;
- tests in `test/*_test.nuc` (as the mobile platform); an invalid body answers 400 (`Invalid`) everywhere;
- a graph state is read as `state.field` in every dialect.

rows.title: ADR-0002: Synapsis has exactly three platforms; dialects are grouped under them and never show in the Nuclear code — Decision
rows.summary: 9. A conformance test per platform: one example project per platform is built with every dialect of the platform from the same `.nuc` files, and each output passes its dialect's checks (`tsc --strict`, `pyright
body: 9. **A conformance test per platform:** one example project per platform is built with every dialect of the
platform from the same `.nuc` files, and each output passes its dialect's checks (`tsc --strict`, `pyright
--strict`, tests, smoke).

rows.title: ADR-0002: Synapsis has exactly three platforms; dialects are grouped under them and never show in the Nuclear code — Decision
rows.summary: The language dialects `typescript`, `dart` and `python` stay as the layer the framework dialects extend, and as targets for a single `.nuc` without Synapsis.
body: The language dialects `typescript`, `dart` and `python` stay as the layer the framework dialects extend, and as
targets for a single `.nuc` without Synapsis.
3. **The Nuclear code of a project never changes when its dialect changes.** The one exception is code that uses a
dialect's type definitions (ADR-lang-0008: `numpy` exists only in Python): it is allowed, and it ties that code
to that dialect; the platform's own kinds and library never do. Kinds and features may differ between platforms,
never between the dialects of one platform. A platform's reference, docs, examples and diagnostics name no
dialect.
4. **A project declares both** in `config.nuc`, the only manifest of a Synapsis project (ADR-synapsis-0001,
ADR-mobile-0001):
```nuclear
synapsis(platform = "backend", dialect = "fastapi")
app(name = "tasks_api", description = "...", version = "0.1.0")
plugins(sqlite = true, ollama = true)

rows.title: ADR-0002: Synapsis has exactly three platforms; dialects are grouped under them and never show in the Nuclear code — Decision
rows.summary: 1. Exactly three platforms: `web`, `mobile` and `backend`.
body: 1. **Exactly three platforms: `web`, `mobile` and `backend`.** A platform is a specification written in Nuclear
only: its project layout, `config.nuc`, kinds, decorators, connections, plugins, tests, errors and the standard
library (ADR-lang-0009). It names no language. The user and the agent write the platform; nothing else.
2. **A dialect is a language and a framework that implements a platform**, grouped under it:
- `backend`: `fastapi` (Python: FastAPI, SQLAlchemy 2 async, pydantic, LangChain, LangGraph) and `nestjs`
(TypeScript: NestJS 12, Sequelize, class-validator, LangChain.js); later `express` and others, and Synapsis's
own backend in Rust.
- `mobile`: `flutter` (Dart); later `react-native`, `kotlin-multiplatform`, native Android.
- `web`: `react` (ADR-web-0001); `vue` and `angular` planned.

rows.title: ADR-0002: Synapsis has exactly three platforms; dialects are grouped under them and never show in the Nuclear code — Decision
rows.summary: `nuclear.toml` stays for projects of a language dialect without Synapsis.
body: `nuclear.toml` stays for projects of a language dialect without Synapsis. The command creates a project with
`nuclear new -p <platform> -d <dialect> <name>` and reads `synapsis(...)` afterwards; it knows no language
(ADR-synapsis-0001: `[toolchain]`).
5. **Folders and contract.** `nuclear-synapsis-framework/platforms/<platform>/platform.toml` is the platform's
contract: its kinds, decorators, plugins and folders. A dialect lives under the language it is written in,
`nuclearlang/dialects/<language>/frameworks/<dialect>/`, and names its platform in `[dialect]`. The loader
refuses a dialect that misses a kind of its platform, or that brings a kind, a consumed decorator or a plugin
its platform does not declare (N0305); a plugin of the platform a dialect does not bring yet is a warning. The
loader test guards it. Kinds a dialect does not bring come as packages on top of it, never inside it
(ADR-synapsis-0004).
6. **One reference per platform** (`platforms/<platform>/docs/07-reference/<platform>.md`), with the rules and the
Nuclear; one per dialect (`nuclearlang/dialects/<language>/docs/07-reference/<dialect>.md`) with only how that
dialect writes it (the equivalences `nuclearlang/tools/spec-check` verifies). `nuclear spec --dialect fastapi`

rows.title: ADR-0002: Synapsis has exactly three platforms; dialects are grouped under them and never show in the Nuclear code — Options considered
rows.summary: 1. Keeping one specification per dialect and asking the two backends to "stay close": nothing would guard it, and the two examples had already drifted in a day.
body: 1. Keeping one specification per dialect and asking the two backends to "stay close": nothing would guard it, and
the two examples had already drifted in a day.
2. A `platform` field in `nuclear.toml`: a Synapsis project has only `.nuc` files (ADR-synapsis-0001).
3. Naming the dialects by language (`python`, `typescript`): `express` is TypeScript too; the framework is what a
dialect is.
4. Three platforms as contracts, with the dialects grouped under them: chosen.

rows.title: ADR-0003: An app is closed components with layers and a facade; dependencies are injected by header; the transpiler checks the…
rows.summary: (`nuclear help layout --dialect <d>`) and what it may use.
body: - Positive: every project has the same shape, so a person, an agent or a generator knows where a file goes
(`nuclear help layout --dialect <d>`) and what it may use.
- Positive: a breach of the architecture is a build error with a code, not a review comment.
- Negative: every rule is an error; there is no warning level and no way to switch a rule off for a file or a
declaration (open in `docs/01-product/roadmap.md`).

rows.title: ADR-0003: An app is closed components with layers and a facade; dependencies are injected by header; the transpiler checks the…
rows.summary: The framework writes the architecture so that Nuclear holds only the business logic (ADR-synapsis-0001), and it warns when something breaks that architecture.
body: The framework writes the architecture so that Nuclear holds only the business logic (ADR-synapsis-0001), and it warns
when something breaks that architecture. That needs one shape for every project: where each declaration lives, how
it gets what it depends on, and who may call whom.

rows.title: ADR-0003: An app is closed components with layers and a facade; dependencies are injected by header; the transpiler checks the…
rows.summary: `components/<c>/{config, data, domain/{models, usecases, aggregates, services}}` plus the platform's entry layer and the component's facade (kind `appcomponent`); `shared/`, `config/` (kind `appConfig`) and, in an app, `main.nuc` at the root.
body: **Component structure.** An app is made of components, one per feature:
`components/<c>/{config, data, domain/{models, usecases, aggregates, services}}` plus the platform's entry layer
and the component's facade (kind `appcomponent`); `shared/`, `config/` (kind `appConfig`) and, in an app, `main.nuc`
at the root. The entry layer is `presentation/<screen>/{managers, state_models}` and `presentation/widgets` where
there are screens, and `api/` in a backend. The exact place of each kind's file is data: `[layout]` of the
platform's contract (ADR-synapsis-0002). The layers exist in the generated code, not as ceremony in Nuclear
(ADR-dart-0001).
**Dependency injection.** A typed parameter in a kind's header (`(repository: CharacterRepository)`) is injected
automatically. Nothing is registered or resolved by hand.
**Architecture rules.** A use case is only called from an appcomponent; a service only from a use case or an
aggregate. From another component only its public kinds are visible. The transpiler checks the rules across the
whole project (it is the framework's linter): they are declared in `[architecture]` of the dialect (`scope`,
`public`, `exempt`, `callers`, `names`); a caller of a kind that may not call it is N0301, a use of something that
is not public in another component is N0302.

rows.title: ADR-0003: An app is closed components with layers and a facade; dependencies are injected by header; the transpiler checks the…
rows.summary: their `@on(Event)` methods run on every event, wherever the user is.
body: **Global components.** Kind `component` in `shared/components/`: cross-cutting use cases any declaration can use;
their `@on(Event)` methods run on every event, wherever the user is.

rows.body: - Replaces: ADR-0042, ADR-0043, ADR-0046, ADR-0053

rows.title: ADR-0004: Kinds are Nuclear's libraries: native kinds in the platform, extension kinds as packages, optional parts as plugins of…
rows.summary: a release of the compiler; the rule is part of the hard rule 11 of the root `AGENTS.md`.
body: - Positive: a project carries only the packages of the plugins it enables; a kind is shared and installed without
a release of the compiler; the rule is part of the hard rule 11 of the root `AGENTS.md`.
- The template engine (a Mustache subset with filters) and the fixed data it receives are kept. The cost is that
new data comes from the compiler; the benefit is that a kind can only produce code an expert reads (the golden
rule, ADR-lang-0001). It is revisited only if the first community packages show that templates are not enough.
- Two generic emitter capabilities came with Genkit: `async_methods` also for methods that await nothing, and
`async` in the `methods` of kind templates.
- Negative: a capability a template lacks waits for the compiler, for every kind author.

rows.title: ADR-0004: Kinds are Nuclear's libraries: native kinds in the platform, extension kinds as packages, optional parts as plugins of…
rows.summary: Kinds are to Synapsis what libraries are to a language.
body: Kinds are to Synapsis what libraries are to a language. There are native kinds and kinds written by a project or
by the community, as extensions of the dialect a developer uses; a developer must never have to touch the parser,
the lexer or the emitter to write one. And a project must not get heavier with what it does not use: full Genkit
support for the mobile platform, database drivers, Kafka or LangChain are wanted only by the projects that ask for
them, through "a section in `config.nuc`, like a pubspec or a package.json but only to enable these packages".
What already held: a kind is data, not code (`[kinds.<word>]` in a TOML file plus a template; no kind name is
written in Rust), and a project could add a kind with a child dialect. What was missing: a unit smaller than a
dialect to share and install; knowing which dialects a kind exists for; keeping the real dialect in `config.nuc`
(a child dialect hid it from the command and the editors); and every framework written so far had needed new
generic emitter capabilities, because templates have no expressions, only sections and filters.

rows.title: ADR-0004: Kinds are Nuclear's libraries: native kinds in the platform, extension kinds as packages, optional parts as plugins of…
rows.summary: the author asks for a generic capability (an `[options]` entry or a template variable) and it is added for every kind; never a case for one kind or one language.
body: the author asks for a generic capability (an `[options]` entry or a template variable) and it is added for
every kind; never a case for one kind or one language.
8. **Project dialects** keep their shortcuts. The kinds they add are extension kinds of that project: allowed,
tied to the dialect they extend, not checked by the platform contract. A kind package is the portable form.
9. **Owed to kind authors:** `nuclear kind new <name>` (the skeleton), `nuclear add <source>` (installs a
package), one `docs.toml` per package read by the editors, the missing-implementation diagnostic, the guide
`docs/08-guides/kinds.md`; and, not delivered yet, `nuclear dialect test` over a package and installing from a
repository with a pinned version.
10. **The editor tells kinds apart.** The loader gives every kind its source (`Dialect.kind_sources`): the
language's (`dart`'s `data`, `mixin`), native of the platform, or an extension package (name, version, the
dialects it implements). The language server lists, for a project, only the kinds of its platform (the native
ones plus the packages its `config.nuc` enables) and shows each kind's source and docs; the same word may mean
different things in two platforms, and the editor always shows the meaning of the project's platform.

rows.title: ADR-0004: Kinds are Nuclear's libraries: native kinds in the platform, extension kinds as packages, optional parts as plugins of…
rows.summary: 1. Plugins.
body: 1. **Plugins.** A dialect declares `[project.plugins.<name>]` (packages, dev packages, type definitions, kinds,
names, requires); `config.nuc` enables them with `plugins(name = true)`. A kind or a name of a plugin that is
not enabled is N0304, with the line to add; an unknown plugin or value is N0303. Project templates get
`plugins.<name>`, `plugins.packages` and `plugins.dev_packages`, so a generated manifest lists only the enabled
packages; the `nuclear` command adds and removes the Flutter packages of the plugins (`.synapsis_plugins`).
The plugins' type definitions are always loaded (their index only), so editors know them. The plugins of a
platform are a list of its contract, the same in every dialect (ADR-synapsis-0002).
2. **Catalogs.** Mobile: `genkit` and one plugin per provider. Backend: `sqlite`, `postgres`, `mysql`, `mariadb`,
`redis`, `kafka`, `events` (in-process publish), `ai`, `openai`, `ollama`, `chroma`. The runtimes keep the
optional parts in their own modules (`synapsis.ai`, `synapsis.events`; `synapsis-nest/ai`,
`synapsis-nest/events`, kafkajs and ioredis loaded when opened), so a project without a plugin does not need
its package.
3. **Genkit for the mobile platform** (the runtime package `synapsis_genkit`): Genkit in the app and remote

rows.title: ADR-0004: Kinds are Nuclear's libraries: native kinds in the platform, extension kinds as packages, optional parts as plugins of…
rows.summary: flows, with the providers Firebase AI, Google AI, Vertex AI, OpenAI and Anthropic.
body: flows, with the providers Firebase AI, Google AI, Vertex AI, OpenAI and Anthropic. Providers are connections of
the project config (descriptors without plugin imports); the generated `lib/synapsis_genkit.g.dart` (only with
the plugin) turns them into plugins and registers a schema per model of the app (`SchemanticType.from` with its
fields and `fromJson`, no schemantic codegen). Kinds: `tools` (doc comment = description, parameters = JSON
schema), `chat` (history, `send`, `stream`, `ChatController`), `flow` (`GenkitFlow`, `generateObject` with a
text fallback for servers without structured output), `remote` (`defineRemoteAction`, call and stream),
`knowledge` (embed and cosine search, `context` for RAG). Tests: `startFakeGenkit`.
4. **Two sources of kinds.** Native kinds are the platform's: listed in its `platform.toml`, implemented
identically by every dialect of the platform. Extension kinds come in packages written by a project or by the
community on top of one or more dialects of a platform. A dialect's own TOML never adds kinds (N0305): what a
dialect would add goes in a package, so any other dialect can implement it.
5. **A kind package is a plugin that is not shipped with the dialect.** It is a folder `kinds/<name>/`: a
`kind.toml` with `[package]` (name, version, platform, description), a `docs.toml`, and one folder per dialect

rows.title: ADR-0004: Kinds are Nuclear's libraries: native kinds in the platform, extension kinds as packages, optional parts as plugins of…
rows.summary: it supports (`fastapi/kind.toml` with `[plugin]`, the dialect sections and the templates).
body: it supports (`fastapi/kind.toml` with `[plugin]`, the dialect sections and the templates). A package belongs to
exactly one platform: its kinds never appear in a project of another platform, even when the word exists there
with another meaning (`repository` is table queries in backend and HTTP calls in mobile). A project enables it
with `plugins(<name> = true)`, exactly like a shipped plugin, and keeps `synapsis(platform = "backend", dialect
= "fastapi")`: the dialect is always the platform's dialect, never a child dialect that wraps it.
6. **Portability.** A package declares the dialects it implements; the Nuclear of the kind is the same in all of
them. A project that enables a package implemented for only some dialects of its platform is tied to those
dialects, the same exception type definitions have; a package enabled without an implementation for the
project's dialect is N0306. A package may gain implementations later without changing its Nuclear.
7. **A kind never touches the compiler.** A package holds TOML, templates, a runtime package in the target
language, type definitions and docs; nothing else. A kind adds no syntax: it is a header and a block of the base
grammar, and its words are kinds, decorators, modifiers and clauses. When a template cannot express something,

rows.title: ADR-0004: Kinds are Nuclear's libraries: native kinds in the platform, extension kinds as packages, optional parts as plugins of…
rows.summary: 1. Kinds inside a child dialect named in `config.nuc`: the real dialect disappears from the manifest, nothing says which dialects the kind exists for, and there is nothing to install.
body: 1. Kinds inside a child dialect named in `config.nuc`: the real dialect disappears from the manifest, nothing says
which dialects the kind exists for, and there is nothing to install.
2. A kind API in Rust or WebAssembly (a plugin computes the output): it would let a kind fake syntax and emit code
no template reviewer reads; it moves the parser problem to the author, the opposite of the goal.
3. Letting each dialect declare extra kinds (dropping N0305): the Nuclear of a platform would drift again between
its dialects, which ADR-synapsis-0002 forbids.
4. Packages of TOML, templates and a runtime, enabled as plugins: chosen.

rows.title: ADR-0005: Every app gets the same services from the framework: events, session, ACL, forms, translations and generic models — Consequences
rows.summary: writes them the same way whatever the dialect.
body: - Positive: an app needs no third-party package for events, session, permissions, forms or translations, and
writes them the same way whatever the dialect.
- Positive: the dictionaries in `assets/` are the one kind of file that is not `.nuc` a project writes by hand
(ADR-synapsis-0001).
- Negative: each platform implements each service natively, so a service exists in a platform only when its
contract and its runtime have it; what a platform still lacks is in that platform's roadmap.

rows.title: ADR-0005: Every app gets the same services from the framework: events, session, ACL, forms, translations and generic models — Context and…
rows.summary: With Synapsis a project does not choose and wire packages: what an app always needs comes with the framework, as the same concepts in every platform, implemented natively by each one.
body: With Synapsis a project does not choose and wire packages: what an app always needs comes with the framework, as
the same concepts in every platform, implemented natively by each one. These are the decisions on what those
services are and how they are written in Nuclear.

rows.title: ADR-0005: Every app gets the same services from the framework: events, session, ACL, forms, translations and generic models — Decision
rows.summary: EventBus or Node's EventEmitter.
body: **Global events.** A global manager (`Events`) with two operations, `publish` and `subscribe`, like Guava's
EventBus or Node's EventEmitter. Delivery is on demand: an event reaches only the visible screen and the global
components at once; a hidden screen gets the last event of each type when it is shown again. Background isolates
of the app also publish.
**Session.** `session.start(data, ...)` and `session.destroy()` (which publishes the end to the global events),
kept in secure storage. It combines with the ACL when the developer wants.
**ACL.** Based on Phalcon (roles that inherit others, permissions per role, everything denied unless allowed) and
on NestJS (guards: kind `guard` with `canActivate`). By default there is only logged in or not; roles are
optional.

**Forms.** Format validation belongs to presentation: a form model (kind `form`, in `presentation/

/forms/`)
with the rules as decorators on its fields (`@required`, `@email`, `@minLength(n)`...), a form manager (kind
`formmanager`, `@form(F)`) that only validates, and widgets (`SynapsisForm`, `FormTextField`...) bound by field
name. Business rules stay in the domain; `@validate("field")` asks the component.

rows.title: ADR-0005: Every app gets the same services from the framework: events, session, ACL, forms, translations and generic models — Decision
rows.summary: `assets/i18n/<locale>/<component>.json`; the key is `<component>.<path>`, used as `"key".tr()`.
body: **Translations.** Native JSON dictionaries (no third-party libraries), one per component and language in
`assets/i18n/<locale>/<component>.json`; the key is `<component>.<path>`, used as `"key".tr()`. Optional remote
dictionaries, stored by version on every platform.
**Generic models.** A model can have type parameters (`Page<T>` with `results: T[]`) and interfaces (`ApiFailure >
Exception`); the dialect writes what is needed (Dart: `genericArgumentFactories` of json_serializable, the
`fromJson` of each argument in repositories). A kind that would not write generics or interfaces is an error
(N0218) instead of losing them.

rows.title: ADR-0006: A backend publishes what it exposes as a contract; a client generates its models and repositories from it — Consequences
rows.summary: change in the API is caught at build time; the editors read every project's endpoints from the same file (ADR-extensions-0002).
body: - Positive: a mobile or web app over a Nuclear backend writes no model and no repository; the rules travel; a
change in the API is caught at build time; the editors read every project's endpoints from the same file
(ADR-extensions-0002).
- Negative, the limits of the decision: entities travel only when a route returns them; a generic in a route's
answer (`Page<Task>`) is generated but not stored locally (`local = true` only for a plain keyed model); the
client's `<Name>Error` has the message only (the status is not in the mobile `Result` error); a url contract
needs `curl`; the generated repository names (`TasksRepository`) may clash with the app's own, and two contracts
that export the same model name clash (each is a top-level declaration); versions are shown, not enforced.

rows.title: ADR-0006: A backend publishes what it exposes as a contract; a client generates its models and repositories from it — Context and problem
rows.summary: A backend written in Nuclear defines its models and routes once; every app that calls it wrote the same models and a repository per controller again, by hand, with nothing checking the copies.
body: A backend written in Nuclear defines its models and routes once; every app that calls it wrote the same models and
a repository per controller again, by hand, with nothing checking the copies. A renamed field or a changed path
compiled on both sides and failed at run time; the validation rules stayed in the backend; an agent spent its
turns transcribing. Backend and app stay two projects, deployed apart and talking over HTTP: what was missing is
the description of the API traveling from one to the other, the way OpenAPI, `.proto` files or tRPC do it.

rows.title: ADR-0006: A backend publishes what it exposes as a contract; a client generates its models and repositories from it — Decision
rows.summary: 1. Every project writes its contract.
body: 1. **Every project writes its contract.** `nuclear build`, `nuclear check`, `nuclear build` and the editors (the
same call that writes the project card, `project::write_metadata`) write `.nuclear/contract.json`: the models
(fields, Nuclear types, optionality, defaults, JSON names, validation rules, the key field, doc comments) and,
for a backend, the controllers with their routes (verb, path, parameters with where they go, body, answer,
error type, status); for a mobile or web app, the repositories with the calls they make. The contract is in
Nuclear's notation and is the same whatever the dialect (checked by a test with `nestjs` and `fastapi`).
2. **A backend also writes OpenAPI 3.1** (`.nuclear/openapi.json`, from the contract: paths, parameters, request
bodies, responses, schemas with the rules, doc comments as summaries). Both files are copied into the output
folder, and the runtimes serve them at `GET /.nuclear/contract.json` and `GET /.nuclear/openapi.json`, so a
client that is not Nuclear (Swagger UI, a generator, an HTTP tool) reads the API as built.
3. **A client declares the backends it talks to** in its manifest: `contracts(tasks_api = "../tasks_api")` (a
path: the backend built next to it, in the same tree or a sibling checkout) or `contracts(tasks_api =

rows.title: ADR-0006: A backend publishes what it exposes as a contract; a client generates its models and repositories from it — Decision
rows.summary: "https://api.x.com")` (the running API: fetched by `nuclear contracts update`, kept in `contracts/<name>/contract.json`, committed so a build never needs the network).
body: "https://api.x.com")` (the running API: fetched by `nuclear contracts update`, kept in
`contracts/<name>/contract.json`, committed so a build never needs the network). The name is the
`connectionName` the generated repositories use.
4. **The build generates Nuclear, not target code.** Before reading the sources, `project::build` writes
`contracts/<name>/`: one model per model the routes carry (transitively), the error model `<Name>Error`
(`message`), one repository per controller with a method per route (`{id}` → `:id`, path, query and body
placement, `Result<<Name>Error, T>`), with the backend's doc comments as comments. Only the decorators the
client's dialect consumes are written (`@primary` and the rules for flutter, `@key` everywhere; a GET that
answers a keyed model gets `local = true` where the local database exists). The files carry a "generated, do
not edit" header and are regenerated on every build from a path contract; stale files are removed. The rest of
the pipeline is untouched: the client's dialect writes the model and the repository as it writes its own.
5. **Drift is a build error.** A field the backend renamed is unknown in the client at its next build (N0116, with
the field's name); a contract that cannot be read is N0307. `nuclear contracts list` shows each contract's
source and the version of the local copy.

body: 6. **Two generic compiler fixes came with it** (no kind name in Rust): named arguments to a method of a value
typed with a project declaration (`repo.all(done = false)`) are reordered by position like any Nuclear call
(they were written as named, which Dart and TypeScript refuse); and a project declaration named like a library

definitions; the `hide` clause of `import_default`).

rows.title: ADR-0006: A backend publishes what it exposes as a contract; a client generates its models and repositories from it — Options considered
rows.summary: 1. OpenAPI as the only contract: it loses `Result` errors, Nuclear types, the key field and the rules' names; kept as an export for clients that are not Nuclear (decision 2).
body: 1. OpenAPI as the only contract: it loses `Result` errors, Nuclear types, the key field and the rules' names; kept
as an export for clients that are not Nuclear (decision 2).
2. Target code generated directly in the client: a second code path per dialect; generating Nuclear reuses the
dialect's own templates and shows the user plain `.nuc` files.
3. A shared Nuclear library imported by both projects: the backend would depend on the client's platform.
4. A contract in Nuclear's notation, read back as generated `.nuc`: chosen.

rows.summary: Step 3 of the competitiveness plan (decided by the user 2026-11-06; what is left of it is in `nuclear-synapsis-framework/docs/01-product/roadmap.md`).
body: Step 3 of the competitiveness plan (decided by the user 2026-11-06; what is left of it is in
`nuclear-synapsis-framework/docs/01-product/roadmap.md`). **Delivered 2026-11-06** (ADR-synapsis-0006): F1–F4 as
below with these differences: the word is `contracts(...)`; the generated folder is committed and regenerated on
every build (path) or on `nuclear contracts update` (url); entities travel when a route returns them; the error
model carries `message` only; F5 shows versions (`nuclear contracts list`) without a drift warning yet. Reference:
`nuclearlang/docs/07-reference/projects.md` §1.2. Paths in this plan start at the root of the tree.

rows.title: 003 — Shared contracts: the backend written once, its clients generated — 1. Goal
rows.summary: A model, an entity and a route are written once, in the backend project.
body: A model, an entity and a route are written **once**, in the backend project. Every client project of the same
app (mobile, web) gets, without writing them, the same models, a typed repository per controller and the routes
with their parameters. When the backend changes, the clients fail to build until they follow, instead of failing
at run time with a 404 or a wrong field.

rows.title: 003 — Shared contracts: the backend written once, its clients generated — 2. Diagnosis: what happens today
rows.summary: Three copies of `Task` (entity, backend model, mobile model), two of `NewTask`, the routes typed twice.
body: Three copies of `Task` (entity, backend model, mobile model), two of `NewTask`, the routes typed twice. A renamed
field (`done` → `completed`) breaks the app at run time. The validation rules (`@minLength(3)`) are lost in the
client, so a form sends what the API will refuse.

rows.title: 003 — Shared contracts: the backend written once, its clients generated — 2. Diagnosis: what happens today
rows.summary: The backend example `nuclear-synapsis-framework/platforms/backend/examples/examples-backend/tasks_api` and a mobile app that uses it write the same thing twice, by hand, with no check between them.
body: The backend example `nuclear-synapsis-framework/platforms/backend/examples/examples-backend/tasks_api` and a mobile
app that uses it write the same thing twice, by hand, with no check between them.
Backend (`components/tasks/`):
```nuclear

entity Task()
@generated()
id: int
@column(length = 120)
title: string
done: boolean = false
// domain/models/new_task.nuc
NewTask
@required
@minLength(3)
title: string
// api/tasks_controller.nuc
@controller("tasks")
controller TasksController(tasks: TasksAppComponent)
@get("{id}")
one(id: int) Result<AppError, Task>
tasks.find(id)
@post
@status(201)
create(body: NewTask) Result<AppError, Task>

@get

@primary

NewTask

rows.title: 003 — Shared contracts: the backend written once, its clients generated — 3. The design in one picture
rows.summary: backend project (tasks_api) client project (tasks_app, mobile or web) components/tasks/data/entities/task.nuc config.nuc: contracts(tasks_api = "../tasks_api") components/tasks/domain/models/new_task.nuc ───► contracts/tasks_api/ (generated, read-only) components/tasks/api/tasks_controller.nuc…
body: backend project (tasks_api)                                client project (tasks_app, mobile or web)
components/tasks/data/entities/task.nuc                   config.nuc: contracts(tasks_api = "../tasks_api")
components/tasks/domain/models/new_task.nuc     ───►      contracts/tasks_api/           (generated, read-only)
components/tasks/api/tasks_controller.nuc                   models/task.nuc
│                                                   models/new_task.nuc
▼ nuclear build                                     tasks_repository.nuc
.nuclear/contract.json  (models, routes)        ───►      then the normal build of the client dialect
The contract is **Nuclear generated into the client**, not target code: the client's dialect already knows how to
write a model and a repository (ADR-mobile-0006 made the mobile model a table too). The compiler only learns to write
the contract and to read it back as `.nuc`; no new kind, no new template variable.

rows.title: 003 — Shared contracts: the backend written once, its clients generated — F3 — The client's build writes the contract as Nuclear
rows.summary: Before building, `nuclear build` (and `nuclear build`) writes `contracts/<name>/` from the contract: // contracts/tasks_api/models/task.nuc — generated from tasks_api 1.0.0; do not edit Task @primary id: int @minLength(3) title: string done: boolean // contracts/tasks_api/models/new_task.nuc…
body: Before building, `nuclear build` (and `nuclear build`) writes `contracts/<name>/` from the contract:
```nuclear
// contracts/tasks_api/models/task.nuc — generated from tasks_api 1.0.0; do not edit
Task
@primary
id: int
@minLength(3)
title: string
done: boolean
// contracts/tasks_api/models/new_task.nuc
NewTask
@required
@minLength(3)
title: string
// contracts/tasks_api/tasks_repository.nuc
@repository(path = "tasks", connection = "tasks_api", saveLocal = true)
repository TasksRepository
@get(path = ":id")
one(id: int) Result<ApiError, Task>
@post
create(body: NewTask) Result<ApiError, Task>
@get
search(done?: boolean, page: int = 1) Result<ApiError, Task[]>
The validation rules travel with the model, so a mobile `form` built on `NewTask` refuses what the API refuses.
`ApiError` (`message`, `status`) is the client-side twin of the backend's `AppError`; `saveLocal` is on because
the models carry their key (ADR-mobile-0006), so every GET gets its `<method>AsLocal()` twin and the app works offline for
what it already fetched.
The generated folder is read-only for the architecture rules: a client component uses the repository as it uses
its own (`N0301`: only from a `usecase` or an `aggregate`), and may not declare a name the contract declares.

rows.title: ADR-0001: Backend data is written with one key decorator, a decorator per relation, `paginate`, `@transactional` and generated migrations…
rows.summary: mobile, and so is a page.
body: - Positive: an entity reads like a TypeORM entity in every backend dialect; the key is one word on backend and
mobile, and so is a page.
- Positive: the rules of the relation decorators are data of the platform, so a new backend dialect gets them by
writing templates.
- Positive: `make` never needs a running database, and the same migration file runs on every database.
- Negative: the join table and the relation column have no custom name; another name would be a later argument.
- Negative: `@transactional` covers the default database only.
- Negative: the members of `Page<T>` are untyped in Nuclear until type definitions carry member types.

rows.title: ADR-0001: Backend data is written with one key decorator, a decorator per relation, `paginate`, `@transactional` and generated migrations…

body: A real backend needs relations between tables, pagination, transactions and migrations of the database schema
([spec 004](../04-specs/004-backend-parity/plan.md), F1–F4). The user's rule for them: the code must look as much
alike as possible across the platforms, at the middle point of cost and benefit, polished step by step. The words
had to be the same in every backend dialect, and the key and the pages also on the mobile local tables
(ADR-mobile-0006).

rows.title: ADR-0001: Backend data is written with one key decorator, a decorator per relation, `paginate`, `@transactional` and generated migrations…
rows.summary: difference between the entities and the last migration, never a live database, in the dialect's tool, under `migrations/` of the project (kept with the sources, not in `build/`).
body: **Migrations are generated from the entities.** `nuclear migrate make "<message>"` writes one migration from the
difference between the entities and the last migration, never a live database, in the dialect's tool, under
`migrations/` of the project (kept with the sources, not in `build/`). `nuclear migrate` applies the pending
ones to the default database; `nuclear migrate down` reverts the last. They are the dialect's `[toolchain]` keys
`migrate_make`, `migrate`, `migrate_down` (placeholders `{{message}}`, `{{migrations}}`), so the command names no
tool. `SQLite(createTables = true)` stays for tests and development. A field default (`done: boolean = false`) is
also the column's SQL default, so a non-null column can be added to a table with rows. A rename shows as a drop
and an add; `make` warns of every drop; the file is the project's to edit.
**How each dialect implements it.**

rows.title: ADR-0001: Backend data is written with one key decorator, a decorator per relation, `paginate`, `@transactional` and generated migrations…
rows.summary: In fastapi related entities are imported only for the type checker; in nestjs a single relation is typed `Related<T>` and the runtime's `Entity` keeps the relations given to the constructor.
body: | | `fastapi` (SQLAlchemy 2) | `nestjs` (sequelize-typescript) |
| `@manyToOne` | `relationship` + `ForeignKey` on `x_id` | `@BelongsTo` + `@ForeignKey` on `xId` |
| `@oneToMany` | `relationship(back_populates=...)` | `@HasMany` |
| `@manyToMany` | `relationship(secondary=...)` | `@BelongsToMany(..., through)` |
| `@oneToOne` | `relationship(uselist=False)` | `@BelongsTo` / `@HasOne` |
| Transaction | an `AsyncSession` in a `ContextVar` | a sequelize transaction in an `AsyncLocalStorage` |

| Migrations | Alembic: `make` brings an empty SQLite in memory to the last migration and lets autogenerate write the difference, in batch mode (SQLite cannot alter a column; the other databases run the same file); the folder's `env.py` is written once; `alembic_version` lists what is applied | the runtime's `synapsis-nest-migrate`: it reads the entities' attributes, diffs them with the `schema` the last migration exports and writes `up` / `down` over `queryInterface`; `SequelizeMeta` lists what is applied |
In fastapi related entities are imported only for the type checker; in nestjs a single relation is typed
`Related<T>` and the runtime's `Entity` keeps the relations given to the constructor. In Dart `Page<T>` is the
runtime's `PageOf<T>` (Flutter has its own `Page`; a project's own `Page` keeps its name).

rows.title: ADR-0001: Backend data is written with one key decorator, a decorator per relation, `paginate`, `@transactional` and generated migrations…
rows.summary: runtime fills it: auto increment for an `int`, a uuid for a `string`) and `length` (a `string` key the app gives).
body: **One key decorator, `@primary(...)`, that takes what it needs as arguments.** `generated` (the database or the
runtime fills it: auto increment for an `int`, a uuid for a `string`) and `length` (a `string` key the app gives).
There is no `@generated` and no key by name, on any platform: `@generated()` is N0309, with
`@primary(generated = true)` as the fix.
```nuclear
@entity("tasks")
entity Task()
@primary(generated = true)     // the database gives it
id: int
@entity("codes")
entity Code()
@primary(length = 8)           // the app gives it
code: string
**A decorator per relation, as TypeORM writes them**, because the explicit form needs no deduction rules to learn.
```nuclear
@entity("tasks")
entity Task()
@primary(generated = true)
id: int
@manyToOne(inverse = "tasks", onDelete = "cascade")
project?: Project
projectId: int                 // the join column of `project` (projectId?: int: a task may have no project)
@manyToMany(inverse = "tasks")
@joinTable()
tags?: Tag[]

rows.title: ADR-0001: Backend data is written with one key decorator, a decorator per relation, `paginate`, `@transactional` and generated migrations…
rows.summary: The related type comes from the field's type, so the decorator does not repeat it.
body: | Decorator | On | Arguments |
| `@manyToOne` | `x?: T`, with a field `xId` | `inverse`, `onDelete` (`"cascade"`, `"set null"`, `"restrict"`) |
| `@oneToMany` | `xs?: T[]` | `inverse` (required: the `@manyToOne` field of `T`) |
| `@manyToMany` | `xs?: T[]` | `inverse`; `@joinTable()` on the side that owns the join table |
| `@oneToOne` | `x?: T` | `inverse`, `onDelete`; `@joinColumn()` and a field `xId` on the side that keeps the column |
The related type comes from the field's type, so the decorator does not repeat it. The join column is a field of
its own (`projectId`): it is set without loading the other row and it is in the JSON answer. The join table is
`<owner table>_<field>` (`tasks_tags`), with the columns `<entity>_id` of both sides; the column of a relation is
`<field>_id`. Both are conventions, the same in every dialect.
Checked at compile time (N0308): a relation field is optional (it is there only when loaded); its type is an entity
(a list for `@oneToMany` / `@manyToMany`, one for `@manyToOne` / `@oneToOne`); `@manyToOne`, and `@oneToOne` with
`@joinColumn`, need the field `<name>Id`; `inverse` names a field of the related entity; one side of a
`@manyToMany` has `@joinTable`, one side of a `@oneToOne` has `@joinColumn`.

rows.title: ADR-0001: Backend data is written with one key decorator, a decorator per relation, `paginate`, `@transactional` and generated migrations…
rows.summary: from the JSON answer: never `null`, never a lazy query.
body: **Loading is explicit**: `relations("tasks")` is one more step of the query builder. An unloaded relation is absent
from the JSON answer: never `null`, never a lazy query. Saving writes what the entity holds: the join column of a
`@manyToOne`, and the rows of the join table when a `@manyToMany` list is set (`task.tags = [a, b]`, then
`save(task)`).
**The rules are data of the platform, with no decorator name in Rust.** `[decorators.args]` and
`[decorators.fields]` of `platform.toml` list them (`optional`, `list`, `target`, `sibling`, `inverse`, `with`);
the loader merges them into every backend dialect. Templates get `tinfo.decor` (the decorators of the field's type:
its table), `owner` / `owner_decor` (the declaration the field is in) and the `unquote` filter.
**Pagination is `paginate(page, size)` → `Page<T>`**, one more step of the query builder (one `count` and one
`limit` / `offset`). `Page<T>` (`items`, `page` from 1, `size`, `total`, `pages`) is a class of the runtimes. The
same line is written in a backend repository and in a mobile local query.
```nuclear
repository TaskRepository
page(page: int, size: int = 20) Page<Task>
orderBy("id")
paginate(page, size)

rows.title: ADR-0001: Backend data is written with one key decorator, a decorator per relation, `paginate`, `@transactional` and generated migrations…
rows.summary: of the default database; an `Err` result or a thrown error rolls it back, an `Ok` commits it.
body: **Transactions are `@transactional` on a use case's `exec`.** Every repository call inside it joins one transaction
of the default database; an `Err` result or a thrown error rolls it back, an `Ok` commits it. The repositories of the
runtimes read the open transaction, so nothing else changes in the code.
```nuclear
usecase MoveTasks(tasks: TaskRepository, projects: ProjectRepository)
@transactional
exec(from: int, to: int) Result<Error, int>
~projects.find(to)
moved = ~tasks.where({ "projectId": from }).update({ "projectId": to })
Ok(moved)

rows.title: ADR-0001: Backend data is written with one key decorator, a decorator per relation, `paginate`, `@transactional` and generated migrations…
rows.summary: 1. A decorator for the key and one per relation, explicit loading — chosen.
body: 1. **A decorator for the key and one per relation, explicit loading** — chosen.
2. **The key and the relations deduced from types and names** (`id` is the key, a field of an entity type is a
relation): less to write, but it needs deduction rules to learn, and the user prefers the explicit form.
3. **A kind by folder for repositories and controllers, with paths from the name**: the kinds stay as they are.
4. **Lazy or eager loading by default**: hidden queries and N+1, against the golden rule (ADR-lang-0001).
5. **Cursor pagination first**: offset pages are what most APIs and the mobile `Page<T>` use; cursors can come later.
6. **umzug for the nestjs migrations**: not needed, `SequelizeMeta` and `queryInterface` are enough.

rows.title: 004 — Backend parity: what a real API needs that the backend platform lacks — 1. Diagnosis
rows.summary: Today a backend is a CRUD over one table per repository with SQLite (Postgres, MySQL and MariaDB are connections but were never run), events and AI agents.
body: Today a backend is a CRUD over one table per repository with SQLite (Postgres, MySQL and MariaDB are connections
but were never run), events and AI agents. It has no relations, no migrations, no transactions, no pagination, no
authentication, no scheduled work, no uploads, no deploy file, no metrics; its CLI builds and tests but cannot
generate a kind, check a project or rebuild on save. A real API needs all of that in its first week.

rows.title: 004 — Backend parity: what a real API needs that the backend platform lacks — F1 — Relations between entities
rows.summary: DONE 2026-11-10 as ADR-backend-0001 (relations); the example below is the first idea, the delivered form is in the ADR.
body: DONE 2026-11-10 as ADR-backend-0001 (relations); the example below is the first idea, the delivered form is in the ADR.
```nuclear
@entity("projects")
entity Project()
@generated()
id: int
name: string
@hasMany(Task)                     // Project.tasks: Task[]
tasks: Task[]
@entity("tasks")
entity Task()
@generated()
id: int
title: string
@belongsTo(Project)                // the column project_id, the field Task.project
project: Project
Repositories load a relation on demand, never by default:
```nuclear
repository ProjectRepository
withTasks(id: int) Result<NotFound, Project>
where({ "id": id })
include("tasks")
getOne()
| | fastapi (SQLAlchemy 2) | nestjs (sequelize-typescript) |
| `@hasMany(Task)` | `relationship("Task", back_populates="project")` | `@HasMany(() => Task)` |
| `@belongsTo(Project)` | `project_id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(ForeignKey("projects.id"))` + `relationship` | `@ForeignKey(() => Project) projectId` + `@BelongsTo(() => Project)` |
| `include("tasks")` | `selectinload(Project.tasks)` | `include: [Task]` |

rows.title: 004 — Backend parity: what a real API needs that the backend platform lacks — F2 — Migrations
rows.summary: DONE 2026-11-10: the delivered form is ADR-backend-0001, migrations (`migrations/` kept with the sources, not `build/`; nestjs without umzug).
body: DONE 2026-11-10: the delivered form is ADR-backend-0001, migrations (`migrations/` kept with the sources, not `build/`; nestjs
without umzug). The example below is the first idea.
Today `createTables = true` creates tables at start (development only). A real database changes by migrations:
```sh
nuclear migrate make "add done to tasks"     # compares the entities with the migrations folder, writes one
nuclear migrate                              # applies the pending ones
nuclear migrate down                         # reverts the last one
The migration is written in the dialect's tool (Alembic for `fastapi`, umzug + Sequelize for `nestjs`), under
`build/migrations/`, from the diff between the entities and the last migration; the user never writes SQL for
the common cases (a column, a table, an index, a relation). `SQLite(createTables = true)` stays for tests.
Done when: the check scripts run `migrate make` + `migrate` on a fresh SQLite and the tests pass against it.

rows.title: 004 — Backend parity: what a real API needs that the backend platform lacks — F3 — Transactions
rows.summary: DONE 2026-11-10 as ADR-backend-0001 (transactions); the example below is the first idea, the delivered form is in the ADR.
body: DONE 2026-11-10 as ADR-backend-0001 (transactions); the example below is the first idea, the delivered form is in the ADR.
Several repositories in one unit of work:
```nuclear
usecase MoveTask(tasks: TaskRepository, projects: ProjectRepository)
@transactional
exec(taskId: int, projectId: int) Result<AppError, Task>
project = ~projects.find(projectId)
task = ~tasks.find(taskId)
~projects.touch(project.id)
~tasks.save(task.copyWith(project = project))
`@transactional` on `exec`: the use case runs inside one transaction of the default database; an `Err` or a
thrown error rolls it back. (`fastapi`: `async with session.begin()`; `nestjs`: `sequelize.transaction` + CLS
namespace so repositories pick it up.) Done when: a test asserts a failed second write leaves the first undone.

rows.title: 004 — Backend parity: what a real API needs that the backend platform lacks — F4 — Pagination
rows.summary: DONE 2026-11-10 as ADR-backend-0001 (pagination); the example below is the first idea, the delivered form is in the ADR.
body: DONE 2026-11-10 as ADR-backend-0001 (pagination); the example below is the first idea, the delivered form is in the ADR.
`Page<T>` exists in the mobile platform (`shared/models/page.nuc` of the example). The backend gets it as a
platform model and repositories a `paginate`:
```nuclear
repository TaskRepository
page(page: int, size: int = 20) Page<Task>
orderBy("id")
paginate(page, size)             // Page<Task>: items, page, size, total, pages
A controller returns it as is; the contract (spec 003) carries `Page<Task>` so the mobile `Page<T>` is generated,
not written. Done when: `tasks_api` has a paged route in both dialects.

rows.title: 004 — Backend parity: what a real API needs that the backend platform lacks — F5 — Authentication, sessions and guards
rows.summary: Mobile has `Session`, ACL and `guard`.
body: Mobile has `Session`, ACL and `guard`. The backend gets the server side of the same words:
```nuclear
// config/project_config.nuc
appConfig ProjectConfig
connections: Connection[] = [SQLite(file = "app.sqlite")]
auth: Auth = Jwt(secret = env("JWT_SECRET"), expires = Duration(hours = 12))
// api/tasks_controller.nuc
@controller("tasks")
controller TasksController(tasks: TasksAppComponent)
@post
@auth                                 // 401 without a valid token; `session` is the caller
create(body: NewTask, session: Session) Result<AppError, Task>
tasks.create(body, owner = session.userId)
@delete("{id}")
@auth(roles = ["admin"])              // 403 without the role
remove(id: int) Result<AppError, void>
tasks.remove(id)
// shared/guards/owner_guard.nuc
guard OwnerGuard(tasks: TaskRepository)
canActivate(session: Session, id: int) boolean
task = ~tasks.find(id)
task.ownerId == session.userId
`Jwt` issues and checks tokens (`POST /auth/login` is the app's own route that calls `auth.issue(userId, roles)`);
`Session(userId, roles, permissions)` is the platform model. `fastapi`: a dependency on the router; `nestjs`: a
guard + `@UseGuards`. Done when: the example has login, an authenticated route and a role-guarded route, tested in
both dialects.

rows.title: 004 — Backend parity: what a real API needs that the backend platform lacks — 4. Decided by the user (2026-11-10)
rows.summary: Reviewing the first draft of ADR-backend-0001 (which deduced keys and relations and gave kinds by folder), the user chose: database gives it), `@primary(length = 8)` (the app gives a code).
body: Reviewing the first draft of ADR-backend-0001 (which deduced keys and relations and gave kinds by folder), the user chose:
- **One key decorator, `@primary`, that takes what it needs as arguments**: `@primary(generated = true)` (the
database gives it), `@primary(length = 8)` (the app gives a code). `@generated` is gone, also on mobile.
- **Relations the TypeORM way** (the user's preference): `@manyToOne` (+ its column `<name>Id`), `@oneToMany`,
`@manyToMany` + `@joinTable`, `@oneToOne` + `@joinColumn`; loading explicit with `relations(...)`.
- Pagination as drafted (`paginate(page, size)` → `Page<T>`).
- **The kinds stay as they are**: no kind by folder for repositories and controllers, no default paths.
- **Transactions in the first step** (`@transactional` on `exec`); migrations are of the database schema, next.
