rows.title: ADR-0001: A project's manifest is `config.nuc`, it lists only third-party packages, and assets follow a convention — Consequences
rows.summary: editor too; the versions of the framework's own packages are never a project's concern; definitions are generated once and shared; a deleted asset leaves the app on the next build.
body: - Positive: a project holds no file of the target; the manifest is checked with the rest of the project, in the
editor too; the versions of the framework's own packages are never a project's concern; definitions are
generated once and shared; a deleted asset leaves the app on the next build.
- Negative: a package the framework uses cannot be listed nor pinned by a project. `nuclear defs show` does not see
a project's packages: a name that gets no import is debugged in `build/defs.lock` and the cache.

rows.title: ADR-0001: A project's manifest is `config.nuc`, it lists only third-party packages, and assets follow a convention — Context and problem
rows.summary: A project of the platform has only `.nuc` files and `assets/` (ADR-synapsis-0001): the app is generated in `build/app` and never edited.
body: A project of the platform has only `.nuc` files and `assets/` (ADR-synapsis-0001): the app is generated in `build/app`
and never edited. The app still needs a package manifest: its name and version, the packages it adds, their type
definitions for the transpiler and the editor, and its fonts, shaders and other assets. None of that may be a
hand-written file of the target.

rows.title: ADR-0001: A project's manifest is `config.nuc`, it lists only third-party packages, and assets follow a convention — Decision
rows.summary: new grammar: `app(name, description, version, usesMaterialDesign)`, `environment(sdk, flutter)`, `dependencies(package = "version")`, `devDependencies(...)`.
body: **The manifest is written in Nuclear.** `config.nuc`, at the project's root, with the language's call syntax and no
new grammar: `app(name, description, version, usesMaterialDesign)`, `environment(sdk, flutter)`,
`dependencies(package = "version")`, `devDependencies(...)`. It is not transpiled; it is checked with the project
(`N0303`). The mechanism is generic: the dialect's `[project.manifest] file, sections`. The same file carries the
platform and dialect line (ADR-synapsis-0002), the plugins (ADR-synapsis-0004) and the contracts of the backends the app reads
(ADR-synapsis-0006).
**Only third-party packages.** A project adds only packages the framework does not use: neither the dialect's (its
`defs`) nor the ones Synapsis adds (`[project.manifest] reserved`), which reach the app by themselves.
`nuclear add` rejects one before changing anything, and `config.nuc` marks it with `N0303` on its line in
`check`, `build` and the editor. A project without `config.nuc` gets one on its first `check` or `build`.

rows.title: ADR-0001: A project's manifest is `config.nuc`, it lists only third-party packages, and assets follow a convention — Decision
rows.summary: `nuclear flutter add`, ADR-lang-0008) adds it to `config.nuc` and to the app, and generates its type definitions with the Dart analyzer (`nuclearlang/tools/defs`) into a global cache, `~/.cache/nuclearlang/defs`, shared by projects.
body: **Every third-party package has type definitions.** `nuclear add <package>` (the same command as
`nuclear flutter add`, ADR-lang-0008) adds it to `config.nuc` and to the app, and generates its type definitions
with the Dart analyzer (`nuclearlang/tools/defs`) into a global cache, `~/.cache/nuclearlang/defs`, shared by
projects. `nuclear remove` removes it from the project and keeps the cached definitions. The project lists its
own in `build/defs.lock`; the language server loads them from there.
**No empty sections.** What is not used is not written: a new project has only `app(...)`. `add` creates
`dependencies` or `devDependencies` with its first package; `remove` deletes the section with its last one.
**Assets by convention.** `config.nuc` declares no assets. `assets/fonts/<Family>/` are fonts, with the weight and
the style taken from the end of the file's name (`Roboto-BoldItalic.ttf`); `assets/shaders/*.frag` are shaders; any
other folder of `assets/` is bundled. `nuclear build` rewrites `assets:`, `fonts:` and `shaders:` of the app's
pubspec on every build. Two fonts of a family with the same weight and style are an error. The project only adds:
no `dependency_overrides`.

rows.title: ADR-0001: A project's manifest is `config.nuc`, it lists only third-party packages, and assets follow a convention — References
rows.summary: (`nuclearlang/dialects/dart/docs/07-reference/flutter.md`).
body: - Rules: [project.md](../02-architecture/project.md); the sections one by one, the flutter reference §3.1 and §3.2
(`nuclearlang/dialects/dart/docs/07-reference/flutter.md`).
- Replaces: ADR-0065, ADR-0066, ADR-0069, ADR-0070, ADR-0071

rows.title: ADR-0002: A screen is declared with `@screen`, navigation belongs to the views, and dialogs and the splash come from the runtime —…
rows.summary: must be in its route.
body: - Positive: everything about a screen is in one place and a new need is a new argument; the domain cannot navigate.
- Negative: a screen whose route is nested is built from the address when a child is opened, so its parameters
must be in its route. `onLoad` has no timeout.

rows.title: ADR-0002: A screen is declared with `@screen`, navigation belongs to the views, and dialogs and the splash come from the runtime — Context…
rows.summary: A screen has an address, the state managers it provides, a session it may require, an access rule, a place in a tab bar, a way to come in.
body: A screen has an address, the state managers it provides, a session it may require, an access rule, a place in a
tab bar, a way to come in. An app also needs dialogs that look alike and a first screen that covers its start. The
project must say all of it in a few words, and the architecture must keep navigation out of the domain.

rows.title: ADR-0002: A screen is declared with `@screen`, navigation belongs to the views, and dialogs and the splash come from the runtime — Decision
rows.summary: `@screen(route = "/", providers = [...], loggedIn = { forward: LoginScreen }, acl = { roles, permissions, guards, forward }, shell = { widget, tab }, notFound, transition = ScreenTransition.fade)`.
body: **One extensible decorator for screens.**
`@screen(route = "/", providers = [...], loggedIn = { forward: LoginScreen }, acl = { roles, permissions, guards, forward }, shell = { widget, tab }, notFound, transition = ScreenTransition.fade)`.
Its objects use `:`, like every Nuclear object. `forward` is required in `loggedIn` and in `acl` (`N0217`).
**Routes: go_router, always from the views.** Never from managers or use cases: `BuildContext`, `GoRouter` and
`appRouter` are used only in a `stateless` or a `stateful` (`N0301`).
**A transition per screen.** `transition` takes `ScreenTransition.fade`, `slide`, `up`, `scale` or `none`; without
it, the platform's. It is an enum: the editor completes it and the target checks it, and the name `Transition`
would clash with bloc's class.
**Nested routes with their own back.** A route is nested in the route with the longest address that starts its
own (never `/`). Going to it stacks the parent below, also from a link, so back returns to the parent. Inside a
`shell` tab it stays in that tab. No argument says it: the address already does.

rows.title: ADR-0002: A screen is declared with `@screen`, navigation belongs to the views, and dialogs and the splash come from the runtime — Decision
rows.summary: warning and danger in the color and icon of the app's theme, the sizes small, medium and large, and localized Accept and Close.
body: **Dialogs.** `SynapsisDialog` is like a Bootstrap modal (header, body, footer), with the types info, success,
warning and danger in the color and icon of the app's theme, the sizes small, medium and large, and localized
Accept and Close. A dialog has an Accept button only with `onAccept`. `Popups.toast` and `Popups.snackbar` are for
messages that go away on their own.
**The splash comes in the package.** `SplashScreen` shows `child` for at least `minDuration` (3 s by default) and
until `onLoad` (the initial data) finishes; then it goes to `next` with the router. An error of `onLoad` shows
`onError` with `retry`; without `onError` it is logged and the app continues to `next`.
**The native splash is `@splash(color, image)`** on the splash screen. The project generates
`flutter_native_splash.yaml` and the CLI runs `flutter_native_splash:create` (Android, also 12+, iOS and web; on
Linux and Windows the window waits for the first frame). `startSynapsis()` removes the native splash on the first
frame; the route of the `@splash` screen is the initial one. Images in `assets/` are copied to the app.

rows.title: ADR-0002: A screen is declared with `@screen`, navigation belongs to the views, and dialogs and the splash come from the runtime — Options…
rows.summary: 1. `@route` + `@provider`, two decorators: replaced by the single `@screen`.
body: 1. `@route` + `@provider`, two decorators: replaced by the single `@screen`.
2. `transition = "fade"`, a text: no completion and no check until run time.
3. An explicit `parent` argument for nested routes: a second way to say what the address already says.

rows.title: ADR-0002: A screen is declared with `@screen`, navigation belongs to the views, and dialogs and the splash come from the runtime —…
rows.summary: with `onAccept`, a transition per screen, nested routes.
body: - An async guard and the router: [ADR-mobile-0007](0007-accepted-rules-of-events-guards-forms-and-state.md).
- Behaviour: [runtime.md](../02-architecture/runtime.md); API: [synapsis.md §6](../07-reference/synapsis.md).
- Of the eleven rules accepted together, this ADR holds four: `forward` required in `acl`, the Accept button only
with `onAccept`, a transition per screen, nested routes.
- Replaces: ADR-0055, ADR-0057, ADR-0059, ADR-0061, ADR-0063, ADR-0085

rows.title: ADR-0003: JSON is generated from the model: `@key` names a field and a `converter` reads and writes a value — Consequences
rows.summary: everywhere.
body: - Positive: a model stays a list of fields; a converter is written once, in `shared/converters/`, and is visible
everywhere.
- Negative: a model has a `part` file and the app needs `build_runner`. The same holds for an `event`, which
carries the same mapping ([ADR-mobile-0007](0007-accepted-rules-of-events-guards-forms-and-state.md)): a field
that is not a JSON type is an error of `build_runner`, not of the transpiler.

rows.title: ADR-0003: JSON is generated from the model: `@key` names a field and a `converter` reads and writes a value — Context and problem
rows.summary: A model in Nuclear is only its definition; reading it from and writing it to JSON is not business logic and must not be written by hand.
body: A model in Nuclear is only its definition; reading it from and writing it to JSON is not business logic and must
not be written by hand. Two things the definition alone cannot say: a field whose name in the JSON is not its name
in the model, and a value whose JSON form is not its type's (a date as text, an address as a string).

rows.title: ADR-0003: JSON is generated from the model: `@key` names a field and a `converter` reads and writes a value — Decision
rows.summary: generated code.
body: **`json_serializable` + `build_runner`.** The transpiler writes the annotations and the `part`; the mapping is
generated code.
**`@key("json_name")`** on a model's field is its name in the JSON (in Dart, `@JsonKey(name:)`).
**A converter is a kind.** `converter Name` with `fromJson(json: J) T` and `toJson(value: T) J` (in Dart, a
`JsonConverter<T, J>`; the types are taken from the signature of `fromJson`). A field uses it with `@Name`. In
Dart, a PascalCase decorator without arguments is a call to its const constructor (`@Name` → `@Name()`).

rows.title: ADR-0003: JSON is generated from the model: `@key` names a field and a `converter` reads and writes a value — References
rows.summary: References
body: - A converter's optional `sample()` for the generated tests: [ADR-mobile-0004](0004-tests-in-nuclear.md).
- Generic models (`Page<T>`): ADR-synapsis-0005.
- Replaces: ADR-0044, ADR-0064

rows.title: ADR-0004: Tests are written in Nuclear, and the build generates the standard ones — Consequences
rows.summary: the twins of the local database are checked without a request (ADR-mobile-0006).
body: - Positive: the tests of an app are in the language of the app; what the framework writes, the framework tests;
the twins of the local database are checked without a request
([ADR-mobile-0006](0006-local-database.md)).
- Negative: a converter of a type the tests cannot invent needs a `sample()` to be covered.

rows.title: ADR-0004: Tests are written in Nuclear, and the build generates the standard ones — Context and problem
rows.summary: A project has only `.nuc` files, so its tests cannot be files of the target.
body: A project has only `.nuc` files, so its tests cannot be files of the target. And a large part of an app's tests is
the same in every app: a model reads its JSON, a repository sends the request it declares, a route asks for a
session or a permission, a screen opens.

rows.title: ADR-0004: Tests are written in Nuclear, and the build generates the standard ones — Decision
rows.summary: `@mock`, `@test`, `@states` (bloc_test) and `@widget`; mocks with mocktail.
body: **Tests are kinds.** `tests` (folder `test/`) and `integration` (folder `integration_test/`, on a device), with
`@mock`, `@test`, `@states` (bloc_test) and `@widget`; mocks with mocktail. A method without a decorator is the
group's setUp or tearDown; `X.m()` in a test is the injected `X`; a `Result` does not propagate in a test.
**The build generates the standard tests**: of the models (their JSON), the repositories (the http contract), the
routes (session and ACL) and the screens.
**The values of a generated test.** An enum field of a model gets its first value (`Plan.values.first.name`). A
field with a converter gets the JSON the converter writes for a value the tests can make; for a type the tests
cannot invent, the converter's optional `sample() T` gives the value; without it, the field gets `null`.

rows.title: ADR-0004: Tests are written in Nuclear, and the build generates the standard ones — References
rows.summary: synapsis.md §7.
body: - What runs where: [testing.md](../05-standards/testing.md); the test helpers of the runtime:
[synapsis.md §7](../07-reference/synapsis.md).
- Of the eleven rules accepted together, this ADR holds one: the values of a generated test.
- Replaces: ADR-0049, ADR-0085

rows.title: ADR-0005: A log is a readable block by component, and the transpiler writes where it was called — Consequences
rows.summary: Consequences
body: - Positive: a log costs no more than its text; its place is the source's, not the generated file's.
- Negative: the call site exists only in a dialect that declares `[call_site]`.

rows.title: ADR-0005: A log is a readable block by component, and the transpiler writes where it was called — Context and problem
rows.summary: A log must say at a glance which component wrote it and from which line of the `.nuc` file, for a person and for an agent that reads the console as text.
body: A log must say at a glance which component wrote it and from which line of the `.nuc` file, for a person and for
an agent that reads the console as text. Finding the caller at run time costs time on every log and gives the
generated file's line, not the source's.

rows.title: ADR-0005: A log is a readable block by component, and the transpiler writes where it was called — Decision
rows.summary: `Log.d/i/s/w/e` write a block with a breadcrumb (`component › kind › Class.method`), the time, the message, the data as JSON and, at the foot, the `.nuc` file and line.
body: `Log.d/i/s/w/e` write a block with a breadcrumb (`component › kind › Class.method`), the time, the message, the
data as JSON and, at the foot, the `.nuc` file and line.
**The transpiler writes the breadcrumb in each call as a constant** (the dialect's `[call_site]`): no cost at run
time and no stack reading.
Each component has a stable pastel color (xterm-256); its `config` changes it with `logColor`. A thick frame and a
level badge use the colors of Bootstrap's dark-mode alerts; the breadcrumb and the data use code colors;
Synapsis's own logs are purple. Only the exact place of an error blinks.
Flutter exceptions use their own format: a double red frame, a `✖ EXCEPTION` bar, the stack in columns with the
app's frames highlighted.
A log is readable without colors (`Log.colors = false`), for people and agents.

rows.title: ADR-0005: A log is a readable block by component, and the transpiler writes where it was called — Options considered
rows.summary: 1. Reading the stack at run time to find the caller: rejected.
body: 1. Reading the stack at run time to find the caller: rejected.
2. The breadcrumb written by the transpiler as a constant: chosen.

rows.title: ADR-0005: A log is a readable block by component, and the transpiler writes where it was called — References
rows.summary: References
body: - Behaviour, levels and masking: [runtime.md](../02-architecture/runtime.md), [security.md](../05-standards/security.md).
- Replaces: ADR-0078

rows.title: ADR-0006: The local database is the backend's ORM on the device: `@primary` models, `@repository(saveLocal)` and `<method>AsLocal()` —…
rows.summary: device; a local-only repository without a new kind; generated tests that check each twin answers without a request.
body: - Positive: offline reading with two words (`saveLocal = true`, `@primary`); the backend's query vocabulary on the
device; a local-only repository without a new kind; generated tests that check each twin answers without a
request.
- Negative:
- a GET that answers a model without `@primary` under `saveLocal` fails at its first call with a `StateError`
that names the fix (the generated tests catch it; there is no compile-time diagnostic);
- `local = false` on a method does not opt out of `saveLocal` (templates compare no values);
- `isNull` of the backend is not a mobile operator: the word is the `flutter_test` matcher already in the
dialect's auto-imports, so a `[functions]` shortcut is refused by `N0204`;
- `hive_ce` keeps a box in memory: a table is for the data a phone shows, not for millions of rows;
- `@created` / `@updated` are ISO-8601 texts; a backend entity's `@column` options (`length`, `unique`, `index`)
have no equivalent in a document store;
- turning `encrypted` on or off after the first run needs the tables cleared (a box is read with the cipher it
was written with);
- on web the key lives in the browser's storage, weaker than a phone's keystore.

rows.title: ADR-0006: The local database is the backend's ORM on the device: `@primary` models, `@repository(saveLocal)` and `<method>AsLocal()` —…
rows.summary: The mobile platform needed the ORM the backend platform has (ADR-python-0002, ADR-typescript-0001: an entity with `@primary`, `@created`, `@updated`, a repository with CRUD and the query builder), but 100 % local: a secure database on the device, automated through the `repository` kind.
body: The mobile platform needed the ORM the backend platform has (ADR-python-0002, ADR-typescript-0001: an entity with `@primary`,
`@created`, `@updated`, a repository with CRUD and the query builder), but 100 % local: a secure database on the
device, automated through the `repository` kind. With `@repository(saveLocal = true)` the transpiler creates the
table from the model a GET answers, saves every answer in it, asks for the minimum of annotations on the model, and
writes for each method a twin that answers from the device instead of the network; one method can turn it on by
itself.
Constraints: the mobile `repository` is http calls, not tables, so the two kinds cannot be merged (ADR-synapsis-0004);
the Nuclear of a project never names the storage engine; the runtime must work on web; the compiler stays generic.

rows.title: ADR-0006: The local database is the backend's ORM on the device: `@primary` models, `@repository(saveLocal)` and `<method>AsLocal()` —…
rows.summary: `find`, `findAll`, `save`, `saveAll`, `remove`, `clear`, and the backend's query builder: `where({ "age": gt(18) })` with `gt`, `gte`, `lt`, `lte`, `ne`, `like`, `ilike`, `oneOf`, `between` (a plain `null` is "is null", `ne(null)` "is not null"), `orderBy(field, desc)`, `limit`, `offset`,…
body: **The table is the ORM.** `local<Character>()` in a repository (and `Character.table` anywhere) is a `LocalTable`:
`find`, `findAll`, `save`, `saveAll`, `remove`, `clear`, and the backend's query builder: `where({ "age": gt(18) })`
with `gt`, `gte`, `lt`, `lte`, `ne`, `like`, `ilike`, `oneOf`, `between` (a plain `null` is "is null", `ne(null)`
"is not null"), `orderBy(field, desc)`, `limit`, `offset`, `getOne`, `getMany`, `paginate` → `Page<T>`, `count`,
`exists`, `update`, `delete`. A repository method with a body writes its queries on it, so a repository can be
100 % local.
**The engine is `hive_ce`, behind the runtime, one database for every platform.** Pure Dart: a file per box on
Android, iOS, Linux, macOS and Windows, IndexedDB on web. Rows are JSON text (the model's `toJson` / `fromJson`,
nested objects intact); in memory and unencrypted in tests. **Encryption is a setting of the config files:**
`local: LocalDatabase = LocalDatabase(encrypted = true)` in `appConfig` (the project) and in a component's `config`
(the tables of its models). The default is encrypted: AES-256, a key generated once and kept in the secure storage
(Keychain, Keystore, libsecret, DPAPI, WebCrypto). Nothing generated names hive: the dialect writes `LocalTable`,
`Local`, `LocalDatabase`, `send(local:)`, `recall`, so the engine can change in the package without touching the
transpiler or any `.nuc`.

rows.title: ADR-0006: The local database is the backend's ORM on the device: `@primary` models, `@repository(saveLocal)` and `<method>AsLocal()` —…
rows.summary: field of the returned model with that decorator) and `field_decor` of each declaration in the project context, plus `{{#a or b}}` in templates (the first alternative that is true).
body: **Two generic template variables, no kind name in the compiler:** `ret_info.fields_decor.<decorator>` (the first
field of the returned model with that decorator) and `field_decor` of each declaration in the project context, plus
`{{#a or b}}` in templates (the first alternative that is true). Everything else is TOML, templates and the
package.

rows.title: ADR-0006: The local database is the backend's ORM on the device: `@primary` models, `@repository(saveLocal)` and `<method>AsLocal()` —…
rows.summary: `@primary(generated = true)` for a key the table gives (an auto-increment: the field is `T?`; ADR-backend-0001), `@created` and `@updated` for stamps the table writes, `@entity("characters")` for the table's name (default: the model's name in snake_case; the box is `synapsis_<name>`).
body: **A model with `@primary` has a local table.** The same words as a backend entity: `@primary` on the key field,
`@primary(generated = true)` for a key the table gives (an auto-increment: the field is `T?`; ADR-backend-0001),
`@created` and `@updated` for stamps the table writes, `@entity("characters")` for the table's name (default: the
model's name in snake_case; the box is `synapsis_<name>`). `@column` has no meaning in a document store (the JSON
name, `@key`, is the column) and is not part of the platform. The dialect writes
`static final LocalTable<M> table` in the model and registers it at startup with its component.
**`@repository(saveLocal = true)`, or `@get(local = true)` on one method.** A GET that answers a model with a table
(or a list of them; not `Page<Character>`, which has no key) passes `local: 'Repo.method'` to `send`: the decoded
rows go to the model's table and a calls table remembers which rows that call (url and query) answered. The
transpiler writes the twin **`<method>AsLocal()`**, with the same signature and return type, which reads those rows
as they are now (`recall`) and never sends a request; without a previous answer it is `Err(E(message))` for a
`Result` method and a thrown `NotFound` otherwise.

rows.title: ADR-0006: The local database is the backend's ORM on the device: `@primary` models, `@repository(saveLocal)` and `<method>AsLocal()` —…
rows.summary: 1. Isar: v3 is unmaintained against current Flutter, v4 unfinished.
body: 1. **Isar**: v3 is unmaintained against current Flutter, v4 unfinished.
2. **Drift / sqflite / sqlite3**: real SQL and SQLCipher, but web needs a wasm bundle and a worker copied into
every app, and drift adds its own code generation per table on top of json_serializable; the backend's query
vocabulary is covered without SQL at mobile sizes.
3. **Hive v2**: frozen. `hive_ce` is its maintained fork with the same API, pure Dart, web and encryption built in:
chosen.
4. **sembast**: queries built in, but no encryption without a third package.
5. **An `entity` kind in mobile**: a second kind for the same model doubled every model (an http model and a table
model); the minimum of annotations on the model the GET returns was asked for.
6. **A twin that reads the table by the method's parameters** (`getOne(id)` → `find(id)`): right only when a
parameter is the key; `search(name)` or `getPage(page)` would need a mapping per method. Remembering which rows
each call answered works for every signature and still returns fresh rows.
7. **A plugin `local`**, with the package added only when used: `hive_ce` is pure Dart and small; a plugin would
add a line to `config.nuc` for a feature two annotations already declare.

rows.title: ADR-0007: Guards may be async, an event travels between engines as JSON, and the names of the session's events, translations, form checks…
rows.summary: with a typed event.
body: - Positive: a guard may ask a server without changing the sync ones; a background task reaches the app's screens
with a typed event.
- Negative: an `event` has a `part` file and needs `build_runner`, like a model
([ADR-mobile-0003](0003-json-models-names-and-converters.md)); an event field that is not a JSON type is an error
of `build_runner`. `canActivate` of a `Guard` written by hand in Dart may return `bool` or `Future<bool>`.

rows.title: ADR-0007: Guards may be async, an event travels between engines as JSON, and the names of the session's events, translations, form checks…
rows.summary: Eleven rules of the platform were accepted together.
body: Eleven rules of the platform were accepted together. Those about screens, routes and dialogs are in
[ADR-mobile-0002](0002-screens-routes-dialogs-and-splash.md) and the one about generated tests in
[ADR-mobile-0004](0004-tests-in-nuclear.md). This ADR holds the six that belong to the services those two do not
cover: access, events, session, translations, forms and state.
Two of them answer a real limit. A guard that asks a server cannot answer at once, but most guards can, and views
and use cases must not all wait because of a few. And an event published from another engine (a background task of
workmanager) cannot be sent as an object: Flutter engines share no objects.

rows.title: ADR-0007: Guards may be async, an event travels between engines as JSON, and the names of the session's events, translations, form checks…
rows.summary: router waits for it (its `redirect` stays sync when no guard is async); `AclBuilder` shows `fallback` until it answers; an async use case with `@acl` uses `Guards.verify`; `Acl.check` is the version of `Acl.can` that waits.
body: **Async guards.** `Guard.canActivate()` returns `FutureOr<bool>`; with `~` in its body it is `Future<bool>`. The
router waits for it (its `redirect` stays sync when no guard is async); `AclBuilder` shows `fallback` until it
answers; an async use case with `@acl` uses `Guards.verify`; `Acl.check` is the version of `Acl.can` that waits.
The sync `Acl.can`, `Acl.canOpen` and `Guards.check` throw a clear error with an async guard.
**Events from another engine.** The `event` kind writes `fromJson` / `toJson` (json_serializable) and `eventName`.
From a background isolate, an event with a name travels as its name and its JSON text, and `Events.decoder`,
registered at startup with the models, reads it back. So the fields of an event are JSON types.
**The session's events.** `GlobalEvents` uses `sessionStarted` and `sessionEnded` (and `onSessionEnded`).
**Translations use `.tr()`.**
**`@validate("field")` takes the field as text**; a bare name is `N0106`.
**Each state model generates its own `<Model>Builder<Manager>`**, not a generic `StateBuilder<Manager>`.

body: 1. Making every guard async: it would force every view and every use case to wait, also for the sync guards.
2. Sending event objects between engines: only JSON-like values travel.

rows.title: ADR-0001: The web platform is the mobile platform in a browser, and its first dialect is `react` — Consequences
rows.summary: minus Flutter's widgets); "three platforms" is true; there is one platform reference more.
body: - Positive: a web app is made from the mobile example in an afternoon (the `characters` example is the mobile one
minus Flutter's widgets); "three platforms" is true; there is one platform reference more.
- Positive: the `nuclear` command gets web projects through the dialect's `[toolchain]` (`nuclear new -p web -d
react`, `build` through `nuclear build .`).
- Negative: no forms, converters, translations, local database, plugins or AI kinds yet; no generated tests file.
- Negative: `@acl(guards)` only in a use case that awaits something (`Guards.verify` is asynchronous).
- Negative: a view's arguments must be named (a positional call to a view is written as positional).
- Negative: `useManager` and `useStateOf` are hooks, so only in `build`.
- Negative: the generated app was not run in a real browser.

rows.title: ADR-0001: The web platform is the mobile platform in a browser, and its first dialect is `react` — Context and problem
rows.summary: Synapsis names three platforms (ADR-synapsis-0002); `web` had no dialect, so "three platforms" was only a promise.
body: Synapsis names three platforms (ADR-synapsis-0002); `web` had no dialect, so "three platforms" was only a promise. The
user asked for the first web dialect to be built on what the mobile platform already does, so the knowledge of one
platform carries to the other, and for an analysis of a simpler design on top of React's own ecosystem.

rows.title: ADR-0001: The web platform is the mobile platform in a browser, and its first dialect is `react` — Decision
rows.summary: use for them: `stateless` / `stateful` (parameters are props, `build() Element`), `appConfig` / `config`, `repository` with the http decorators, `usecase` / `appcomponent` / `service` / `aggregate`, state models and `statemanager` with `@stateModel` / `@state` / `@before` / `@after`,…
body: **The web platform is the mobile platform in a browser.** The same kinds with the same words where a browser has a
use for them: `stateless` / `stateful` (parameters are props, `build() Element`), `appConfig` / `config`,
`repository` with the http decorators, `usecase` / `appcomponent` / `service` / `aggregate`, state models and
`statemanager` with `@stateModel` / `@state` / `@before` / `@after`, `@screen(route, providers, loggedIn, acl,
notFound)`, `event` and `component` with `@on`, `guard`, `tests` with `@test` / `@states` / `@widget` / `@mock`.
The contract is `platform.toml`; the rules are `docs/07-reference/web.md`. Forms, converters, translations, the
local database, plugins and AI are left out of the first version: they come with the mobile words.

rows.title: ADR-0001: The web platform is the mobile platform in a browser, and its first dialect is `react` — Decision
rows.summary: 19 without JSX, React Router 7, Vite 7, Vitest 4 + jsdom + Testing Library.
body: **The first dialect is `react`** (`nuclearlang/dialects/typescript/frameworks/react/`, extends `typescript`): React
19 **without JSX**, React Router 7, Vite 7, Vitest 4 + jsdom + Testing Library. Nuclear has no JSX: elements are
the runtime's HTML functions (`div(className = ..., children = [...])`) and views are called like functions. A view
is a class (`StatelessView` / `StatefulView`) shown through `createElement`, so hooks work inside `build` and a
`stateful` keeps its fields between renders (`setState`, `initState`, `dispose`), the way a Flutter `State` does. A
state model generates a `<Model>Builder` component; `@screen(providers)` wraps the screen in `Providers`, and
`Manager.method()` inside its views is `this.manager(Manager).method()` (no hook in a callback).
**The runtime is `packages/synapsis-web`** (npm `synapsis-web`, ESM): `Result`, the injector, configuration and
the `Http` connection, `Repository` over fetch (cache, retries, `result` / `attempt`), `StateManager`, the view
bases and hooks, the HTML functions, events, session / ACL / guards, the router (`buildRouter`, `goTo`, `goBack`),
`Log`, and `synapsis-web/testing` (`SynapsisTest` with canned fetch, `mock` / `when` / `verify`, `renderScreen`,
`statesOf`). Its type definitions and those of React, React Router, Vitest and Testing Library are in
`nuclearlang/dialects/typescript/defs/`.

rows.title: ADR-0001: The web platform is the mobile platform in a browser, and its first dialect is `react` — Decision
rows.summary: declaration of that kind is built when called: a view is a function call, not `new`), and named arguments to a kind with `named_params` stay one object in a dialect whose named arguments are an object, instead of being reordered by position.
body: **Two generic emitter rules came with it, with no kind name in Rust:** `[kinds.<k>.syntax] construct` (how a
declaration of that kind is built when called: a view is a function call, not `new`), and named arguments to a kind
with `named_params` stay one object in a dialect whose named arguments are an object, instead of being reordered by
position.
**It is checked** by `checks/react-check/check.sh` (the runtime's `tsc`, the example built, `tsc --strict`, vitest,
`vite build`, the runtime's vitest) and the golden `examples/expected/characters/`.
**The platform's words stay; the dialect may use the ecosystem underneath where it costs no word.** They are what
makes mobile and web code read the same and what the agents already know. Open to the user: zod + react-hook-form
for `form`; zustand as the engine of `StateManager` (the same Nuclear, selectors for free) if the builder's
re-render cost shows up; TanStack Query only as an opt-in for a `repository` method (`@get(query = true)` → a
`useX` hook) once a real app asks for background refetch. JSX stays out.

rows.title: ADR-0001: The web platform is the mobile platform in a browser, and its first dialect is `react` — Options considered
rows.summary: 1. The mobile platform's words, written by a React dialect — chosen.
body: 1. **The mobile platform's words, written by a React dialect** — chosen.
2. **A web platform designed from React up** (hooks, stores, JSX as the kinds): the Nuclear of a web app would
share nothing with a mobile one; the user asked for the opposite.
3. **react-native as the first web dialect**: it is a mobile dialect (ADR-synapsis-0002 lists it under mobile).
4. **Vue or Angular first**: React has the largest ecosystem, and the type definitions came from `@types/react`
with the existing generator; the platform's contract is ready for them.
5. **A `.tsx` output with JSX**: it needs JSX in Nuclear (a parser change for one dialect) or a second syntax for
views.
What the first version copies from mobile, and what React's libraries would replace, piece by piece:

rows.title: ADR-0001: The web platform is the mobile platform in a browser, and its first dialect is `react` — Options considered
rows.summary: Options considered
body: | `form` + `formmanager` (not in the first version) | **react-hook-form** + **zod** | the standard of the ecosystem; the validation rules (`@required`, `@email`...) map to a zod schema one to one | none: the recommended path (the Nuclear stays the mobile `form` words; the dialect writes a zod schema and a `useForm`) |

| HTML functions without JSX | JSX in `.tsx` | what every React developer reads | Nuclear would need JSX in the parser, which never changes per dialect, or a template string; the functions keep Nuclear's call syntax, the same the mobile widgets use |
| `Providers` + `this.manager(X)` (context) | zustand stores are global: no provider | less wiring | a store per screen instance (a detail opened twice) needs a factory anyway |

| `goTo(Screen, params)` | react-router's `<Link>` / `useNavigate` with paths | idiomatic | navigation by address breaks when a route changes; the mobile platform navigates by screen on purpose (ADR-mobile-0002) |
| `tests` with `SynapsisTest` + `@mock` | MSW for http, vitest mocks | the ecosystem's tools | `SynapsisTest.respond` is MSW's role with no package; `@mock` already uses `vi.fn` |

rows.title: ADR-0001: The web platform is the mobile platform in a browser, and its first dialect is `react` — Options considered
rows.summary: Options considered
body: | Mobile piece (copied) | React's alternative | Gain | Cost |

| `statemodel` + `statemanager` + `<Model>Builder` (a Cubit) | a **zustand** store: `create((set) => ({ characters: [], load: async (page) => set({ ... }) }))` and `useStore((s) => s.characters)` in the view | less generated code (no builder, no status enum), selectors re-render only what changed, devtools | the state is a bag of fields, not a list of named states: `loading` / `full` / `error` become flags the view checks; the `@states` test (ordered states) loses its meaning; Nuclear would need a `store` kind, a new word for both platforms or a web-only one |

| `repository` with `cache` / `retry` / `purge` | **TanStack Query**: `useQuery({ queryKey, queryFn })` gives cache, retries, refetch and loading / error state in the view | removes the manager for read-only screens (the query's state is the screen's), background refetch | ties data fetching to the view (the platform keeps http in `data/` and state in `presentation/`); a use case between them has no place; mobile has nothing equivalent |

rows.title: ADR-0001: The `flutter` dialect is a framework: it generates the app over official libraries and the independent Dart package `synapsis` —…
rows.summary: Two questions are decided together: how much of a Flutter app is written in Nuclear, and where the code that Flutter itself lacks lives.
body: Two questions are decided together: how much of a Flutter app is written in Nuclear, and where the code that
Flutter itself lacks lives. The records this ADR replaces hold the decisions without their discussion.

rows.title: ADR-0001: The `flutter` dialect is a framework: it generates the app over official libraries and the independent Dart package `synapsis` —…
rows.summary: (`nuclear-synapsis-framework/platforms/mobile/packages/synapsis`), publishable on pub.dev and also usable by hand, without Nuclear; its API is `nuclear-synapsis-framework/platforms/mobile/docs/07-reference/synapsis.md`.
body: **`synapsis` is an independent Dart package.** What does not exist in Flutter lives in the package `synapsis`
(`nuclear-synapsis-framework/platforms/mobile/packages/synapsis`), publishable on pub.dev and also usable by
hand, without Nuclear; its API is
`nuclear-synapsis-framework/platforms/mobile/docs/07-reference/synapsis.md`. The `flutter` dialect generates code

rows.title: ADR-0001: The `flutter` dialect is a framework: it generates the app over official libraries and the independent Dart package `synapsis` —…
rows.summary: light clean architecture.
body: **The dialect minimizes Flutter.** Nuclear holds the business logic and the transpiler generates the app with a
light clean architecture. The layers exist in the generated Dart, not in Nuclear. The `flutter` dialect is the
dialect of the mobile platform (ADR-synapsis-0002): the platform says which kinds, decorators and folders exist; the
dialect (`nuclearlang/dialects/dart/frameworks/flutter/`) says how each is written in Dart, with its project
structure, architecture rules and tests (`nuclearlang/dialects/dart/docs/07-reference/flutter.md`).
**Official ecosystem libraries, not code of our own.** The generated app relies on `bloc` / `flutter_bloc`
(state), `json_serializable` / `json_annotation` (JSON), `get_it` (dependency injection) and `dio` (network).
Later decisions added, on the same rule, `fpdart` for `Result` (ADR-lang-0006) and `hive_ce` for the local database
(ADR-mobile-0006); the dialect also relies on `go_router` (routes), `connectivity_plus` and `flutter_secure_storage`.
**The Flutter CLI underneath.** The SDK, packages, builds and devices are handled by `flutter`; the `synapsis`
command calls it inside the generated app.

rows.title: ADR-0001: Python is a dialect made with the dialect system, and what it needs becomes generic emitter options — Context and problem
rows.summary: The user asked for a dialect with Python completely in its base, made with the dialect system, and with the type definitions of LangChain, LangGraph, FastAPI, Chroma, Postgres, Ollama and OpenAI by default.
body: The user asked for a dialect with Python completely in its base, made with the dialect system, and with the type
definitions of LangChain, LangGraph, FastAPI, Chroma, Postgres, Ollama and OpenAI by default. Python is the first
target whose blocks have no braces, whose lambdas are one expression and whose classes set their fields in
`__init__`. The plan for dialects (`nuclearlang/docs/04-specs/002-dialects-with-agents/`, D7) says such needs
become generic `[options]`, never a case of one language in the compiler.

rows.title: ADR-0001: Python is a dialect made with the dialect system, and what it needs becomes generic emitter options — Decision
rows.summary: never changes the language.
body: **Names.** The `.nuc` keeps Nuclear's `camelCase` (`nuclearlang/docs/07-reference/nuclear-base.md` §2.4): a dialect
never changes the language. `snake_case_names` writes the names in Python's `snake_case` (`getOne` → `get_one`):
the compiler renames the AST before emitting and keeps the names that exist as they are in the type definitions;
strings and map keys are data.
**Type definitions** come from the installed modules: `nuclearlang/tools/defs/python/gen.py` reads them with
`inspect`, from the virtual environment `nuclearlang/tools/python/.venv` pinned by
`nuclearlang/tools/python/requirements.txt`. `python@3.14` (the standard library; builtins implicit) for this
dialect, and for `fastapi`: pydantic, pydantic-settings, starlette, fastapi, sqlalchemy, asyncpg, redis, aiokafka,
openai, ollama, chromadb, langchain_core, langchain, langgraph, langchain_openai, langchain_ollama,
langchain_chroma and the runtime.

rows.title: ADR-0001: Python is a dialect made with the dialect system, and what it needs becomes generic emitter options — Decision
rows.summary: shared mutable defaults); a subclass without its own constructor keeps class defaults.
body: - `hoist_block_lambdas` + `local_function`: a lambda with a block becomes a local function before its statement.
- `init_fields` + `field_init`: constructor parameters and fields with a default are set in the constructor (no
shared mutable defaults); a subclass without its own constructor keeps class defaults.
- `super_ctor`; `doc_inside` (the doc comment goes to the template's `doc`).
- `interp_prefix` + `interp_brace_escape` (f-strings); `module_separator`; `toplevel_gap`; `file_prelude`
(`from __future__ import annotations`).
- `type_args_as_args`: `inject<Repo>()` → `inject(Repo)`.
- `builtin_result`: a child dialect uses a library's `Result`.
- `snake_case_names`.
- Template variables `names` (lambda parameters without types), `types` (function types), `items_list` (enums);
the filter `strip_suffix`.
- A named argument of a decorator is written with the dialect's `named_arg`. The scan of the words a file writes
reads f-string interpolations and `#` comments.
**`Result`.** The file's own runtime (`templates/result.tpl`), with explicit covariant type variables: a frozen
dataclass is invariant from Python 3.13 on because of `__replace__`.

(`redis.asyncio`).

`nuclear-synapsis-framework/platforms/backend/packages/synapsis-py`): the injector, the connections opened by the
app's lifespan, `create_app`, testing helpers (`running`, `client`, `FakeModel`, in-memory databases). The build
writes `app/main.py`, `tests/conftest.py` and `pyproject.toml`; the optional parts are plugins of `config.nuc` (old

rows.title: ADR-0002: The `fastapi` dialect writes the backend with FastAPI, SQLAlchemy 2 async, pydantic, LangChain and LangGraph — Decision

the same architecture as the mobile framework: components, `usecase` (one `exec` returning `Result`),
`appcomponent` (aliases through `inject`), `service`, `aggregate`, `config` / `appConfig`, architecture rules; kinds
by folder for `entity`, `model`, `state` and `tests`.
**Data.** The ORM is SQLAlchemy 2 async, decided with the user. An `entity` is a SQLAlchemy 2 table whose field
decorators are TypeORM's (`@entity`, `@primary`, `@column(...)`, `@created`, `@updated`; the generated key and the
relations are ADR-backend-0001's). A `repository` is `Repository[Entity]` with CRUD (`find`, `findAll`, `save`,

`Result`, `getMany`, `count`, `exists`, `update`, `delete`): the kind writes `q = self.query()` and

answered by a controller goes through `ResultInterceptor`.
**Messaging and AI.** kafkajs (`publish`, listeners with `@consumer`, missing topics created; without Kafka the
listeners of the process receive it) and ioredis (`cacheGet` / `cacheSet`); LangChain.js `tool` + zod schemas from
the parameters (`doc_text` / `doc_literal`), `createAgent`, LangGraph.js `StateGraph` over `Annotation.Root`,

`VectorStore` in the runtime.
**Type definitions of TypeScript.** `nuclearlang/tools/defs/typescript/gen.js` runs the TypeScript compiler over
the `.d.ts` files: the standard library (implicit) and NestJS, Sequelize, class-validator, class-transformer, RxJS
and the runtime. The order of `defs` decides a name two packages export (class-validator's `IsInt`, Nest's

rows.title: ADR-0001: One golden rule judges every proposal; Nuclear is modules and functions, not objects; the compiler writes the map of a project —…
rows.summary: A language made for AI agents and the people who work with them gets a constant flow of proposals: a rule, a shortcut, a kind for a framework.
body: A language made for AI agents and the people who work with them gets a constant flow of proposals: a rule, a
shortcut, a kind for a framework. Without one test for all of them the language grows two ways to write each thing.
The targets are object-oriented languages, but agents and readers work better with plain modules and functions. And
an agent that must read every file of a project to change one of them spends its context before it starts.

rows.title: ADR-0001: One golden rule judges every proposal; Nuclear is modules and functions, not objects; the compiler writes the map of a project —…
rows.summary: rule, a shortcut or a kind is accepted only if it respects the three: the generated code runs as fast as what an expert in the target would write, transpiling is immediate, and Nuclear code reads effortlessly.
body: **The golden rule.** Performance, speed and readability of the syntax, for the base language and every dialect. A
rule, a shortcut or a kind is accepted only if it respects the three: the generated code runs as fast as what an
expert in the target would write, transpiling is immediate, and Nuclear code reads effortlessly.
**Not object oriented.** Nuclear is like Elixir: components, modules and functions. It still has modules with
constructors and inheritance, only so that it transpiles to object-oriented languages.
**Generated context maps.** The compiler generates the context documentation of the code, so an agent goes to the
concrete code instead of reading all of it. Today it writes one map per project, `.nuclear/map.md`: every
declaration with its kind, its description (its doc comment) and its members, grouped by component, in Nuclear, the
same for every dialect of a platform.

rows.title: ADR-0002: Files are `.nuc`, blocks are two spaces, words for logic and symbols for arithmetic and bits — Consequences
rows.summary: form for each thing.

form for each thing.
- Negative: `%`, integer widths and rounding differ between targets; the editors' grammars (TextMate, tree-sitter)

rows.title: ADR-0002: Files are `.nuc`, blocks are two spaces, words for logic and symbols for arithmetic and bits — Context and problem
rows.summary: The lexical layer decides how many tokens a program costs and how often an agent hesitates between two forms.
body: The lexical layer decides how many tokens a program costs and how often an agent hesitates between two forms.
Nuclear also had to "have nothing to envy any language" in math, text, regular expressions, bytes and physics
without breaking its rules: the syntax lacked power, integer division, bitwise operators, shifts, binary and
scientific literals and raw text.

rows.title: ADR-0002: Files are `.nuc`, blocks are two spaces, words for logic and symbols for arithmetic and bits — Decision
body: **Extension.** Nuclear source files use `.nuc`.
**Indentation.** Two spaces, as in Elixir: fewer tokens, a common standard.
**Quotes and interpolation.** `"..."` and `'...'` are the same, also for interpolation and multi-line text (`"""`
or `'''`). Interpolation is `"${expr}"`, as in Dart.
**Comments.** A multi-line comment continues on lines that start with ` * `, the `*` right below the second `/` of
`//` (like `/** */`). A lone `*` is an empty line; `@example` code has more space after the `*`. A line indented
another way is N0021, with its fix. In the editor, Enter inside a comment adds the ` * ` and Enter on an empty ` * `
line ends it.
**Logical operators.** `and`, `or`, `not`. One form only: two forms would be ambiguous.
**Arithmetic and bitwise operators.** The same grammar for every dialect; each dialect writes them in
`[operators]`: `a ** b` (right associative, above unary minus: `-2 ** 2` is -4), `a ~/ b` (integer division,
Dart's token), `&`, `|`, `^`, `<<`, `>>`, `>>>`, and `^x` for the complement (`~` is await, as in Go). Precedence as
in Python and Dart: comparisons < `|` < `^` < `&` < shifts < `+`. Compound `%= &= |= ^= <<= >>= >>>=`. `>>` and
`>>>` are `>` tokens written together, joined by the parser, so `List<List<int>>` keeps working.
**Literals.** `0b1010`, `1.5e-3`, and raw text `r"\d+"` (no escapes nor interpolation), for regular expressions.

rows.title: ADR-0002: Files are `.nuc`, blocks are two spaces, words for logic and symbols for arithmetic and bits — Decision
rows.summary: negative), the integer width of bitwise operators (32 bits in TypeScript, 64 in Dart), the rounding of halves.
body: **Semantics that stay the target's**, documented: `%` (TypeScript keeps the dividend's sign, Dart is never
negative), the integer width of bitwise operators (32 bits in TypeScript, 64 in Dart), the rounding of halves.
**What the emitter gives the operator templates.** The operands' numeric kind (`int`/`double`, for Dart's `pow`
returning `num`) and bare operands (`left_arg`); `in` knows maps; `is` gets the type's info; `try` as the last line
is a value; a Dart top-level variable used by a declaration stays top-level; statements plus a `main` are N0113.
Every area of the library has one program in `examples/stdlib/` that prints the same output in every target, run by
`tools/stdlib-check.sh`. Which library those programs call is decided in ADR-lang-0009.

rows.title: ADR-0002: Files are `.nuc`, blocks are two spaces, words for logic and symbols for arithmetic and bits — Options considered
rows.summary: 1. `.nl` or `.nuclear` as the extension: rejected.
body: 1. `.nl` or `.nuclear` as the extension: rejected.
2. `&&`, `||`, `!`: rejected, one form only.
3. Words for the operators (`div`, `xor`, `shl`, as in Kotlin): more reserved words; C symbols are what every agent
knows.
4. `~x` for the complement: `~` is await.
5. Defining `%` the same in every target: either the Dart or the TypeScript output would stop being the expert's.

rows.title: ADR-0003: A function is a header plus a block, returns its last line when it declares a type, and awaits with `~` — Consequences
rows.summary: facade is one line per function (`list() = ListTasks.exec`).
body: - Positive: a function costs its name, its parameters and its body; async can never be forgotten or misplaced; a
facade is one line per function (`list() = ListTasks.exec`).
- Negative: `~` before a call that is not asynchronous is not reported yet and fails in Python
(`docs/01-product/roadmap.md`).

rows.title: ADR-0003: A function is a header plus a block, returns its last line when it declares a type, and awaits with `~` — Context and problem
rows.summary: Functions are most of a program.
body: Functions are most of a program. Every keyword they need (`function`, `return`, `async`, `await`) is a token an
agent pays in every file and a place where two styles appear.

rows.title: ADR-0003: A function is a header plus a block, returns its last line when it declares a type, and awaits with `~` — Decision
rows.summary: is no `fn`/`def` keyword (the "header + block" rule).
body: **No keyword.** A function is a header plus a block: `greet(x: string) string` followed by an indented body. There
is no `fn`/`def` keyword (the "header + block" rule).
**Implicit return.** The last line is returned only when the function declares a return type. It avoids returning
something by accident from `void` functions.
**Automatic async.** `async` is never written. A function that awaits another (`user = ~callUser()`) becomes async.
**Await with `~`.** `~` before a call awaits it: `users = ~getUsers.get()`. `@` is only for decorators.
**No nested functions.** Functions are not declared inside a body; an anonymous function assigned to a name is used
instead: `log = (message: string)` plus a block.
**One-line lambdas** are kept: `numbers.map(n => n * 2)`.
**Only explicit parameters.** Only the parameters written in the signature exist.
**Parameters between `{ }`** are optional in a signature; only Dart uses them (named parameters). Other dialects
ignore them.
**Generators.** `yield value` and `yield ...other()`; a function with `yield` is a generator (async when it uses
`~`); the return type is the type of each value.

rows.title: ADR-0003: A function is a header plus a block, returns its last line when it declares a type, and awaits with `~` — Decision
rows.summary: async).
body: **Function aliases.** `name() = Module.method`: `name` is the same function as `method` (same parameters, return,
async). A non-`static` method is called on a new `Module()`, whose constructor cannot have required parameters
(N0112). Only when the body is `Module.method` of a module of the file; otherwise the one-line form keeps its
meaning.

rows.title: ADR-0003: A function is a header plus a block, returns its last line when it declares a type, and awaits with `~` — Options considered
rows.summary: 1. A keyword before the function: rejected.
body: 1. A keyword before the function: rejected.
2. Returning the last line always, or never: rejected.
3. `await`, or `@` before the call: rejected.
4. Inferred parameters: existed and were removed.

rows.title: ADR-0003: A function is a header plus a block, returns its last line when it declares a type, and awaits with `~` — References

body: - `docs/07-reference/nuclear-base.md` §4.1, §4.1.1, §4.1.2, §6.4; `docs/02-architecture/result.md` (aliases).

rows.title: ADR-0004: A variable is an assignment, a block has its own scope, `if` and `match` are values, and there are no records nor `type` —…
rows.summary: built where it is used (`x = if ...`, `[a, if cond b]`).
body: - Positive: no declaration keyword to choose; a typo in a name is N0106 instead of a new variable; a value is
built where it is used (`x = if ...`, `[a, if cond b]`).

rows.title: ADR-0004: A variable is an assignment, a block has its own scope, `if` and `match` are values, and there are no records nor `type` —…
rows.summary: mutable when it is reassigned in its block); there is no `const`/`let`/`var` in Nuclear.
body: **Variables.** `x = 1` declares a variable. The transpiler decides whether it is a constant or mutable (it is
mutable when it is reassigned in its block); there is no `const`/`let`/`var` in Nuclear.
**Block scope and values.** A variable created inside `if`, `for`, `while`, `match` or `try` does not exist
outside (N0105). A name nothing defines is an error (N0106). `if` and `match` are values, as in Elixir:
**Map type.** `<Key, Value>` anywhere a type goes: `get(name: string) <string, string>`. A map value is always
written between `{ }`.
**No `type`.** It is not reserved and does not declare type aliases.
**No records.** Several values go in a map `<K, V>` or a list.
**Enum item without a value.** In a key-value enum, an item without a value takes its own name: `medium` →
`"medium"`.
**`x as T`, `x!`, `X<T>(...)`** are kept as in TypeScript and Dart. The `<` of a generic call goes right after the
name; with a space it is a comparison.
**Bounded generics.** `<T: Comparable>` (`:` means extends, as in inheritance).
**Cascades.** Lines that start with `..` below an expression; `..` on the same line is still a range.
**Destructuring.** Lists (`[a, ...rest] = xs`, `_` ignores) and maps (`{ a, "k": b } = m`), Elixir style with
TypeScript syntax: `...` instead of `|` (already union types and `match` alternatives). Names are all new or all
existing (N0107).

its constructor with as little noise as possible (`this.`, `new`, `private`, `@override`), also when its base is a
class of a library that is not in the file.

rows.title: ADR-0005: A module uses its members by name, has no visibility words, is constructed by calling its PascalCase name and inherits from…
rows.summary: member and the dialect adds `this`/`self` when the target needs it.
body: **Implicit `this`.** Inside a module, members are used by name; the resolver knows with certainty when a name is a
member and the dialect adds `this`/`self` when the target needs it. Less noise.
**No visibility modifiers.** No `private`, `public` or `protected`. Visibility between components is a project rule
(ADR-synapsis-0003 and the `[architecture]` section of a dialect).
**Construct with PascalCase.** There is no `new`: calling a PascalCase name constructs an object; the dialect writes
whatever the target needs.
**Constructor of an inheriting module.** `super(...)` as the first line of the body (its arguments are the received
parameters); without it the base is called without arguments. A parameter named like a member of the base is that
member, not a new field.
**External classes.** Versioned type definitions (like `.d.ts`), generated from the SDK (format and repository: old
ADR-0040), mark overrides and give the inherited members of classes that are not in the file.

`Result<E, T>` is fpdart's `Either<E, T>` (`Ok` → `Right`, `Err` → `Left`); async is `Future<Either<E, T>>` with

(`tools/spec-check`); a dialect is data a third party can write.

body: Imports are the part of a file an agent gets wrong most often and reads least. The libraries of a target change
with each version. The rules of the base must not fill with one target's details. And a new target should not need

rows.title: ADR-0007: The transpiler writes the imports from versioned definitions; each dialect has its own reference; a new dialect is created by an…
rows.summary: (type definitions, ADR-lang-0008) and organizes them per component, module or function.
body: **Imports written by the transpiler.** The transpiler writes the imports: it knows the libraries of the dialect
(type definitions, ADR-lang-0008) and organizes them per component, module or function. `use` exists for shortcuts
(`use flutter.ui`).
**Versioned technologies.** The transpiler keeps versions of each technology with their dictionaries (the type
definitions packages `name@version`).
**Optional agents.** Optionally the transpiler can connect to a coding agent (Claude, Codex, OpenCode) to optimize
and personalize the generated code. The compiler has no such connection today.
**Dialect references.** The base reference (`docs/07-reference/nuclear-base.md`) describes no dialect; every
dialect has its own reference (`dialects/<language>/docs/07-reference/<dialect>.md`), which inherits from the base.
**New dialects with agents.** A new dialect is created by a coding agent (Claude, Codex, OpenCode) following the
rules, the process and the restrictions of `docs/07-reference/dialects.md` §8; each rule of its reference has at
least one verified example. Per-project kinds and decorators are postponed.

rows.title: ADR-0008: The target's libraries are described by versioned type definitions, and any package of the target is added through Nuclear with…
rows.summary: ADR-0088); a cloned backend or web project compiles before anything is installed.
body: - Positive: the API is exact for the installed versions; an invented class or argument fails in Nuclear (old
ADR-0088); a cloned backend or web project compiles before anything is installed.
- Negative:
- A dialect without `package_*` commands cannot add packages; the command says which key is missing.
- Projects with a `nuclear.toml` (the base dialects, built with `nuclear build`) have no command: they have no
environment of their own to install into. They still keep definitions by hand in `defs/`.
- The definitions describe the version installed when the package was added; `nuclear add <package>` again
regenerates them after an upgrade.
- TypeScript: what a CommonJS package hangs from its exported value is reached through the default export
(`lodash.chunk(...)`), not by name; a module other than the package's own is named with `--module`
(`date-fns/locale`); a package with no types of its own nor an `@types` package cannot be described.
- Python: the definitions are what the package's top modules export; a sub-module is named with `--module`.
- The editors bundle the compiler: they are released with it.

rows.title: ADR-0008: The target's libraries are described by versioned type definitions, and any package of the target is added through Nuclear with…
rows.summary: The compiler only knows the names its type definitions give it: any other name is N0106. Hand-written lists of symbols did not scale, and a project uses libraries nobody described for Nuclear: `lodash` under nestjs, `humanize` under fastapi, `cached_network_image` under flutter.
body: The compiler only knows the names its type definitions give it: any other name is N0106. Hand-written lists of
symbols did not scale, and a project uses libraries nobody described for Nuclear: `lodash` under nestjs, `humanize`
under fastapi, `cached_network_image` under flutter. The user's rule: any library of the dialect's technology is
installed through Nuclear and only through Nuclear, with that technology's own package manager underneath; Nuclear
takes the package and creates every definition the compiler, the language server and the dialect need, as
TypeScript does with a package's types. By a command or by asking the agent.

rows.title: ADR-0008: The target's libraries are described by versioned type definitions, and any package of the target is added through Nuclear with…
rows.summary: (`express` under nestjs: the `controller` kind).
body: **Advice, never a refusal.** `[project.manifest.advice]` of a dialect names packages the platform already covers
(`express` under nestjs: the `controller` kind). Adding one says so and adds it. Only what the framework itself
uses stays refused (`reserved`, the dialect's `defs`).
**The tools read the project's packages.** `nuclear defs show|list|search` inside a project include them, as
`nuclear check`, `nuclear build` and the language server do.
**Through the agent.** The MCP tool `synapsis` runs `add` and `remove`; `nuclear_defs` takes the project's folder;
the skill and a project's `AGENTS.md` say that a missing library is added with `nuclear add`, never by hand in
`build/`.
**Not decided: a library of another language** (a Python library inside a project of the TypeScript dialect). It is
not a matter of definitions (`gen.py` already describes the library): what is missing is where its code runs. To
decide when a project needs it.

rows.title: ADR-0008: The target's libraries are described by versioned type definitions, and any package of the target is added through Nuclear with…
rows.summary: `defs/<language>/<name>/<version>/`, with the sources: a project just cloned compiles before anything is installed.
body: **Where a project's definitions live.** A backend or web project keeps them in the project,
`defs/<language>/<name>/<version>/`, with the sources: a project just cloned compiles before anything is installed.
`nuclear install` generates the ones that are missing (a package written by hand in `config.nuc`). Mobile keeps
the shared cache and `build/defs.lock`.
**A name is imported as what it is.** `index.json` has `defaults`: the symbols that are the default export of their
library (`import dayjs from 'dayjs'`). Every other symbol is a name of its library, also one called like it
(`import { nanoid } from 'nanoid'`, `from tqdm import tqdm`). A module written as itself in a dialect file
(`[auto_imports] "math" = ["math"]`) stays the module (`import math`). The default export is called as the package
declares it (`dayjs`, `React`) or, when that is no name to write (`_`, `e`, none), like the module (`lodash`,
`express`).
**Any package name is written in `config.nuc`.** `name = "version"` when the name is an identifier,
`"name@version"` otherwise (`"date-fns@^4.1.0"`, `"@nestjs/axios@^12.0.0"`): split at the first `@` that is not the
first character. The parser does not change.

rows.title: ADR-0008: The target's libraries are described by versioned type definitions, and any package of the target is added through Nuclear with…
rows.summary: `dialects/<language>/defs/<package>/<version>/`: `package.toml`, `index.json` for the transpiler, `api.json` with the full API for the language server and the agents.
body: **The format.** Like TypeScript's `.d.ts` / `@types`: packages `name@version`, per language, in
`dialects/<language>/defs/<package>/<version>/`: `package.toml`, `index.json` for the transpiler, `api.json` with
the full API for the language server and the agents. Types in Nuclear notation. A dialect lists them in
`[dialect] defs`; they give the automatic imports, the inherited members and the overrides. One generator per
language (`tools/defs/`).
**One command on every platform.** `nuclear add <package>[@version]... [--module <module>]...` and
`nuclear remove <package>...`. A folder is still a kind package (ADR-synapsis-0004); a name is a package of the target.
The package is installed in the generated project, written in `dependencies(...)` of `config.nuc` with the version
the package manager resolved, and described: its definitions are generated from what is installed.
**The dialect says how; Rust knows no package manager.** A backend or web dialect gives the commands in
`[toolchain]`: `package_add`, `package_remove`, `package_version`, `package_defs`, the texts `package_requirement`,
`package_constraint`, `package_exact`, and `package_companion` (the package that carries the types of one that
ships none: `@types/lodash`, added and removed with it). The mobile platform keeps its own path (`flutter pub add`,
definitions by Dart's analyzer).

rows.title: ADR-0008: The target's libraries are described by versioned type definitions, and any package of the target is added through Nuclear with…
rows.summary: 1. Hand-written symbol lists (`symbols.toml`): replaced by the definitions packages.
body: 1. Hand-written symbol lists (`symbols.toml`): replaced by the definitions packages.
2. For a library of another language, a second process: the library behind a small service the generated code
calls. It needs the emitter to write every call to a foreign name as an awaited call to a generated client, and
the toolchain to keep a second environment and start and stop the process with the app, its tests and its
container. Only data that travels as JSON; a class becomes a remote handle with a lifetime; no callbacks; every
call is asynchronous and slower. The only general way; its plain form works today by hand (a fastapi project that
exposes the library and the nestjs project reading its contract, ADR-synapsis-0006). One command for it is weeks of
work for functions with plain data on the backend platform, much more for objects with state; in a browser or a
phone it is only ever a call to a backend.
3. For a library of another language, the interpreter inside Node (a native bridge, or Pyodide): a native build per
system, or WebAssembly; fragile to install; Pyodide runs pure Python and few compiled packages.
4. Translating the library: not feasible in general.

rows.title: ADR-0009: Nuclear has its own standard library for its base types, translated by every language dialect — Consequences
rows.summary: (the templates write `len(xs)`, `[f(x) for x in xs]`, `xs.where(f).toList()`); the guide, the references, the briefs and the examples use one vocabulary, kept honest by `tools/spec-check`.
body: - Positive: the Nuclear code of a project does not change with its dialect; the generated code stays the expert's
(the templates write `len(xs)`, `[f(x) for x in xs]`, `xs.where(f).toList()`); the guide, the references, the
briefs and the examples use one vocabulary, kept honest by `tools/spec-check`.
- Negative: a second vocabulary to learn next to the targets'; a member on a receiver whose type is not known is
not translated (`docs/01-product/roadmap.md`).
- Dart's fpdart-style `Result` and Flutter's widget API are not library members: they are type definitions.
- The operators stay as decided in ADR-lang-0002.

rows.title: ADR-0009: Nuclear has its own standard library for its base types, translated by every language dialect — Context and problem
rows.summary: Calling the target's library (`xs.push(x)` in TypeScript, `xs.add(x)` in Dart, `xs.append(x)` in Python) ties a `.nuc` to one target.
body: Calling the target's library (`xs.push(x)` in TypeScript, `xs.add(x)` in Dart, `xs.append(x)` in Python) ties a
`.nuc` to one target. With three platforms whose Nuclear must not change between dialects (ADR-synapsis-0002), a `.nuc`
that calls `xs.length` cannot be the same file that calls `len(xs)`. The user chose Nuclear's own vocabulary over
TypeScript's or Python's.

rows.title: ADR-0009: Nuclear has its own standard library for its base types, translated by every language dialect — Decision
rows.summary: `Set<T>`, `Bytes`) and a small set of objects (`Math`, `Json`, `Regex`, `DateTime`, `Duration`, `delay`, `awaitAll`, `print`): `docs/07-reference/library.md`.
body: **Nuclear defines the members of its base types** (`string`, `int`, `double`, `boolean`, `T[]`, `<K, V>`,
`Set<T>`, `Bytes`) and a small set of objects (`Math`, `Json`, `Regex`, `DateTime`, `Duration`, `delay`,
`awaitAll`, `print`): `docs/07-reference/library.md`. One name per operation, camelCase, properties for cheap
queries (`length`, `isEmpty`, `first`, `keys`), methods for everything else; the most widespread name wins when the
targets disagree (`contains`, `add`, `upper`, `trim`, `join`, `sorted`).
**Every language dialect translates it** (`[library.<type>]`, a template per member with the receiver and the
arguments, including the lambda's parameters and body so Python can write a comprehension). The emitter rewrites a
member of a base type when the receiver's type is known (declared, a literal, or the result of a library member or
a declared function); when it is not known and the name belongs to more than one type with different translations,
it reports that the receiver needs a type.
**A target's library name on a base type is an error** in every dialect, with the Nuclear name as the fix:
`xs.push(x)` → "use add". The type definitions of libraries (ADR-lang-0008) are untouched: `numpy`, `dio`,
`Text(...)` are written as they are; only the base types are Nuclear's.

rows.title: ADR-0009: Nuclear has its own standard library for its base types, translated by every language dialect — Decision
rows.summary: with the same expected output.
body: **One `examples/stdlib/` set for every target**, checked by `tools/stdlib-check.sh` in TypeScript, Dart and Python
with the same expected output.

rows.title: ADR-0009: Nuclear has its own standard library for its base types, translated by every language dialect — Options considered
rows.summary: 1. The target's library, with no library of Nuclear's own (no wrapper between the code and the platform; agents already know those APIs): it was the first decision; it makes the same `.nuc` impossible to build for two targets.
body: 1. The target's library, with no library of Nuclear's own (no wrapper between the code and the platform; agents
already know those APIs): it was the first decision; it makes the same `.nuc` impossible to build for two
targets.
2. TypeScript's vocabulary as the standard (agents know it best): it would make the Python output read as a
translation and tie the language to one target's naming.
3. Python's vocabulary: the same, the other way; and `len(xs)` as a function reads worse than a property.

rows.title: ADR-0009: Nuclear has its own standard library for its base types, translated by every language dialect — References
rows.summary: `dialects/<language>/library.toml`.
body: - `docs/07-reference/library.md`, `docs/07-reference/dialects.md` §5.8, `crates/nuclear-dialect/src/library.rs`,
`dialects/<language>/library.toml`.

rows.title: ADR-0010: Every word is documented for the editor, and the compiler corrects what an agent writes by reflex or invents — Consequences
rows.summary: a cascade of N0013; an invented widget or argument fails in Nuclear, not later in the target's compiler; the editor and the command line show the same text for a word.
body: - Positive: an agent that writes TypeScript, Dart or Python by reflex gets one exact correction per line instead of
a cascade of N0013; an invented widget or argument fails in Nuclear, not later in the target's compiler; the
editor and the command line show the same text for a word.
- Negative: a false positive of the habits scan is a bug: every `.nuc` of the tree and every `nuclear` block of the
documents must give none, checked by hand when the rules change. How much it helps agents is not measured yet
(`docs/01-product/roadmap.md`).

rows.title: ADR-0010: Every word is documented for the editor, and the compiler corrects what an agent writes by reflex or invents — Context and problem
rows.summary: The user asked that agents read and understand Nuclear, the framework and every dialect "as if the model had been trained on them".
body: The user asked that agents read and understand Nuclear, the framework and every dialect "as if the model had been
trained on them". A model cannot be trained here, and a measurement showed that a brief alone changes little:
agents copy the project's `.nuc` and fail where they write by reflex. So the knowledge goes where the agent and the
developer already look: the editor's hover, the errors of the compiler and the shell.

rows.title: ADR-0010: Every word is documented for the editor, and the compiler corrects what an agent writes by reflex or invents — Decision
rows.summary: PascalCase call nothing defines is N0220 (did you mean: edit distance over the project, the auto-imports and the globals) and a named argument the constructor lacks is N0219 (it lists the real ones).
body: **Invented APIs.** In a file of a project (a single file cannot see its neighbours) with type definitions, a
PascalCase call nothing defines is N0220 (did you mean: edit distance over the project, the auto-imports and the
globals) and a named argument the constructor lacks is N0219 (it lists the real ones). `index.json` carries
`params` (the unnamed constructor) per class, so the build stays as fast (no `api.json` read);
`tools/defs/index_params.py` adds them to existing packages and the generators write them. A class imported under
that name from another package is not checked (`Dialect::def_libraries`). The names of `implicit` libraries are
`globals`.
**Words on demand.** `nuclear help <word> --dialect <d>` prints the `docs.toml` entry of a kind, a decorator or a
header word (the same text as the editor's hover); `nuclear help words --dialect <d>` lists them with their first
line.
**llms.txt.** The website publishes `/llms.txt` (llmstxt.org: the sheets first, then the reference) and
`/llms-full.txt` (every brief + the reference), generated from the same files.
The skill, the `AGENTS.md` template and the base brief say that the compiler corrects habits and how to look up
words.

rows.title: ADR-0010: Every word is documented for the editor, and the compiler corrects what an agent writes by reflex or invents — Decision
rows.summary: text`, `@return`, `@throws`, `@example` with code on the following lines, `@see`, `@deprecated`, `@since`; the type comes from the signature).
body: **Doc comments.** The comment right above a declaration is its documentation, with JSDoc-like tags (`@param name
text`, `@return`, `@throws`, `@example` with code on the following lines, `@see`, `@deprecated`, `@since`; the type
comes from the signature). The editor shows it in hover, completion and signature help; the dialect writes it with
the optional `doc_comment` template.
**Every word has documentation.** Every word of the base (`base/docs.toml`) and of each dialect (`docs.toml` next
to `dialect.toml`) has it; a build never reads it.
**Habits (N0022, `crates/nuclear-syntax/src/habits.rs`).** A line scan, before the parser's errors, of the forms of
TypeScript, Dart, Python, Java and Go: `{ }` blocks, `await`, `const/let/var/final x =`, `new`, `class A extends
B`, `class A(B):`, the return type first (`int f(int x)`, `Widget build(BuildContext context)`),
`def`/`function`/`fn`, trailing `:`, `elif`, `except E as e`, `None/True/False/undefined/nil`, `self`, `pass`,
`lambda x:`, `#` comments, f-strings, backticks, `x++`, `import`/`from ... import`, `switch`, C `for (`. Each one
gives the Nuclear form and, when exact, a `fix` (the agent hook and the language server apply it). The other errors
of those lines are dropped.

2. The brief alone: measured, it changes little.
