rows.title: ADR-0011: A `.nuc` is debugged through the target's debugger with a line map, not with aligned output nor a debugger of its own —…
rows.summary: target's debugger keeps working; the same map serves every dialect.
body: - Positive: the generated text does not change because of debugging (the golden tests prove it); every tool of the
target's debugger keeps working; the same map serves every dialect.
- Negative: the editor's native call stack shows the target's frames; each editor has to implement the mirror
breakpoints and the stepping on its side.

rows.title: ADR-0011: A `.nuc` is debugged through the target's debugger with a line map, not with aligned output nor a debugger of its own — Context…
rows.summary: A developer sets a breakpoint in the `.nuc`, but what runs is the generated code.
body: A developer sets a breakpoint in the `.nuc`, but what runs is the generated code. Either the generated code is
bent to match the source line by line, or a debugger is written for Nuclear, or the target's debugger is kept and
told which line is which.

rows.title: ADR-0011: A `.nuc` is debugged through the target's debugger with a line map, not with aligned output nor a debugger of its own — Decision
rows.summary: statement, member, declaration and argument on its own line.
body: **A line map.** The emitter records, for each generated file, the pairs (generated line → Nuclear line) of each
statement, member, declaration and argument on its own line. The generated code is not aligned line by line with
the `.nuc`: it stays readable. A build writes the map: a mobile app to `build/app/.dart_tool/nuclear_lines.json`,
any other project to `<output>/.nuclear/lines.json`. Editors set a mirror breakpoint in the generated file, show
the `.nuc` line of each pause and can mark an error of the target on its `.nuc` line with a side window that
explains it (`nuclear explain`).
**Mixed debugging, on top of the target's session.** In a Flutter app the session is the Dart extension's: steps
go by Nuclear line (the Dart step is repeated until another `.nuc` line), active when the pause came from a `.nuc`
breakpoint or the focus is on a `.nuc`; a `.dart` breakpoint gives Dart steps. Variable values are shown in the
`.nuc`, with a Nuclear call stack and a command to go to the same line in Nuclear or Dart. VS Code's native stack
still shows Dart.

rows.title: ADR-0011: A `.nuc` is debugged through the target's debugger with a line map, not with aligned output nor a debugger of its own — Options…
rows.summary: 1. Generated code aligned line by line with the source: rejected, the output would stop being readable.
body: 1. Generated code aligned line by line with the source: rejected, the output would stop being readable.
2. An own debug adapter that translates messages: rejected, it would lose devices, DevTools and the Inspector.

body: - `docs/02-architecture/emitter.md` (the line map), `crates/nuclear-transpile/src/project.rs`
(`LINE_MAP_FILE`, `line_map`); the editors' side is documented in `../extensions/`.
- Replaces: ADR-0068, ADR-0076

rows.title: Architecture Decision Records — the language
rows.summary: Why the language, the compiler and the language server are the way they are.
body: Why the language, the compiler and the language server are the way they are. The rules themselves are in
`docs/07-reference/`; how the code implements them is in `docs/02-architecture/`. Open an ADR only when its title
answers your question.
- A new decision gets the next number, in the format of the tree's
[`0000-template.md`](../../../docs/03-adr/0000-template.md), and a row in this table.
- An accepted ADR is never edited: a change is a new ADR, and the old one is marked
`superseded by ADR-lang-NNNN`.
- Cite one with the project's key: `ADR-lang-0006`.

rows.title: Architecture Decision Records — the language
rows.summary: Architecture Decision Records — the language
body: | ADR | Decision | Status | Date |
| [0001](0001-principles.md) | One golden rule judges every proposal; Nuclear is modules and functions, not objects; the compiler writes the map of a project | accepted | 2026-11-03 |
| [0002](0002-files-and-lexical-syntax.md) | Files are `.nuc`, blocks are two spaces, words for logic and symbols for arithmetic and bits | accepted | 2026-11-03 |
| [0003](0003-functions-lambdas-and-async.md) | A function is a header plus a block, returns its last line when it declares a type, and awaits with `~` | accepted | 2026-11-03 |
| [0004](0004-variables-types-and-expressions.md) | A variable is an assignment, a block has its own scope, `if` and `match` are values, and there are no records nor `type` | accepted | 2026-11-03 |

| [0005](0005-modules.md) | A module uses its members by name, has no visibility words, is constructed by calling its PascalCase name and inherits from classes the type definitions describe | accepted | 2026-11-03 |
| [0006](0006-results.md) | Errors are values: `Result<E, T>` with the error first, propagated on its own, handled with `.ok()` / `.error()` by what the callback returns | accepted | 2026-11-03 |

rows.title: Plan: new dialects created by agents — 1. Goal
rows.summary: A developer tells a coding agent (Claude, Codex, OpenCode) "turn Crystal and Amber into Synapsis", the agent creates the dialect following Nuclear's rules as we did with `flutter` and `nestjs`, pushes it to a repository, and anyone uses it with `nuclear new -d amber`.
body: A developer tells a coding agent (Claude, Codex, OpenCode) "turn Crystal and Amber into Synapsis", the agent
creates the dialect following Nuclear's rules as we did with `flutter` and `nestjs`, pushes it to a repository,
and anyone uses it with `nuclear new -d amber`.
- The user **does not program nor edit the dialect by hand**: they describe the *what for* and review.
Everything goes through the agent.
- The agent **cannot leave** the rules, philosophy nor restrictions of Nuclear and Synapsis
(`docs/07-reference/dialects.md` §8.4). What cannot be expressed is reported; it is not faked.
**Out of scope (postponed):** kinds, decorators and shortcuts of each project (detecting repeated code,
extension points in the framework's templates, derived kinds). They are taken up later; the project dialect
format of `docs/07-reference/dialects.md` §7 stays the same and is not extended.

`nuclear spec [--dialect]` (the full contract for agents); `nuclear build --dialect <path>`.

the source of truth the agent reads.
- User tutorial: `docs/08-guides/create-a-dialect-with-an-agent.md`.
- `tools/spec-check/check.py` checks that a spec's equivalences are the real output, but only inside the
NuclearLang repository.

rows.title: Plan: new dialects created by agents — Gaps
rows.summary: 1. The `nuclear` CLI has Flutter written in Rust (`Manifest::infer(root, "flutter", ...)`, `doctor`, the SDK, the pubspec, build/run/test).
body: 1. **The `nuclear` CLI has Flutter written in Rust** (`Manifest::infer(root, "flutter", ...)`, `doctor`, the
SDK, the pubspec, build/run/test). A new dialect cannot have its own `nuclear new -d <d>`.
2. **Synapsis's rules as a concept are mixed with Flutter** in `dialects/dart/docs/07-reference/flutter.md` (§1, §3, §4, §6). An agent
building `crystal/amber` has no neutral spec of what Synapsis is.
3. **There is no example checking outside the repository**: a user's agent has no `spec-check`.
4. **Agents do not load the rules by themselves**: the tutorial's prompt has to be pasted.
5. **A dialect cannot be shared**: there is no way to install it from a repository.
6. **Targets with emitter needs**: something that does not come out of a template (Python: single-expression
lambdas, `pass` in empty blocks) needs a new option in Rust, which only the NuclearLang team can add, never
the user's agent (§8.4.1).

rows.title: 005 — The language to 1.0: formatter, definitions, constructors, patterns, freeze
rows.summary: Step 6 of the competitiveness plan (`../docs/01-product/roadmap.md`, decided by the user 2026-11-06).
body: Step 6 of the competitiveness plan (`../docs/01-product/roadmap.md`, decided by the user 2026-11-06). Status: F1 (`nuclear fmt`)
done 2026-11-10 (only reflow, decided by the user; the editor's format on save is the language server's, `docs/01-product/roadmap.md`); F2–F6
not started. Each feature changes `crates/` and `docs/07-reference/nuclear-base.md`; the dialect side is small.

rows.title: 005 — The language to 1.0: formatter, definitions, constructors, patterns, freeze — 1. Diagnosis
rows.summary: `docs/02-architecture/limits.md` lists what Nuclear cannot say yet; the agent evaluation and the external projects show which of those an agent hits first: a named constructor (`Character.fromJson` can be called, not declared), a pattern in a `for` or a `match` branch, a value of a library class…
body: `docs/02-architecture/limits.md` lists what Nuclear cannot say yet; the agent evaluation and the external
projects show which of those an agent hits first: a named constructor (`Character.fromJson` can be called, not
declared), a pattern in a `for` or a `match` branch, a value of a library class whose members are unknown
(`text.split(",")` is "unknown" until typed, so no `N0106` and no completion). There is no formatter, so two
agents write the same code two ways and diffs are noise. TypeScript has no type definitions, so the NestJS and
future web dialects check less than Flutter. And nothing says what is stable: specs change daily.

rows.title: 005 — The language to 1.0: formatter, definitions, constructors, patterns, freeze — F1 — `nuclear fmt`
rows.summary: One canonical layout, the one the specs already use: 2 spaces, one blank line between declarations, members without blank lines unless the author left one, (trailing commas in multi-line calls: left as written, only reflow), decorators on their own line, doc comments kept.
body: One canonical layout, the one the specs already use: 2 spaces, one blank line between declarations, members
without blank lines unless the author left one, (trailing commas in multi-line calls: left as written, only reflow), decorators on their own
line, doc comments kept. `nuclear fmt <file|dir>` rewrites; `nuclear fmt --check` for CI and the editor (format on
save through the LSP).
```nuclear
// before
usecase GetUser(repo:UserRepository)
exec(id:int)   Result<UserError,User>
~repo.find( id )
// after
usecase GetUser(repo: UserRepository)
exec(id: int) Result<UserError, User>
~repo.find(id)
Built on the parser's AST plus the comments and blank lines the lexer already keeps (`DocComment`, the `*`
comment lines of ADR-lang-0002). Done when: every `.nuc` of the repository is a fixed point of `fmt` and a test
guards it.

rows.title: 005 — The language to 1.0: formatter, definitions, constructors, patterns, freeze — F2 — TypeScript type definitions for the base dialect,…
rows.summary: `dialects/typescript/defs/typescript/5.9.3` exists for the nestjs dialect; the `typescript` and `nodejs` dialects get `defs = ["typescript@5.9.3", "node@26"]` so `.nuc` files targeted at TypeScript get `N0219`/`N0220` (unknown member, wrong arguments) like Dart.
body: `dialects/typescript/defs/typescript/5.9.3` exists for the nestjs dialect; the `typescript` and `nodejs` dialects get
`defs = ["typescript@5.9.3", "node@26"]` so `.nuc` files targeted at TypeScript get `N0219`/`N0220` (unknown
member, wrong arguments) like Dart.
Member types: today `index.json` lists members by name only, so a value returned by a library method is
"unknown". The generators (`tools/defs/bin/defs.dart`, `tools/defs/typescript`, `tools/defs/python`) write the return type
of every member in Nuclear notation (`api.json` already has them in TypeScript; Dart's generator loses them), and
the emitter's `static_type` follows a chain:
```nuclear
parts = "a,b".split(",")        // list<string>: known, so
first = parts.first              // string → `first` is typed, N0106 and completion work
Done when: `examples/stdlib` programs type every intermediate value (a test prints the inferred types), and the
LSP's open request (c) "inferred type of an expression" is served by the same function.

rows.title: 005 — The language to 1.0: formatter, definitions, constructors, patterns, freeze — F3 — Named and factory constructors
rows.summary: Point x: double y: double // a named constructor: Point.origin() new origin() this(x = 0, y = 0) // a factory: computes before building new fromJson(json: <string, any>) Point Point(x = json["x"] as double, y = json["y"] as double) `new name(params)` with `this(...)` as the body is a redirecting…
body: ```nuclear
Point
x: double
y: double
// a named constructor: Point.origin()
new origin() this(x = 0, y = 0)
// a factory: computes before building
new fromJson(json: <string, any>) Point
Point(x = json["x"] as double, y = json["y"] as double)
| Dart | TypeScript | Python |
| `Point.origin() : this(x: 0, y: 0);` | `static origin(): Point { return new Point(0, 0); }` | `@classmethod def origin(cls) -> "Point": return cls(x=0, y=0)` |
| `factory Point.fromJson(...)` | `static fromJson(json): Point` | `@classmethod def from_json(cls, json)` |
`new name(params)` with `this(...)` as the body is a redirecting constructor; with a return type it is a factory.
Done when: the flutter dialect's `model` keeps generating `fromJson` and a hand-written `new` on a model is
allowed next to it (`N0xxx` when they clash).

rows.title: 005 — The language to 1.0: formatter, definitions, constructors, patterns, freeze — F4 — Patterns everywhere
rows.summary: Today patterns exist only in assignments (`(a, b) = pair`).
body: Today patterns exist only in assignments (`(a, b) = pair`). They become legal in `for`, in `match` branches and
in lambda parameters:
```nuclear
for (name, score) in scores            // a list of pairs, or map entries
print("${name}: ${score}")
match point
Point(x = 0, y = 0) -> "origin"
Point(x = 0) -> "on y"
_ -> "elsewhere"
users.map(({ name, age }) => "${name} (${age})")
Dart 3 patterns, TypeScript destructuring, Python 3.10 `match`. Done when: `examples/stdlib` has a program per
form that prints the same in the three languages.

rows.title: 005 — The language to 1.0: formatter, definitions, constructors, patterns, freeze — F5 — `const` inference in Dart and a `switch` on…
rows.summary: Dart-only output quality: a widget tree whose arguments are all constants gets `const` (today only literals do), so `flutter analyze` with `prefer_const_constructors` stays at 0 infos.
body: Dart-only output quality: a widget tree whose arguments are all constants gets `const` (today only literals do),
so `flutter analyze` with `prefer_const_constructors` stays at 0 infos. `match` over a sealed value writes a
pattern `switch` (today `if` chains with casts, the `unnecessary_cast` warnings in the `dart` dialect's roadmap).

rows.title: 005 — The language to 1.0: formatter, definitions, constructors, patterns, freeze — F6 — Freeze 1.0
rows.summary: `docs/07-reference/` get a version line and a changelog file (`CHANGELOG.md`, keep-a-changelog).
body: - `nuclear-base.md`, `dialects.md`, `library.md`, `projects.md`, `definitions.md` and `diagnostics.md` of
`docs/07-reference/` get a version line and a changelog file (`CHANGELOG.md`, keep-a-changelog).
- Semantic versioning: a change that makes a valid `.nuc` invalid or changes its meaning is a major; a new
construct is a minor; a diagnostic text or a generated-code improvement is a patch.
- A compatibility test: every `.nuc` of `examples/` and the external projects builds with 1.0 and keeps building
with every 1.x.
- The platforms (`backend.md`, `mobile.md`, `web.md`) version separately from the language.
Done when: `nuclear --version` prints `1.0.0`, the website has a "What is stable" page, and the first external
project builds from the published release.

rows.title: 005 — The language to 1.0: formatter, definitions, constructors, patterns, freeze — 3. Work order
rows.summary: 1. F1 `fmt` (independent, high value for agents and reviews).
body: 1. F1 `fmt` (independent, high value for agents and reviews).
2. F2 definitions (unblocks the web dialect's checks and the LSP).
3. F3 constructors, F4 patterns, F5 Dart quality.

does not load a dialect to know where a project answers.
- Negative: the mobile path of the CLI still calls Flutter directly (its SDK lookup, devices and hot reload);
moving it to `[toolchain]` is its own step ([roadmap](../01-product/roadmap.md)).

rows.title: ADR-0001: A project's commands come from its dialect's data; a dialect's own commands go under its name — Context and problem
rows.summary: The `nuclear` CLI, the VS Code extension and the website each carried their own copy of how a dialect's generated project is installed, run, debugged and served: ports, urls, framework commands and dialect names written in Rust and TypeScript.
body: The `nuclear` CLI, the VS Code extension and the website each carried their own copy of how a dialect's generated
project is installed, run, debugged and served: ports, urls, framework commands and dialect names written in Rust
and TypeScript. A new dialect needed code in three places. The CLI also needs one shape for its commands that holds
for every dialect: some commands are the same in all of them, some belong to one.

rows.title: ADR-0001: A project's commands come from its dialect's data; a dialect's own commands go under its name — Decision
rows.summary: 1. Common commands stay at the first level (`build`, `check`, `make`, `run`, `test`...): the project already says its dialect.
body: 1. **Common commands stay at the first level** (`build`, `check`, `make`, `run`, `test`...): the project already
says its dialect. **A dialect's own commands go under its name**: `nuclear <dialect> <command>`
(`nuclear flutter add`). A subcommand the dialect does not define goes to its own CLI as it is
(`nuclear flutter doctor` → `flutter doctor`).
2. **A dialect's `[toolchain]` is the only source** of how its generated project is installed, compiled, run,
tested, served by an editor and debugged: the commands, `url`, `ready`, `installed`, `[[toolchain.launch]]`,
`[toolchain.settings]`, `extensions`, with `[toolchain.<os>]` overrides (the format is in
`nuclearlang/docs/07-reference/dialects.md`). `synapsis` runs those commands and writes the editor workspace
from them; nothing in Rust or TypeScript names a port or a framework command.
3. **A platform names its default dialect** (`[platform] default_dialect` of its `platform.toml`):
`nuclear new -p <platform>` uses it, and so does an older Flutter app whose `config.nuc` has no
`synapsis(...)` line.
4. **The project card carries `toolchain`** (`url`, `serve`, `installed` in `.nuclear/project.json`): an editor
reads it instead of loading the dialect (the web device's server, the base urls of the HTTP Connections tool, "needs
install").

rows.title: ADR-0001: A project's commands come from its dialect's data; a dialect's own commands go under its name — Decision
rows.summary: 5. `nuclear build` removes the output of a removed `.nuc`, from the previous build's line map.
body: 5. **`nuclear build` removes the output of a removed `.nuc`**, from the previous build's line map.
The release archives and the one-line installers were decided together with this; they are the installer's
decision: ADR-installer-0001.

2. The dialect declares it as data, and every tool reads it. Chosen.

rows.title: ADR-0002: Agents learn Nuclear from a short brief, one skill, a project's agent files and the compiler's errors — Consequences
rows.summary: errors without asking.
body: - Positive: an agent learns Nuclear with about 3k tokens instead of the 50k of the full Flutter spec, and sees its
errors without asking.
- Negative: running the evaluation spends the user's quota (about USD 5 per mode in API-equivalent cost): ask
first.
- Measured once: baseline 10 of 10 green, 9.8 turns, about 460k tokens per task; with the skill, `AGENTS.md` and
the hook 10 of 10, 10.6 turns, about 456k tokens. Agents already learn from the project's own `.nuc` files, so
these tasks do not separate the modes: harder tasks are needed (a project from scratch, nothing to copy;
[the plan](../04-specs/001-agent-support/plan.md), F7).

rows.title: ADR-0002: Agents learn Nuclear from a short brief, one skill, a project's agent files and the compiler's errors — Context and problem
rows.summary: No model was trained on NuclearLang, and none is trained or fine-tuned for it.
body: No model was trained on NuclearLang, and none is trained or fine-tuned for it. The language saves about four times
the tokens of the equivalent Dart, but explaining it with the full spec cost more than the saving: the Flutter spec
is about 50k tokens, 2.5 times a whole project. An agent also could not see its own mistakes without being told to
run the check.

`agent`; the results are `results/<mode>.json`.

rows.title: ADR-0002: Agents learn Nuclear from a short brief, one skill, a project's agent files and the compiler's errors — Decision
rows.summary: 1. The brief.
body: 1. **The brief.** A sheet per dialect, written by hand, holding only what changes from TypeScript / Dart / Python,
kept in the `docs/07-reference/brief/` of the language, of each language dialect and of each platform, checked
by `spec-check` like the references. `nuclear spec --brief --dialect <d>` concatenates the base and the chain
(flutter is about 3k tokens; a test keeps it ≤ 16 KB). A dialect outside NuclearLang may bring its own
`brief.md`.
2. **The skill.** One `SKILL.md` in the open Agent Skills format (`tools/cli/agent-files/skills/nuclear/`),
installed by the installers in `~/.claude/skills` (Claude Code; Cursor and OpenCode also read it),
`~/.agents/skills` (Codex, Cursor, OpenCode) and `~/.codex/skills` (older Codex). It does not copy the brief: it
asks the installed binary for it.
3. **Per project.** `nuclear agent init` (and `nuclear agent init`, also run by `nuclear new`) writes the
NuclearLang section of `AGENTS.md` (between markers, the rest kept), `CLAUDE.md` with `@AGENTS.md`,
`.cursor/rules/nuclear.mdc` and a Claude Code `PostToolUse` hook (`nuclear agent hook`) that checks each edited
`.nuc` with its project and gives the errors back, one line each, with exit code 2.
4. **The evaluation.** `nuclear-synapsis-framework/eval/agent-eval/` (10 tasks: 7 Synapsis on a copy of an app, 2

rows.title: ADR-0002: Agents learn Nuclear from a short brief, one skill, a project's agent files and the compiler's errors — Options considered
rows.summary: 1. A brief generated from the specs: less control over what an agent needs first.
body: 1. A brief generated from the specs: less control over what an agent needs first.
2. A copy of the skill in every project: it would go stale; the global skill asks the binary.
3. An MCP server instead of the shell: more fixed tokens, and the CLI already answers through the shell. (An MCP
server was built later for another purpose, the generators and the local agents: `ADR-platform-0003`,
`ADR-codegen-0001`.)
4. The hand-written brief, one global skill, the project files and the hook. Chosen.

rows.title: ADR-0003: One command line tool, `nuclear`, with the framework's commands — Consequences
rows.summary: `nuclear run`, `nuclear test`.
body: - Positive: one command to install, to learn and to give an agent; the framework's guides read `nuclear new`,
`nuclear run`, `nuclear test`.
- Negative: `build` and `check` without a path outside a project are an error ("no main.nuc or config.nuc"), where
the compiler alone used to print its usage.

rows.title: ADR-0003: One command line tool, `nuclear`, with the framework's commands — Context and problem
rows.summary: NuclearLang had two binaries: `nuclear` (the compiler's: build, check, fix, fmt, help, spec, defs, contracts) and `dragonfly` (the framework's: new, make, gen, run, test, migrate, packages, devices).
body: NuclearLang had two binaries: `nuclear` (the compiler's: build, check, fix, fmt, help, spec, defs, contracts) and
`dragonfly` (the framework's: new, make, gen, run, test, migrate, packages, devices). A person or an agent had to know
which of the two a task needed, and two of their commands had the same name with different meanings: `nuclear build
app.nuc --dialect dart` transpiles a file, `dragonfly build apk` builds a project. The user decided that everything
is `nuclear`, and that the framework is called Synapsis.

rows.title: ADR-0003: One command line tool, `nuclear`, with the framework's commands — Decision
rows.summary: 1. One binary, `nuclear`.
body: 1. **One binary, `nuclear`.** The framework's commands are commands of `nuclear`, in the module `framework/` of this
crate. The `dragonfly` binary does not exist.
2. **A command line is the framework's** when its command is one only the framework has (`new`, `make`, `gen`,
`run`, `test`, `install`, `migrate`, `add`, `remove`, `device`, `terminal-device`, `watch`, `code`, `analyze`,
`clean`, `repair`, `explain`, `pub`, `flutter`, `doctor`, `setup`...), or when there is no command (the landing
page).
3. **`build` and `check` decide by their argument.** With a path (`nuclear build app.nuc`, `nuclear check .`) they are
the compiler's, as they always were. Without one, or with a target of the platform's own tool (`nuclear build
apk`), they work on the project of the framework they run in.
4. **`agent init`** reads the project's manifest when it runs inside a project of the framework; elsewhere it is the
compiler's (`--dialect`).
5. `nuclear help` lists both: the compiler's commands and topics, then the framework's commands.
6. The generators (`make`, `gen`) are the code generator's library (`tools/code_generator`) and the devices the
devices' (`device-emulators`); the command only parses, calls them and prints.

rows.title: ADR-0003: One command line tool, `nuclear`, with the framework's commands — Options considered
rows.summary: 1. Two binaries: two names to learn, and an agent picks the wrong one.
body: 1. Two binaries: two names to learn, and an agent picks the wrong one.
2. One binary where the framework's commands get a prefix (`nuclear project build`): longer commands for the common
case, and every guide changes twice.
3. One binary that tells the two meanings of a name by its argument.

rows.title: Plan: agents master Nuclear and Synapsis without spending tokens — 1. Goal
rows.summary: An agent (Claude Code or another) writes correct Nuclear/Synapsis on the first or second try, without having been trained on the language, and the cost of "teaching" it is much lower than the token savings of the `.nuc` itself.
body: An agent (Claude Code or another) writes correct Nuclear/Synapsis on the first or second try, without having
been trained on the language, and the cost of "teaching" it is much lower than the token savings of the `.nuc`
itself.
No model is trained nor fine-tuned: it is not possible with Claude and it is not needed. The knowledge arrives
three ways: **minimal context** (what changes compared with Dart/TS), **on-demand lookups** (the CLI already
answers everything) and **compiler feedback** (errors that say how to fix themselves).

rows.title: Plan: agents master Nuclear and Synapsis without spending tokens — Success metric
rows.summary: Measured with the evaluation suite (F1), against today's baseline:
body: Measured with the evaluation suite (F1), against today's baseline:
| Metric | Target |
| `check` errors until green, per task | ≤ 1 on average |
| Total tokens per task | ≤ the baseline's, even loading the skill |
| Fixed context tokens (skill) | ≤ 5k |
| Tasks that end green | 100% |

rows.title: Plan: agents master Nuclear and Synapsis without spending tokens — 2. Diagnosis (measured on 2026-10-27 on `flutter/rick_and_morty`)
rows.summary: The last two are the most serious: the error shows up only in `flutter analyze`, on the generated Dart and with lines the agent never wrote.
body: | What an agent coming from Dart writes | Result today | Problem |
| `Text("a", style: TextStyle())` | N0013 + `fix: replace ':' with ' ='` | ✅ good |
| `return Text("a");` | N0009 + `fix: delete ';'` | ✅ good |
| `build(...) Widget {` | N0013 `expected end of line, found '{'` | no hint: "blocks go by indentation" |
| `Widget build(BuildContext context)` | N0013 `expected end of line, found '('` | no hint: "the return type goes at the end" |
| `x = await g()` | N0013 `found 'g'` | no hint: "use `~g()`" |
| `var x = 3` | N0013 `found 'x'` | no hint: "write `x = 3`" |
| `class Bar extends Foo` | N0201 + a list of 35 kinds | no hint: "`Bar: Foo`" or the right kind |
| `Textt("a")` | **no error** | nonexistent constructor: an invisible hallucination |
| `Text("a", styl = TextStyle())` | **no error** | nonexistent argument: an invisible hallucination |
The last two are the most serious: the error shows up only in `flutter analyze`, on the generated Dart and with
lines the agent never wrote.
There is no agent integration either: `nuclear new` generates no `CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md`, skill nor hooks.

rows.title: Plan: agents master Nuclear and Synapsis without spending tokens — 2. Diagnosis (measured on 2026-10-27 on `flutter/rick_and_morty`)
rows.summary: notation.

- `nuclear defs show|search <Name> --dialect flutter`: the API of Flutter, Synapsis and the packages in Nuclear
notation. `defs show Text` takes about 700 tokens: a cheap, precise lookup.
- `nuclear help <topic>`: a guide split into chapters of 1–4k tokens.
- `nuclearlang/tools/spec-check/check.py`: checks that the Nuclear → target examples are the real output.
- `nuclear make`: generates the skeleton of each piece (screen, usecase, repository...), so the agent does not
write the structure from scratch.
- LSP + VS Code extension (`nuclearlang/crates/nuclear-lsp`, `extensions/`).
**Gaps found** (tested with `nuclear check --dialect flutter`):

rows.title: Plan: agents master Nuclear and Synapsis without spending tokens — 2. Diagnosis (measured on 2026-10-27 on `flutter/rick_and_morty`)
rows.summary: About 4 times less than the equivalent Dart.
body: **The language already saves what it promises:**
| | Size | Approx. tokens |
| The project's `.nuc` source (37 files) | 18.7 KB | ~5k |
| Generated Dart (48 files) | 75.4 KB | ~20k |
About **4 times less** than the equivalent Dart.
**The problem is what explaining it costs:**
| Document | Size | Approx. tokens |
| `nuclear spec` (base) | 71 KB | ~18k |
| `nuclear spec --dialect flutter` | 196 KB | ~50k |
| `nuclear help flutter` | 103 KB | ~26k |
| every reference together (`docs/07-reference/` of the language, the dialects and the platforms) | 280 KB | ~70k |
Loading the Flutter spec costs **2.5 times the whole project**. Principle 5 of `nuclear-base.md` ("the whole spec
fits in the context") holds today only in theory: it fits, but it takes all the savings. The spec is the right
reference for humans and for the transpiler; the agent needs something else.
**What already exists and works as it is** (no need to reinvent it):

rows.summary: Ordered by the work sequence.
rows.body: Ordered by the work sequence. Each one with its "done" criterion.

rows.title: Plan: agents master Nuclear and Synapsis without spending tokens — F1. Evaluation suite and baseline (first: without it, there is no way…
rows.summary: location", "a usecase with a 5-minute cache", "a form with validation", "a global event when the network changes".
body: - 10–15 real tasks on a copy of `rick_and_morty`. Examples: "add search to episodes", "a detail screen for a
location", "a usecase with a 5-minute cache", "a form with validation", "a global event when the network
changes". Also 2–3 NestJS tasks so it is not biased towards Flutter.
- A script that runs each task with `claude -p --output-format json` (clean, headless session) and records:
input/output tokens, turns, number of red `check`s and whether it ended green.
- Location: `nuclear-synapsis-framework/eval/agent-eval/` (tasks in TOML, runner in Python like `spec-check`).
- **Done when:** the baseline without the skill is stored in
`nuclear-synapsis-framework/eval/agent-eval/results/baseline.json`.

rows.title: Plan: agents master Nuclear and Synapsis without spending tokens — F2. A differences sheet: `nuclear spec --brief [--dialect <d>]`
rows.summary: The center of the plan.
body: The center of the plan. A short document (target: ≤ 4k tokens with Flutter) written **for someone who already
knows Dart/TypeScript**. It includes only what changes:
- A table of rules: blocks by indentation, return type at the end, `name = value` in arguments, `~` for await
and automatic async, implicit return, `if`/`match` as values, `Result`/`Ok`/`Err` with propagation, aliases
`f() = Module.method`, constructors `(dep: Type)`, kinds instead of `class`.
- 10–15 **Nuclear → Dart pairs** chosen from what is used most, generated from the transpiler's real output
(checked with `spec-check`, as today).
- Synapsis kinds in one line each (`repository`, `usecase`, `statemanager`, `stateless`, `appcomponent`...) and
the architecture rules (screen → component → usecase → repository).
- "How to look up the rest": `nuclear help <topic>`, `nuclear defs show X`, `nuclear make`.
Source: `docs/07-reference/brief/<dialect>.md` next to each reference, embedded with `include_str!` like the other
topics.
`--brief` concatenates the briefs of the dialect's chain (flutter → dart → base), like `spec`.
- **Done when:** `nuclear spec --brief --dialect flutter` measures ≤ 4k tokens, `spec-check` gives 0 problems on
the briefs, and an agent with only the brief solves a simple F1 task.

rows.title: Plan: agents master Nuclear and Synapsis without spending tokens — F3. Claude Code skill + `AGENTS.md`
rows.summary: `nuclear.toml`) and the work cycle: 1. `nuclear make ...` for the skeleton.
body: - A `nuclear` skill (folder `SKILL.md` + references). Its body is short: when it applies (`*.nuc`,
`nuclear.toml`) and the work cycle:
1. `nuclear make ...` for the skeleton.
2. Write following the brief.
3. `nuclear check --json` → fix until green.
4. On a doubtful API: `nuclear defs show/search`, never guess.
- The brief **is not copied** into the skill: the skill asks for `nuclear spec --brief --dialect <d>`, so it is
never out of date with the installed binary.
- `installer/install.sh` installs the skill in `~/.claude/skills/nuclear/` (option `--no-agent` to skip it).
- `nuclear new` generates in the project an `AGENTS.md` of 10–20 lines (it works for any agent, not only
Claude) and a `CLAUDE.md` that imports it with `@AGENTS.md`. A `nuclear agent init` command is added for
existing projects like `rick_and_morty`.
- **Done when:** in a new project, Claude Code activates the skill by itself when it touches a `.nuc`, and the F1
tasks have fewer errors than the baseline.

rows.title: Plan: agents master Nuclear and Synapsis without spending tokens — F4. Automatic check hook
rows.summary: A Claude Code `PostToolUse` hook for `Edit|Write` on `*.nuc`: it runs `nuclear check <file> --json` (or the project's) and, if there are errors, gives them back to the agent in the same turn.
body: A Claude Code `PostToolUse` hook for `Edit|Write` on `*.nuc`: it runs `nuclear check <file> --json` (or the
project's) and, if there are errors, gives them back to the agent in the same turn. The agent does not have to
remember to check.
- Installed with the skill (F3) inside the project's `.claude/settings.json` through `nuclear agent init`.
- Compact output: only code, line, message and `fix`, without the source code block. Few tokens.
- **Done when:** a `.nuc` with an error, edited by the agent, gets the diagnostic without the agent asking.

rows.title: Plan: agents master Nuclear and Synapsis without spending tokens — F5. Diagnostics with fixes for Dart/TS habits
rows.summary: In the parser/diagnostics (`nuclear-syntax`, `nuclear-diag`), detect and give a `fix`: `nuclearlang/docs/07-reference/diagnostics.md` (the test `every_code_is_documented` requires it).
body: In the parser/diagnostics (`nuclear-syntax`, `nuclear-diag`), detect and give a `fix`:
| Pattern | Suggested message |
| `{` at the end of a header | `blocks use indentation, not braces` + fix: delete `{` / `}` |
| `Type name(params)` | `the return type goes after the parameters: name(params) Type` |
| `await expr` | `use ~expr (async is automatic)` |
| `var/final/let/const x = ` in a body | `assign directly: x = ...` |
| `class X extends Y` | `use a kind or 'X: Y'` + the most likely kinds, not all 35 |
| `new X(...)` | `NuclearLang does not use 'new'` |
- Probably N0013/N0201 are reused adding `fix`/`help`, or new codes are created and documented in
`nuclearlang/docs/07-reference/diagnostics.md` (the test `every_code_is_documented` requires it).
- **Done when:** each pattern has a test, `cargo test` and `cargo clippy` are green, and the F1 tasks show fewer
correction turns.

rows.title: Plan: agents master Nuclear and Synapsis without spending tokens — F6. Validation against type definitions (the strongest defense against…
rows.summary: Care: nothing is reported: zero false positives before full coverage.
body: Care:
- Only when the type resolves with certainty. If the module stays `open` (unknown base or a whole-module `use`),
nothing is reported: zero false positives before full coverage.
- It goes in N01xx (resolver), documented in `nuclearlang/docs/07-reference/diagnostics.md`.
- If `ast.rs` changes, the language server (`nuclearlang/crates/nuclear-lsp`) follows the variants that changed.
- **Done when:** `Textt("a")` and `styl = ...` fail in `nuclear check`; the 37 files of `rick_and_morty`, the
examples and the golden files still have no errors; `cargo test` is green.

rows.title: Plan: agents master Nuclear and Synapsis without spending tokens — F6. Validation against type definitions (the strongest defense against…
rows.summary: The transpiler already loads the defs (`Dialect.defs`, `index.json`) for auto-imports and overrides.
body: The transpiler already loads the defs (`Dialect.defs`, `index.json`) for auto-imports and overrides. They are
also used to validate:
- `PascalCase(...)` that is not in the file, the project nor the defs → an error with "did you mean `Text`?"
(edit distance over the known names).
- A named argument the constructor or method does not have → an error with the valid parameters.
- (Optional, later) A nonexistent member on a known type: `Icons.casinoo`.
Available base (`ADR-mobile-0001` to `ADR-mobile-0001`): project defs are added with
`Loader::add_defs(&mut Dialect, &project::defs_lock(root))` (reads `build/defs.lock`, refs `name@version`),
`nuclear_dialect::defs_cache_dir()` and `Package::from_project`. The validation must look up the dialect
**after** `add_defs`; otherwise the project's third-party packages (`nuclear flutter add`) would give false
positives. The LSP already calls `add_defs` before `project::build`.

rows.title: Plan: agents master Nuclear and Synapsis without spending tokens — F7. Final measurement and tuning
rows.summary: Repeat F1 with everything on.
body: Repeat F1 with everything on. Tune the brief according to where agents still fail: each repeated error is a
missing line in the brief or a missing `fix` in a diagnostic.

rows.title: Plan: agents master Nuclear and Synapsis without spending tokens — 4. Out of scope (for now)
rows.summary: schemas.
body: - **Fine-tuning or training:** not possible with Claude; context + compiler give the same practical result.
- **MCP server:** the CLI already answers everything through Bash, and an MCP adds fixed tokens with its tool
schemas. It is reconsidered only if an agent without a shell needs it.
- **`llms.txt`, a public site and example repositories:** the way for future models to learn Nuclear by
themselves. Worth it when the language is published, but it takes months and does not help today.
- **Rewriting the specs:** they stay the source of truth; the brief is a short view on top.

rows.title: ADR-0001: The CLI and the MCP generate the standard code; an agent writes only what is not standard — Consequences
rows.summary: well.
body: - Positive: a standard feature costs no model tokens; the local 3B model only fills what is specific, where it does
well. The backend has an HTTP client in both runtimes (`synapsis-py` over httpx, `synapsis-nest` over fetch).
- Negative: each platform keeps generator templates next to its kinds, and a new kind or decorator must update
them (a test builds a generated resource with every dialect of every platform).
- Limits known when it was delivered: the backend platform has no `@mock`, so a REST resource of the backend gets
no generated tests (a test there would call the real API), and the local tester's own test of such a resource is
often wrong; the nestjs HTTP repository answers the API's JSON as it came (a use case that reads a renamed field
gets `undefined`). Both are in the [roadmap](../01-product/roadmap.md).

rows.title: ADR-0001: The CLI and the MCP generate the standard code; an agent writes only what is not standard — Context and problem
rows.summary: A feature such as "list the characters of an API, paged" is mostly code that follows from its data: a component, the models of the answer, a repository over the API, one use case per action, the aliases of the component's facade, a controller or a screen with its state manager, the tests.
body: A feature such as "list the characters of an API, paged" is mostly code that follows from its data: a component,
the models of the answer, a repository over the API, one use case per action, the aliases of the component's facade,
a controller or a screen with its state manager, the tests. Frameworks generate that code (Phoenix
`mix phx.gen.json`, Laravel `artisan make:model -mcr`, Symfony `make:crud`), and NuclearLang exists so that the
deterministic work is done by a tool. Yet `nuclear make` wrote one nearly empty file per kind (no fields, nothing
wired, no REST in the backend) and the Builder asked a 3B model to write every file: it failed on what is plain
procedure.
The user's rule: the CLI and the MCP do most of the code; the agent writes only use cases with their own logic and
the interface; a frontier model (whatever the user has) understands the global context and the spec; the agent must
know where the fields come from (the spec, the API's answer, the API's documentation) and look them up, or ask.

rows.title: ADR-0001: The CLI and the MCP generate the standard code; an agent writes only what is not standard — Decision
rows.summary: 1. `nuclear gen` generates finished code that compiles, never placeholders.
body: 1. **`nuclear gen` generates finished code that compiles, never placeholders.**
- `gen component <component>`: the component's folder, its facade (`appcomponent`) and its config.
- `gen resource <component> <Name>`: the models (with their fields; nested objects become models), the
repository (`--source rest:<base url> --path <path>`: an HTTP repository; `--source db`: an entity and its
queries), one use case per action (`--actions list,get,search,create,update,delete`), their aliases in the
facade, the entry of the platform (backend: a controller with the routes; mobile and web: `--screen <screen>`,
a screen with its state manager and state model) and the tests of each action. A component that does not exist
is created first; a file that exists is never overwritten (the facade gets the missing aliases added).
- The fields come from `--fields "id:int name:string origin:Origin"`, from `--from-json <file or url>` (an
example answer of the API: a list under `results` is a paged answer, a nested object a model, `null` an
optional field) or from `--from-spec <spec.md>` (its example answer, else its `Key | Type | Description` table;
a table with objects it does not detail reads the API's answer from the spec's `GET <url>` line, which also

rows.title: ADR-0001: The CLI and the MCP generate the standard code; an agent writes only what is not standard — Decision
rows.summary: place and the form to write it: a use case with a hole in it would be a placeholder.
body: place and the form to write it: a use case with a hole in it would be a placeholder. What a screen shows of a
use case (a state manager's method and its state) is the interface, written by hand.
- `gen inspect`: what the project has (components, declarations by kind) as JSON, so an agent checks before it
generates. A screen that is not a resource's list is `nuclear make screen` (mobile, web); a resource's list
screen comes with `gen resource --screen`.
2. **The templates are the platform's** (`[[generators.<what>]]` of its `platform.toml`), never the CLI's code: the
Nuclear a generator writes is the same for every dialect of a platform. The CLI only reads the fields, picks the
templates and writes the files at the platform's `[layout]` paths. A merge (`merge = true`) adds whole members,
told by their head line, so a route keeps its decorator and its body.
3. **The backend has HTTP repositories** with the mobile platform's words: a repository whose methods carry `@get`,
`@post`, `@put`, `@patch`, `@delete` and no body calls the `Http(baseUrl)` connection (path parameters `:id`,
the others in the query or the body; an error status is the `Err` of a `Result`), in fastapi and nestjs.
4. **A generated route does not depend on the order it was written in.** A generator appends a route to a

rows.title: ADR-0001: The CLI and the MCP generate the standard code; an agent writes only what is not standard — Decision
rows.summary: controller, so both backend runtimes add a fixed segment before a parameter (`search` before `{id}`), whatever the order in the `.nuc`.
body: controller, so both backend runtimes add a fixed segment before a parameter (`search` before `{id}`), whatever
the order in the `.nuc`.
5. **The MCP exposes the generators and what a model needs to fill them**: `project_inspect`, `generate_component`,
`generate_resource`, `generate_usecase`, `generate_screen`, `api_inspect` (fetches a url and answers its JSON's
shape and the files it implies), `web_search` and `web_read` (the API's documentation). Its instructions tell
the client to generate first and give `developer_task` only what is left.
6. **The Builder generates before it writes**: a *Generate* stage between the spec and the plan runs
`nuclear gen resource` for each resource the spec names (a `## Resources` section, else each `GET <url>` line
of the description). The planner is told what was generated and plans only the rest (a piece that repeats a
generated file is dropped), the agents write only that, and the tests check the whole. The generated files go to
the run's write ledger, so a crash undoes them like an agent's.

rows.title: ADR-0001: The CLI and the MCP generate the standard code; an agent writes only what is not standard — Decision
rows.summary: gives the API).
body: gives the API). A JSON key that is not the field's camelCase name gets `@key("air_date")`; the backend platform
has `@key` for it (pydantic aliases, class-transformer `@Expose`), as mobile and web had.
- Before writing anything it refuses a field type nobody declared, a name another file declares (N0303) and a
source the platform has no pieces for (mobile and web read APIs; a database resource is backend only). The
`Http` connection is added from the platform's `[gen] http` (or `http_named`, a named one, when the app has
another), and the repository then names it.
- `gen usecase <component> <Name>` wires a use case into its component: its alias in the facade and, on the
backend, with `--route "POST orders/{id}/cancel"`, its route in the controller of the route's prefix (made when
missing; a `{name}` of the path must be a parameter of the use case). The signature is read from the project,
never typed again: a use case with rules of its own is written first (by hand or by the coder) and this wires
it, calling it with `~` only when its `exec` awaits. `--calls <Repository>.<method>` writes the use case too,
because one that only calls a repository method follows from that method (a method that answers no `Result`
goes inside an `Ok`: backend). A use case that is neither declared nor given `--calls` is refused with the

rows.title: ADR-0001: The CLI and the MCP generate the standard code; an agent writes only what is not standard — Options considered
rows.summary: 1. Skeletons with placeholders for the model to fill (what `nuclear make` did).
body: 1. Skeletons with placeholders for the model to fill (what `nuclear make` did). Measured: worse than writing from
scratch, 29 of 42 against 37: the model copies the holes.
2. Generators written in each dialect: the Nuclear would differ between the dialects of a platform.
3. Letting the model write the standard code with more examples: it costs tokens and fails on procedure a command
does exactly.
4. Generators of finished code whose templates are the platform's data. Chosen.

rows.title: ADR-0001: The MCP server is a Nuclear project of its own, `nuclear-mcp` — Consequences
rows.summary: set-up runs again.
body: - Positive: the server's code, tests and dependencies are in its project; the graph's package is lighter.
- Negative: two packages to install where there was one; the old registrations name `nuclear-graph mcp` until the
set-up runs again.

rows.title: ADR-0001: The MCP server is a Nuclear project of its own, `nuclear-mcp` — Context and problem
rows.summary: The MCP server was a module of the Smart Graph's package (`mcp_server.nuc`, started with `nuclear-graph mcp`), so the graph's package carried the `mcp` library and a machine of remote agents only installed the graph's package to get it (ADR-installer-0002).
body: The MCP server was a module of the Smart Graph's package (`mcp_server.nuc`, started with `nuclear-graph mcp`), so the
graph's package carried the `mcp` library and a machine of remote agents only installed the graph's package to get
it (ADR-installer-0002). The user ordered every project into its own folder with its code (`tools/mcp`).

rows.title: ADR-0001: The MCP server is a Nuclear project of its own, `nuclear-mcp` — Decision
rows.summary: 1. The server is the Nuclear project `tools/mcp` (`python` dialect), command `nuclear-mcp`: no argument serves MCP on stdio; `nuclear-mcp tools` prints its instructions and tools as JSON.
body: 1. The server is the Nuclear project `tools/mcp` (`python` dialect), command `nuclear-mcp`: no argument serves MCP on
stdio; `nuclear-mcp tools` prints its instructions and tools as JSON.
2. It reaches the graph through the graph's package as a dependency (its type definitions in `defs/`), never the
other way: the graph's knowledge base reads the server's tools by running `nuclear-mcp tools`.
3. The graph's package has no MCP server and no `mcp` extra. `nuclear-graph mcp` runs `nuclear-mcp`, so a client
registered before keeps working.
4. A machine of remote agents only installs `tools/mcp` (it pulls the graph's package without its `server` extra:
33 MB, as before); a machine with the local agents installs the graph's `server` extra and `tools/mcp`.
5. Every client is registered with `nuclear-mcp` and no argument (the editor's setting `nuclear.ai.mcpCommand`).

rows.title: ADR-0001: The MCP server is a Nuclear project of its own, `nuclear-mcp` — Options considered
rows.summary: 1. Keep it inside the graph's package: the MCP server's code and dependencies in a project that is not the server.
body: 1. Keep it inside the graph's package: the MCP server's code and dependencies in a project that is not the server.
2. A project of its own that the graph's package depends on: the graph would import its own client back (a cycle).
3. A project of its own that depends on the graph's package.

rows.title: ADR-website-0001: The site sells the idea: hooks first, then a page per tool and per platform — Consequences
rows.summary: user guide; the site cannot claim what the tools do not do, since it runs them.
body: - Positive: a visitor sees the value in one scroll and reaches any tool or platform in one click; every tool got a
user guide; the site cannot claim what the tools do not do, since it runs them.
- Negative: `site.toml` grows (the tools and the platforms are data); the pages of the tools and the platforms are
screens of the app, so they have no plain HTML copy in `/static/` yet ([roadmap](../01-product/roadmap.md)).

rows.title: ADR-website-0001: The site sells the idea: hooks first, then a page per tool and per platform — Context and problem
rows.summary: The site published the documentation well, but its home page only compared a sample in three languages.
body: The site published the documentation well, but its home page only compared a sample in three languages. Everything
else NuclearLang offers (the generators, the MCP server, the editors, the Smart Graph, the local agents, three
platforms from one codebase) was not shown, so a visitor could not see the value. NuclearLang is free: "selling"
means making the value proposition obvious and leading each interested visitor to where it is explained.

rows.title: ADR-website-0001: The site sells the idea: hooks first, then a page per tool and per platform — Decision
rows.summary: 1. The home page is a series of hooks, from the most general to the most concrete, each a small interactive block that links to its page: why Nuclear (six one-line hooks), the same code in TypeScript, Dart and Python, an agent's mistake fixed by `nuclear fix`, the commands that make an app…
body: 1. **The home page is a series of hooks**, from the most general to the most concrete, each a small interactive
block that links to its page: why Nuclear (six one-line hooks), the same code in TypeScript, Dart and Python, an
agent's mistake fixed by `nuclear fix`, the commands that make an app replayed in a terminal with the numbers
they give, the same file built for two dialects, the platforms, the tools, a library of the target, install.
2. **Each tool has a page** (`/tools/<key>`) with its pitch, three highlights, how it starts, and the index of its
documents (its user guides, `docs/08-guides/`, which every tool now has); `/tools` is the index of the tools by
job (build, edit, run, AI). The detail lives in the tool's own guides; the page only leads to them.
3. **Each platform has a page** (`/platforms/<key>`) that goes down level by level, as in the C4 model: the context
(the app, its users and what it talks to), the containers (the project, the compiler and dialect, the generated
app, the runtime), the components (the layers of a component), and the code (a real file of its example and what
each dialect writes from it). Its onboarding (`/start/<key>`) builds the example app step by step.
4. **Every claim is real.** A number is measured when the site is built (lines written by the tools, lines the

rows.title: ADR-website-0001: The site sells the idea: hooks first, then a page per tool and per platform — Decision
rows.summary: dialect writes) or comes from a measured report (the run time of generated code, 0.98× to 1.11× of an expert's); an output is the compiler's or a command's, never written by hand.
body: dialect writes) or comes from a measured report (the run time of generated code, 0.98× to 1.11× of an expert's);
an output is the compiler's or a command's, never written by hand. A claim that does not hold is not made (the
thesis that Nuclear is shorter than hand-written code for a small program does not hold, so it is not sold).
5. **The texts stay data**: every word of the hooks, the tools and the platforms is in `site.toml`; the pages of
documentation stay the projects' `.md`.

rows.title: ADR-website-0001: The site sells the idea: hooks first, then a page per tool and per platform — Options considered
rows.summary: 1. Hooks, then pages per tool and per platform, every claim measured (chosen).
body: 1. Hooks, then pages per tool and per platform, every claim measured (chosen).
2. A longer home page with everything on it: one page to scroll, but nothing to link to and no place for detail.
3. Marketing copy written freely: faster, and impossible to keep true.

rows.title: ADR-website-0001: The site sells the idea: hooks first, then a page per tool and per platform — References
rows.summary: References
rows.body: - [ADR-website-0002](0002-onboardings-are-run-when-the-site-is-built.md), [ADR-website-0003](0003-libraries-of-the-target-through-nuclear-add.md).

rows.title: ADR-website-0002: Each onboarding is run when the site is built, and gives the example of the tree — Consequences
rows.summary: diff; the onboardings are a test of `new`, `gen` and `check` on the three platforms.
body: - Positive: the onboarding can never lie; a change of a generator shows up as a failed site build or a golden
diff; the onboardings are a test of `new`, `gen` and `check` on the three platforms.
- Negative: the site build runs the compiler a dozen times (a few seconds); a deliberate change of a generator
means `UPDATE_EXAMPLES=1` and `UPDATE_GOLDEN=1`.

rows.title: ADR-website-0002: Each onboarding is run when the site is built, and gives the example of the tree — Context and problem
rows.summary: Each platform needed an onboarding and an example app.
body: Each platform needed an onboarding and an example app. A tutorial written by hand drifts from the tools: a command
changes its output or its options, and the page keeps showing the old one. And an example app written by hand
proves nothing about the tools ([ADR-platform-0004](../../../docs/03-adr/0004-products-are-made-with-the-tools.md)).

rows.title: ADR-website-0002: Each onboarding is run when the site is built, and gives the example of the tree — Decision
rows.summary: 1. Each example app is made only by commands: `nuclear new`, `nuclear gen resource`, `nuclear check`.
body: 1. **Each example app is made only by commands**: `nuclear new`, `nuclear gen resource`, `nuclear check`. The steps
are data in `site.toml` (`[[onboarding]]`); the apps are the platforms' `examples/onboarding/` (`todos_api`,
`todos_web`, `todos_app`), one story: an API of todos and two clients that list them.
2. **The site runs the steps again on every build** (`tools/content.mjs`), in a scratch folder, with the installed
`nuclear`. It shows each step's real output, builds the shown file with every dialect of the platform, and
measures the lines. **The build fails** when a step fails or when the `.nuc` files the steps make are not the
example of the tree; `UPDATE_EXAMPLES=1` writes the example from them when a tool changes on purpose.
3. **The examples are also goldens** of the compiler's conformance test (`nuclear-transpile/tests/projects.rs`) and
each platform has a user guide of the same steps (`docs/08-guides/onboarding-<platform>.md`).
4. The steps need no network and no target toolchain (no Flutter, Node.js or Python): a step that needs one (build,
install, run) is shown as a command to run, not replayed.

rows.title: ADR-website-0002: Each onboarding is run when the site is built, and gives the example of the tree — Options considered
rows.summary: 1. Replayed steps, the example checked against them (chosen).
body: 1. Replayed steps, the example checked against them (chosen).
2. Outputs recorded once in a file: no cost at build time, and silently stale.
3. Examples written by hand: against ADR-platform-0004.

rows.title: ADR-website-0002: Each onboarding is run when the site is built, and gives the example of the tree — References
rows.summary: References
rows.body: - [ADR-website-0001](0001-the-site-sells-the-idea.md); ADR-codegen-0001 (the generators).

rows.title: ADR-website-0003: A library of the target comes through `nuclear add`; the site stays 100% Nuclear — Consequences
rows.summary: (no DOM globals such as `window` or `document` in the react dialect's definitions; an arrow whose value is not `void` cannot be passed where a callback returns `void`, so the call goes through a method).
body: - Positive: the site is a working example of a target library used from Nuclear; the gaps it found are recorded
(no DOM globals such as `window` or `document` in the react dialect's definitions; an arrow whose value is not
`void` cannot be passed where a callback returns `void`, so the call goes through a method).
- Negative: the bundle grows by the library; the type definitions in `defs/` are regenerated when its version changes.

rows.title: ADR-website-0003: A library of the target comes through `nuclear add`; the site stays 100% Nuclear — Context and problem
rows.summary: The site should look and move better than a plain documentation page, and it is the place to prove that any library of a dialect can be used, tested and built from Nuclear.
body: The site should look and move better than a plain documentation page, and it is the place to prove that any
library of a dialect can be used, tested and built from Nuclear. The web platform has no animation words, and
writing TypeScript by hand would break both the site's promise (written in Nuclear) and
[ADR-platform-0004](../../../docs/03-adr/0004-products-are-made-with-the-tools.md).

rows.title: ADR-website-0003: A library of the target comes through `nuclear add`; the site stays 100% Nuclear — Decision
rows.summary: 1. Animations come from the npm package `motion`, added with `nuclear add motion`: it installs the package, writes it in `config.nuc` (`dependencies(motion = "^14.14.0")`) and generates its type definitions into `defs/`, so the Nuclear calls `animate`, `inView` and `stagger` checked like its own…
body: 1. **Animations come from the npm package `motion`, added with `nuclear add motion`**: it installs the package,
writes it in `config.nuc` (`dependencies(motion = "^14.14.0")`) and generates its type definitions into `defs/`,
so the Nuclear calls `animate`, `inView` and `stagger` checked like its own code.
2. **One view moves a page**: `Reveal` wraps the content once it is loaded; blocks of class `rise` come up one after
the other, blocks of class `reveal` fade in when they scroll into view. Where animations cannot run (the tests,
an old browser) it catches the error and leaves every block visible; a reader who asks for less motion gets none.
3. **Only the styles are not Nuclear**: `public/styles.css`, a static file the web platform serves as it is (the
platform has no styling words). Everything else of the app is `.nuc`.

rows.title: ADR-website-0003: A library of the target comes through `nuclear add`; the site stays 100% Nuclear — Options considered
rows.summary: 1. `motion` through `nuclear add`, one view that runs it (chosen).
body: 1. `motion` through `nuclear add`, one view that runs it (chosen).
2. CSS animations only: no library to prove, and no scroll-triggered motion without script.
3. React's motion components (`motion.div`): need the `motion/react` entry, which `nuclear add` does not describe
(it generates the package's main entry).

rows.title: ADR-website-0003: A library of the target comes through `nuclear add`; the site stays 100% Nuclear — References

rows.body: - [ADR-website-0001](0001-the-site-sells-the-idea.md); ADR-lang-0008 (packages of the target in a project).
